text:
Your weekly resource to learn what the environmental movement is saying about the news of the day and the political fight of our generation. This week, we’re covering a massive clean energy success story, Big Oil’s Q2 profits and the cost to consumers, and Todd Blanche’s confirmation process.

Be sure to follow LCV on Facebook, Instagram, BlueSky, and TikTok.

QUOTES OF THE WEEK:

“This is a serious mistake for the Senate to approve Todd Blanche as the next Attorney General.”

— Senator Dick Durbin (IL) on Senate Republicans moving Todd Blanche’s nomination forward.

“[Utility bills are] up 18% since Trump came into office. Remember, he promised to cut them in half.”

— LCV President Pete Maysmith on Trump’s attacks on the climate and rising energy bills.

“Every time we burn fossil fuels, it adds more chemicals to the atmosphere that trap more heat, creating a positive feedback loop that makes everything hotter and drier.”

— Salon National Affairs Editor Troy Farah on the wildfires in Spokane, Washington.

TOP NEWS IN ENERGY AFFORDABILITY

STATE NEWS

NEW MEXICO’S ENERGY TRANSITION ACT BOOSTS RENEWABLE ENERGY: New Mexico’s Energy Transition Act has successfully bolstered clean energy in the state, shifting the state’s electricity supply from climate-warming fossil fuels to a majority renewables in just five years.

NEW YORK ADOPTS RULES LOWERING CAP ON CLIMATE POLLUTION FROM FOSSIL FUEL POWER PLANTS: New York adopted updated regulations for the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) that lower the cap on climate emissions from the power sector. RGGI is a cooperative, market-based, cap-and-invest program between 11 states on the East Coast from Virginia to Maine. Under the new rules, the greenhouse gas emissions cap will decrease by around 10% annually through 2033, and by around 3% from 2034 through 2037, dropping to about 89% below its 2024 level by 2037. As a result of RGGI, New York has already reduced carbon dioxide emissions from its power sector by 50% below 2005 levels and generated more than $3 billion in program revenue that has been reinvested into cost-saving projects including energy efficiency, clean energy, and electrification efforts. New York ratepayers will save nearly $12 billion due to the program’s success.

NYLCV TAKE: New York LCV President Julie Tighe said, “As the federal government continues to retreat from climate action, programs like the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) are more essential than ever. For over two decades, RGGI has saved families billions of dollars in energy costs, substantially reduced pollution, and supported thousands of jobs while providing significant health benefits by cleaning up our air.

“By updating the regulations – including an 85% reduction in the emissions cap over time, as well as more robust reporting, monitoring, and enforcement mechanisms – New York is helping to ensure RGGI will continue to deliver even more benefits for participating states in the coming years. We applaud Governor Hochul, DEC, and NYSERDA for leading the way in this bipartisan, multi-state effort, and for their strong commitment to building an affordable, clean energy future for all.”

GOVERNOR SPANBERGER SEEKS TO INTERVENE IN DOMINION-NEXTERA MERGER: Virginia governor Abigail Spanberger announced that she will seek to intervene in the $67 billion merger between Dominion and NextEra Energy. A new survey found that three in four Virginians instinctively opposed merger because of fear that it will raise their electricity bills and are looking to their state leaders to protect them from high energy costs.

VALCV TAKE: Virginia LCV Executive Director Michael Town said, “Virginians are sending a crystal-clear message: they do not want a mega-utility monopoly that pads corporate profits by driving up our monthly power bills even further. Our state leaders must give regulators the time and power they need to thoroughly scrutinize this merger and protect everyday Virginians from footing the bill for creating the largest utility in the world.”

NATIONAL NEWS

OIL AND GAS COMPANIES REPORT OVER $46 BILLION IN EXCESS QUARTERLY PROFITS: Quarter two profit reports have shown that major oil and gas companies have made over $46 billion in excess profits so far this year while families and everyday people are struggling to pay their bills and fill up their tanks.

OUR TAKE: LCV Senior Federal Advocacy Campaigns Director Leah Donahey said, “Across the country, everyday people are being forced to make impossible decisions between putting food on the table and gas in the tank. Meanwhile, oil and gas CEOs are raking in their highest profits in years: over $40 billion and counting in just the last three months. This money is coming straight out of our pockets. Trump promised to cut energy bills in half in his first year office, but the average family has spent an additional $504 on gas just since April.

“Trump and congressional Republicans have the power to stop Big Oil from price gouging and return windfall profits to working families, as well as to bring down our costs by investing in cleaner, more affordable alternatives. Instead, they are canceling clean, affordable energy projects, rolling back fuel efficiency standards, making electric vehicles less accessible, and using billions of our taxpayer dollars to subsidize the very companies gouging us at the pump.

“We cannot let Big Oil continue to amass staggering profits at our expense. We urge Congress to pass the Big Oil Windfall Profits Tax to prioritize our families and communities over polluter profits.

DEMOCRATS REJECT REPUBLICAN FARM BILL: Senate Democrats rejected Senator Boozman’s (AR) latest partisan draft of the Senate Farm Bill, the Agricultural Act of 2026. The bill would have failed to address the harmful SNAP cuts from the Republicans’ harmful tax law while also cutting conservation programs that help farmers fight and adapt to climate change.

OUR TAKE: LCV Healthy Communities Program Director Madeleine Foote said, “Today, Senate Democrats stood up for struggling families, small farmers, rural communities, and the environment by opposing Republicans’ harmful Farm Bill. Not only would this bill have failed to address congressional Republicans’ manufactured SNAP crisis, but it also included devastating funding cuts to critical, already-oversubscribed conservation programs that help farmers engage in sustainable and regenerative practices. This bill would have made it more difficult for farmers to continue feeding our families, resulting in higher costs when people are already struggling to put food on the table. LCV applauds Senate Democrats for continuing to fight for a bipartisan Farm Bill that truly delivers for our farmers, communities, and the environment.”

Ahead of the vote, LCV released a statement opposing the bill.

TAKE 2: LCV Healthy Communities Program Director Madeleine Foote said, “Farmers and ranchers nationwide are struggling with crises on multiple fronts, including rapidly rising costs and extreme weather events fueled by climate change, but Senator Boozman’s latest Farm Bill draft fails to provide the lifelines producers need to keep putting food on our tables. Not only does this bill inadequately address the upcoming SNAP crisis that Congressional Republicans created with the Republican Tax Law, but it still includes devastating cuts to critical, already-oversubscribed conservation programs that help farmers engage in more sustainable and regenerative farming practices. Now more than ever, Congress should be increasing investments in the programs and agencies that help farmers thrive while fighting and adapting to the climate crisis. We urge the Senate to reject this proposal and to pass a truly bipartisan Farm Bill that will actually help farmers who are impacted by Trump’s affordability crisis and the climate and other environmental disasters he’s only making worse.”

ELECTRICITY BILLS SET AN ALL TIME RECORD: In July, the average electricity bill across the country hit a new all-time high of $217. Record high energy bills are the result of Trump and congressional Republicans’ policies bolstering expensive, dirty energy while trying to ban clean, affordable alternatives.

CLIMATE ATTACKS FROM THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AND CONGRESS

SENATE REPUBLICANS BLOCK ATTEMPT TO MAINTAIN PFAS REPORTING DEADLINES: Senate Republicans voted against S.J. Res. 187, which would have reverted to the reasonable timeline for chemical manufacturers to report PFAS data to EPA after the agency pushed back reporting deadlines for the third time.

OUR TAKE: LCV Healthy Communities Program Director Madeleine Foote said, “Congress should be working to keep toxic chemicals out of our drinking water, but instead, Senate Republicans are helping hide the truth that chemical companies are polluting our water with dangerous PFAS. PFAS are known as ‘forever chemicals’ because they don’t break down and have been linked to numerous issues including cancers, kidney and liver diseases, hormone disruption, neurological developmental problems, and more. With this vote, Senate Republicans sided with Trump’s corrupt administration to put chemical industry profits ahead of our communities’ health and safety. We appreciate Senator Whitehouse’s leadership to shine the spotlight on whether Senators are standing with our communities or with Big Polluters.”

ICYMI: NATIONAL NEWS

SENATE JUDICIARY COMMITTEE ADVANCES TODD BLANCHE’S NOMINATION FOR ATTORNEY GENERAL: Despite initial Republican holdouts over concerns about Blanche’s involvement in Trump’s $1.8 billion so-called anti-weaponization fund, Senate Judiciary Committee Republicans voted to advance his deeply flawed nomination for Attorney General.

OUR TAKE: LCV Senior Director of Judiciary and Democracy Doug Lindner said, “Todd Blanche continues to be Trump’s personal lawyer, not the American people’s lawyer. At Trump’s direction, Blanche has systematically defied laws, norms, and ethics to undermine our democracy and our environment, purge huge numbers of civil servants, weaponize and politicize law enforcement, harass Trump’s perceived enemies, and protect Trump’s illegal conduct. He has handed billions of taxpayer dollars to energy companies to cancel domestic clean energy projects and redirect funds to fossil fuel export projects at a time of rapidly rising energy prices for American families. And he has worked to hand more billions of taxpayer dollars to Trump and his fellow insurrectionists.

“Nothing in this latest deal with Senate Judiciary Republicans prevents the Trump-Blanche Justice Department from continuing to reach taxpayer-funded settlements with Trump cronies, which it has done as recently as last week. Instead, this deal green-lights the corrupt tax audit immunity Blanche gave Trump, his family, and his business, as well as the sabotage of equal justice under law by an attorney general who serves Trump instead of the American people. Make no mistake: the Republican Senators voting to confirm Todd Blanche are doing so because they support Trump and Blanche’s continued corruption of justice, not because they’ve done anything to stop it. The Senate must reject this nominee and demand an attorney general who works for the people, not just the president and his corporate billionaire friends.”

LCV ACTION FUND CONGRATULATIONS ENDORSED CANDIDATES ON WINNING PRIMARIES: The League of Conservation Voters Action Fund (LCVAF) congratulates Hillary Scholten (MI-03), Debbie Dingell (MI-06), Kristen McDonald Rivet (MI-08), Rashida Tlaib (MI-12) and Donavan McKinney (MI-13) on their wins in Michigan, Wesley Bell (MO-01) on his win in Missouri, Mark Warner (Senate), Shannon Taylor (VA-01), Elaine Luria (VA-02), Jennifer McClellan (VA-04), Tom Perriello (VA-05), Beth Macy (VA-06), Eugene Vindman (VA-07), Don Beyer (VA-08), Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10), James Walkinshaw (VA-11) on their wins in Virginia, and Suzan DelBene (WA-01), Rick Larsen (WA-02), Emily Randall (WA-06), Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), and Kim Schrier (WA-08) in Washington.

LCVAF TAKE: LCV Action Fund Senior Vice President of Government Affairs Sara Chieffo said, “LCV Action Fund congratulates these candidates who understand the impacts their communities are facing from climate change fueled extreme weather and will fight to lower the energy and other costs that are crushing people across the country. The future of our environment and our democracy are at stake while Republicans in Congress continue to prioritize Trump’s personal interests and helping his corporate billionaire friends. Voters have made it clear: they want candidates who will fight for our communities, and stand up to Big Polluters and other greedy special interests.”

FEDERAL APPEALS COURT BARS EPA FROM TAKING BACK $20 BILLION IN GRANTS: A federal appeals court upheld a lower court’s injunction barring EPA from freezing grants under the Inflation Reduction Act’s Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, one of the signature pieces of the Biden administration’s climate and clean energy law.

title: PUC rejects HECO's power-generation proposal 'without demonstration of need' | Honolulu ...
description:
“We appreciate the PUC considering our request and we think this is a prudent path forward,” said Jim Kelly, HECO’s vice president of government and community relations and corporate communications.
JERA Americas Vice President of Development Erik Montague told the Honolulu Star-Advertiser that the PUC’s decision on HECO does not impact its proposal.
In its request letter to the PUC, HECO criticized JERA’s application, alleging the company was attempting to circumvent the competitive bidding process.

text:
The Hawaii Public Utilities Commission declined Hawaiian Electric Co.’s request to expand fuel-­flexible power generation on Oahu by 500 megawatts from any developer, finding that it would not be in the public’s best interest to move forward without identifying whether Oahu needs it.

“Without a demonstration of need, such a request can have far-reaching consequences, not only for Oahu customers, but for the State of Hawaii,” PUC officials said in a Wednesday letter to HECO. “The Commission also notes that the resolution of such crucial issues must consider substantial stakeholder feedback, transparency and thoroughness within the determinative processes.”

HECO also would have to provide “a reasonable justification for the urgency” of procuring the additional capacity on an expedited schedule, the commission said.

The decision is the first indication of how the PUC may evaluate a plan by JERA Americas, a subsidiary of Japan’s largest energy company, JERA Co., to bring liquefied natural gas power generation to Oahu.

JERA filed a notice of intent Opens in a new tab with the PUC on July 17 to establish its own power generation utility, called “GenCo,” that would include a $2 billion, 500-megawatt LNG-fueled plant and offshore infrastructure it pitched to state officials in March. The filing was outside of a request for proposals, or RFP, process and instead through “a certificate of public convenience and necessity.” The company hopes the plan will be approved and online by 2030.

On the same day, HECO filed its own request which sought, in part, an expedited regulatory approval to expand fuel-­flexible firm generation on Oahu by up to 500 megawatts. The commission rejected that proposal Wednesday.

“We appreciate the PUC considering our request and we think this is a prudent path forward,” said Jim Kelly, HECO’s vice president of government and community relations and corporate communications.

JERA Americas Vice President of Development Erik Montague told the Honolulu Star-Advertiser that the PUC’s decision on HECO does not impact its proposal. JERA’s proposal, he said, aims to replace aging and inefficient infrastructure.

“Oahu is in need of an upgraded thermal infrastructure and needs to benefit from the efficiency of new modern generation,” he said. “We’re still committed to putting forward all the details of that in front of the PUC for them to evaluate and determine if it’s in the best interest of the people of Hawaii.”

In an emailed statement, the Hawaii State Energy Office (HSEO) said it agreed with the PUC’s finding, and added that it has identified “a clear need to address Oahu’s aging, inefficient, polluting and increasingly unreliable oil-fired generation fleet.”

HECO’s 650-megawatt Kahe plant and 402- megawatt Waiau plant are both operating beyond their original anticipated service lives, while the logistics of the repowering project remains uncertain, the office said.

Together, the office said, federal data showed both plants consumed about 6.64 million barrels of oil in 2025 while operating at efficiencies below the national average and new power plants, ranking among the most greenhouse-gas- intensive power plants in the country when measured by the amount of electricity produced.

“This isn’t just an environmental issue — it affects Hawaii families and businesses. Every barrel of fuel that is burned but not effectively converted into electricity adds to the cost of generating power,” the agency said. “Because fuel costs are recovered through electric rates, customers ultimately pay for this inefficiency and HECO profits.”

The agency said JERA’s prospective application for a 500-megawatt plant is different from HECO’s request to repower Waiau and establish a 500-megawatt plant through an RFP process and agreed that a procurement of this scale should be informed by “a transparent assessment of system capacity and reliability needs, costs and benefits, lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions, alternative resource portfolios, and community impacts.”

“HSEO has consistently maintained that Oahu needs a genuinely competitive, utility-level process that evaluates how generation can be made more efficient, affordable, reliable, and meaningfully less carbon- intensive,” the agency said.

In its request letter to the PUC, HECO criticized JERA’s application, alleging the company was attempting to circumvent the competitive bidding process. But both the state, which is a staunch supporter of JERA’s plan, and JERA say the plan actually introduces competition.

“All processes are imperfect, and I think we are fully supportive of competition,” Montague said. “We believe that by putting this in front of the PUC that we are driving another choice and another form of competition that is actually even more transparent than what would go through the existing process.”

At the same time, Montague questioned whether the competitive bidding process was actually competitive when it came to thermal generation.

The only big thermal generation project to get approved recently was the Waiau Repower project that “went in a process mandated by HECO, (then) went to HECO,” Montague said.

But the Waiau plan was just the first to be approved by the PUC. Two other thermal generation projects, Ameresco’s Puuloa Energy 99-megawatt plant and Kalaeloa Partner’s 208-megawatt plant, are still in negotiations with the commission, as noted in the PUC’s letter denying HECO’s request for the 500-megawatt addition.

HECO spokesperson Darren Pai said the competitive bidding process is mandated and overseen by the PUC, which appoints an independent observer to monitor the process and that PUC negotiations are independent from HECO.

“We are required to submit a competing bid for firm generation. Our procurements are all subject to extensive regulatory oversight and project selection is based on the merits of competing proposals, not ownership,” Pai said. “We can point to a number of renewable and firm generation projects on Oahu, Maui and Hawaii Island that Hawaiian Electric bid into the competitive process and weren’t selected, despite our supposed control of the process.”

Montague said filing JERA’s notice independently from the RFP process is a way to put another option on the table that could be evaluated against any other current or future project that may come out of an RFP process. He added that nothing is stopping another developer from taking a similar approach.

“Our big concern with following the process, as we stated, was that it hasn’t, I don’t think, been deemed to be fully transparently competitive in the past,” Montague said.

He said the RFP process can drag on for years, which is counter to the state’s goals, and that the long timeline can lead to higher attrition of developers who are not HECO in the latter phases of the RFP process. The RFP process that is currently approving and negotiating projects began in 2017.

Hawaii State Energy Chief Energy Officer Mark Glick told the Star-Advertiser that the implementation of renewable sources thus far has been too slow, and more needs to be done to accelerate the transition.

Pai told the Star-Advertiser that final regulatory approval takes time because it includes “robust stakeholder input and review.” He said the final RFP reflects this, and that the PUC often modifies RFPs to ensure competitors are not limited from bidding. There are also several projects slated to come online through 2033. He added that developers have withdrawn their proposals in the past, but their reasons were not related to the length of the procurement process.

HECO agrees that the process could move faster and be less complex. Streamlining it should be made a state priority, Pai said.

“By badmouthing the competitive bidding process overseen by state regulators, JERA and its partner, the State Energy Office, must think no one is paying attention to their alternative: a no-bid, sole-source, noncompetitive arrangement to build a huge, multibillion- dollar power plant for which the need hasn’t yet been determined.” Pai said.

text:
Washington D.C. — U.S. Senators Cynthia Lummis (R-WY), Eric Schmitt (R-MO), Pete Ricketts (R-NE), and Jon Husted (R-OH) today introduced four joint resolutions under the Congressional Review Act (CRA), each disapproving a separate Environmental Protection Agency waiver that has allowed the California Air Resources Board (CARB) to impose its regulatory agenda far beyond California’s borders.

Together, the four resolutions target CARB’s small off-road engine (SORE) mandate, the Advanced Clean Cars I program, the 2013 Advanced Clean Car Program waiver, and the 2009 waiver that first allowed California to regulate vehicle greenhouse gas emissions.

“California’s climate zealots have run roughshod over the rest of the country for too long,” said Senator Lummis. “Under Governor Newsom, Sacramento has decided it can dictate what Wyoming families drive and what equipment our small businesses use. That ends today. I’m proud to lead this fight to reclaim Congress’s authority and stop California from legislating for the entire nation.”

“California’s burdensome emissions requirements continue to punish American manufacturers, reduce consumer choice, and raise prices for American families,” said Senator Schmitt. “One state should not have the power to set national policy and dictate what products Americans use far beyond its borders. Overturning these climate alarmist rules will not only restore common sense, but also prevent a future administration from attempting to grant similar waivers. I’m proud to lead the Congressional Review Act resolution to repeal the EPA-California State Motor Vehicle Control Standards Waiver and join Senators Ricketts, Husted, and Lummis in our effort to help make life more affordable for American families.”

“Biden’s overregulation and red tape regime cost Nebraskans millions of dollars,” said Senator Ricketts. “They used California policies as a backdoor EV mandate and even tried to control how we cut our grass. I am proud to lead the effort to overturn these restrictions and restore commonsense. I will continue to fight for policies that empower our families, farmers, and ranchers.”

“Ohioans shouldn’t be forced to follow California’s lead when it comes to policies that make everyday life more expensive and less convenient,” said Senator Husted. “These resolutions are part of our work to make life more affordable for working families, restore common sense, cut unnecessary red tape and put consumers back in control. I’m proud to support this effort to lower costs and protect consumer choice.”

Endorsements

“For over a decade, California has tried to abuse the Clean Air Act waiver process to set national policy that Congress never approved, unilaterally deciding what cars Americans can buy and what equipment they can own in their own garages. These four CRAs, led by Senators Ricketts, Husted, Schmitt, and Lummis, undo that end-run and restore a single national standard set by Congress instead of CARB regulators. We urge the full Senate to pass all four and give American consumers back the final say over the vehicles and equipment they choose. Affordability should be top-of-mind for Congress into the fall.” – Brent Gardner, Chief Government Affairs Officer, Americans for Prosperity

“Affordability is the number one issue for Latinos and Americans, and it should be top-of-mind issue for Congress. For years, California has leveraged the Clean Air Act waiver process to set burdensome regulations on everything from vehicles, gas-powered equipment, and other products. The four Congressional Review Act resolutions led by Senators Ricketts, Husted, Schmitt, and Lummis restore Congressional oversight of this process. And we urge the Senate to pass all four to give American consumers the flexibility they deserve when purchasing goods.” – Sandra Benitez, Executive Director, The LIBRE Initiative

Background:

The Clean Air Act gave California a narrow carve-out to seek EPA waivers for emissions rules stricter than federal law — a modest exception meant to address the state’s unique smog problem in the 1970s. California has since hijacked that carve-out, weaponizing its market share to force manufacturers nationwide to build to Sacramento’s rules rather than maintain separate production lines. An unelected state board now dictates national policy that Congress never approved, and most Americans never voted for.

Under Governor Newsom, CARB has abandoned any pretense of addressing local air quality and turned the waiver process into a backdoor for imposing a radical climate agenda on the entire country — banning the gas-powered cars, trucks, and equipment that American families and small businesses rely on every day, without a single vote in Congress.

These four resolutions build on the precedent Congress set last year, when lawmakers used the CRA to strike down three other California power grabs — Advanced Clean Cars II, Advanced Clean Trucks, and the Omnibus NOx Rule. It’s time to finish the job and end California’s hijacking of national policy for good.

Small Off-Road Engine (SORE) CRA: California has increasingly used its Clean Air Act waiver authority to adopt regulations with effects extending beyond the state’s borders. This CRA would overturn EPA’s waiver for California’s Small Off-Road Engine (SORE) rule, reversing the state’s phaseout of gas-powered small engines. As a result, products such as chainsaws, lawn mowers, and power washers would no longer be required to transition to zero-emission technology.

California State Motor Vehicle Control Standards CRA: In 2009, the Obama EPA granted California a Clean Air Act waiver allowing the state to regulate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from vehicles as pollutants California may regulate, creating a pathway for California’s standards to influence national vehicle regulations without new legislation from Congress. That waiver underpinned several subsequent federal vehicle emissions regulations, including those addressed in other CRAs. This resolution would disapprove the 2009 waiver and prohibit EPA from issuing substantially similar waivers in the future.

Click here for text.

Advanced Clean Cars I (ACC I) CRA: This EPA rule allows California to impose vehicle emissions requirements stricter than federal standards for passenger vehicles through model year 2025. This has resulted in a push towards electric vehicles across the nation.

Click here for text.

ACC I Reconsideration CRA: In 2022, the Biden EPA reinstated California’s Clean Air Act waiver for its Advanced Clean Cars (ACC I) program after the Trump administration had revoked it, restoring the state’s authority to enforce its greenhouse gas emissions and zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) sales requirements for model years 2017–2025. This resolution would disapprove the 2022 EPA rule reinstating the ACC I waiver.

title: NH Vehicle Inspection Repeal Gets Green Light From EPA
description:
Kelly Ayotte signed legislation in June 2025 repealing New Hampshire’s annual safety and emissions inspections for most passenger vehicles.
New Hampshire petitioned EPA in December to leave the ozone region and revise its air quality plan.
The out-of-state corporation referenced by Osborne is Gordon-Darby, the Kentucky-based contractor that operated New Hampshire’s emissions testing system.
In the meantime, regular passenger vehicles do not need inspection stickers, and stations cannot conduct official state inspections.
Police can cite drivers for defective brakes, tires, lights and other equipment, while commercial vehicles remain subject to applicable federal inspection requirements.
text:
“Live Free and Drive.”

That’s the response from New Hampshire GOP leaders to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s move Thursday to clear the last major federal roadblock to the state’s repeal of mandatory vehicle inspections.

The EPA proposed removing New Hampshire from the federal Ozone Transport Region (OTR) and conditionally approved the state’s request to eliminate its vehicle emissions inspection program from its federally enforceable air quality plan.

If both proposals are finalized, New Hampshire will be free to end the emissions testing requirement without violating the federal Clean Air Act.

“EPA is committed to working collaboratively with states to reduce unnecessary regulatory burdens while maintaining strong environmental protections and following our statutory obligations,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin. “This is the best way to provide clean air for all Americans.”

The proposals are not yet final. EPA will hold separate 45-day public comment periods on the two actions, along with a public hearing on removing the Granite State from the OTR.

Gov. Kelly Ayotte signed legislation in June 2025 repealing New Hampshire’s annual safety and emissions inspections for most passenger vehicles. Her Democratic opponent, former Executive Councilor Cinde Warmington, also supports ending the inspection mandates.

The program was suspended in February, but the emissions component remained part of New Hampshire’s federally approved State Implementation Plan, or SIP.

That created a conflict between the state repeal and federal clean air regulations.

New Hampshire has been part of the OTR, a collection of northeastern states required to maintain certain ozone-reduction measures even when they meet federal air quality standards. Because vehicle emissions testing is one of the measures included in New Hampshire’s plan, the state needed EPA approval to remove it.

New Hampshire petitioned EPA in December to leave the ozone region and revise its air quality plan. Zeldin pledged during a March visit to the state to accelerate the review.

“The Trump EPA understands states are best positioned to understand the needs of their local communities and therefore should be given the flexibility to implement air quality programs within the scope of the Clean Air Act,” the agency said Thursday.

The issue, opponents of inspection mandates say, is not air quality. New Hampshire has some of the cleanest air in the country. A recent analysis using EPA fine-particle pollution data ranked the Granite State third nationally, behind Wyoming and Hawaii.

House Majority Leader Jason Osborne (R-Auburn), one of the leading advocates for repealing the inspection mandate, celebrated EPA’s announcement.

“Today’s decision by the EPA is a victory for Granite Staters,” Osborne said. “No matter how much out-of-state corporations and unaccountable federal judges tried, House Republicans fought to ensure that mandatory vehicle inspections stay six feet under the asphalt.”

“It’s a rare day when I can say it, but the feds actually got it right,” Osborne joked.

The out-of-state corporation referenced by Osborne is Gordon-Darby, the Kentucky-based contractor that operated New Hampshire’s emissions testing system. The company sued to stop the repeal, arguing the state could not end testing while it remained part of the federally approved air quality plan.

U.S. District Court Judge Landya McCafferty initially issued an injunction requiring New Hampshire to continue the program. However, the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals later halted that order, concluding Gordon-Darby’s Clean Air Act lawsuit was premature. The company subsequently dismissed the case while leaving open the possibility of future litigation.

EPA’s proposed actions would largely eliminate the federal conflict underlying that lawsuit if they become final.

“EPA is grateful for New Hampshire’s partnership as we work together to protect human health and the environment,” said EPA Regional Administrator Mark Sanborn.

State Rep. Henry Giasson III (R-Goffstown), a member of the House Transportation Committee, said the lengthy federal rulemaking process had made it practically impossible for lawmakers to change the inspection law without facing litigation.

“With the EPA’s rulemaking taking 18 months to two years and the New Hampshire legislature serving in biennial terms, there was no practicable way to address the law while maintaining compliance,” Giasson said.

Executive Councilor John Stephen (R-Manchester), one of the leaders in the fight to end the inspection mandate, praised the EPA’s announcement.

“I thank Administrator Zeldin and Regional Administrator Sanborn for respecting the will of New Hampshire’s elected officials and for moving on this in months rather than years. That is what it looks like when the federal government works with a state instead of against it. I am also grateful to Gov. Ayotte, Department of Environmental Services Commissioner Bob Scott, and Attorney General Formella for making New Hampshire’s case every step of the way.”

EPA’s approval of the emissions program repeal would be conditional. New Hampshire would have one year to submit another air quality plan revision listing vehicle inspections as a possible contingency measure if ozone pollution in southern New Hampshire rises substantially in the future.

That condition would not reinstate annual inspections. It would preserve them as one option federal and state officials could consider if New Hampshire were to fall out of compliance with air quality standards.

In the meantime, regular passenger vehicles do not need inspection stickers, and stations cannot conduct official state inspections. Motorists are still required to keep their vehicles safe. Police can cite drivers for defective brakes, tires, lights and other equipment, while commercial vehicles remain subject to applicable federal inspection requirements.

“I am confident that this decision will be finalized and reach the finish line expeditiously,” Osborne said. “In the meantime, I encourage all Granite Staters to join me to ‘Live Free and Drive!’”

title: Thinking about trading your car in for an EV? Here's a compelling new reason to do it now
description:
Research shows the carbon emissions benefits are far greater than you might imagine.
Traditional cars have “internal combustion engines” that burn gasoline in order to produce the energy that turns the wheels.
Prior studies have shown ​​that manufacturing and driving battery electric vehicles produces substantially less carbon emissions than internal combustion engine vehicles.
Together they worked to compare several different timelines for replacing an internal combustion engine vehicle with an EV.
As renewable energy grows to provide a larger share of U.S. electricity generation, the carbon emissions benefits of driving an EV will grow accordingly.
text:
Research shows the carbon emissions benefits are far greater than you might imagine.

Press Contact

In recent months, American drivers have felt the pain of increased prices at the gas pump. There’s some evidence that may be fueling interest in greener ways of getting around. Battery electric cars, more commonly called electric vehicles or EVs, can be cheaper to own and operate than gas-powered internal combustion engine cars, and they offer considerable sustainability benefits. But just how much better for the planet are electric vehicles, really?

As it turns out, from a carbon emissions standpoint, you’d be better off sending a brand new internal combustion engine car directly to the scrap heap in order to replace it with a battery electric car. That’s the surprising new finding from research led by the University of California, Santa Cruz, that explored the carbon footprint trade-offs of vehicle trade-ins.

Now, of course, the research team doesn’t actually recommend scrapping a car you just bought, especially amidst a nationwide cost-of-living crisis. But for drivers who are already in the process of making a decision about future transportation, the new study, published in the journal Science, makes the sustainability case for EV ownership crystal clear.

“In some ways, I think this is really a definitive study about the carbon emissions benefits of EVs, because it shows that even in such an extreme scenario, the EV is still the obvious winner,” explained UC Santa Cruz Environmental Studies Professor Elliott Campbell, lead author of the paper. “So if you’re someone who’s trying to decide whether or not to put money into keeping your gas car going, switching to an EV as soon as a financially viable opportunity comes up is absolutely the right thing to do for the environment.”

High environmental stakes

This research comes at a time when transportation has recently become the largest source of carbon emissions in the U.S. Personal vehicles, in particular, are responsible for a larger share than all other forms of transportation combined.

Traditional cars have “internal combustion engines” that burn gasoline in order to produce the energy that turns the wheels. But when gasoline and other fossil fuels are burned, they produce large amounts of carbon emissions — exhaust gasses that build up in our atmosphere, trapping heat around our planet and causing climate change.

Given the scale of carbon emissions from personal internal combustion engine vehicles, one of the most effective solutions to addressing climate change is helping drivers switch to battery electric cars. Battery electric cars run on stored electricity and are recharged from the local power grid, like a cellphone or a laptop. The mix of energy sources used to produce that electricity varies by location and usually involves some amount of fossil fuels. But it can also include a significant amount of renewable energy and cleaner-burning fossil fuels, like natural gas.

Prior studies have shown ​​that manufacturing and driving battery electric vehicles produces substantially less carbon emissions than internal combustion engine vehicles. So for climate-conscious consumers, the case for choosing an electric vehicle over a gas-powered vehicle for a new purchase has long been clear. What’s trickier has been figuring out the best timing for retiring existing gas vehicles, in order to maximize the climate benefits.

A question of timing

Campbell first developed the idea for the current study while he was working on a different project, interviewing people about their perceptions of electric vehicles.

“This question of when to retire your current vehicle kept coming up,” he recalled. “Some people said they thought it would be most sustainable to keep driving their current car until the wheels fall off, and others were really unsure what timing was best. But it seemed to be a question on many people’s minds.”

And, surprisingly, there wasn’t existing research-based guidance.

“Personally, I’m someone who repairs and reuses just about everything,” Campbell said. “Keeping gear going makes sense in so many contexts, but not in every context. Sometimes it’s better to just make a shift to a newer, more efficient option, and it wasn’t clear yet which was the case with transitioning to an EV.”

Replacing a functional gas-powered vehicle with an EV might seem “wasteful” from a carbon emissions standpoint, because the process of manufacturing a new EV is energy intensive, resulting in carbon emissions that could have been avoided by simply keeping the current vehicle in service longer. But on the other hand, getting internal combustion engine vehicles off the road sooner, rather than later, means more mileage will ultimately be driven with fewer emissions.

So at what point do the emission reduction benefits of driving electric outweigh the drawback of manufacturing a new vehicle? That’s what researchers set out to discover.

Comparing carbon emissions

Campbell and his coauthor, UC Santa Barbara Professor Roland Geyer, both specialize in finding answers to exactly these types of tricky sustainability questions. Campbell is an environmental engineer with a background in large-scale computer modeling of ecological impacts, while Geyer is an industrial ecologist with deep experience in systems of product manufacturing and consumption.

Together they worked to compare several different timelines for replacing an internal combustion engine vehicle with an EV. They calculated the percent difference in emissions that would result if a gas-powered vehicle was driven for its full useful life (about 16 years), or scrapped and replaced at earlier years.

To do this, they looked at how carbon emissions for more than 400 internal combustion engine and battery electric vehicle models were affected by different vehicle efficiencies, grid electricity sources, vehicle mileages, and battery electric vehicle manufacturing emissions and battery sizes.

Their results showed that the climate benefits were generally greatest when gas-powered vehicles were retired at year one, resulting in a 58% reduction in carbon emissions over a 16-year period. It typically took about three years for the lower emissions of driving a battery electric vehicle to offset the emissions required to produce it. Then the climate benefits added up quickly from there.

“What it comes down to is just that gas vehicles require so much more energy to operate,” Campbell explained. “Only 20% of the energy in the gasoline that most of our cars burn actually goes toward moving the vehicle — the rest is just lost as heat. So it really puts internal combustion engines in a totally different class than EVs when it comes to efficiency, and that leads to a situation where you want to retire the gas-powered vehicle as soon as you can.”

Diving into the details

The exact benefits of retiring any particular internal combustion engine vehicle vary based on location and the specific type of vehicle. But 92% of the scenarios that researchers modeled for replacing gas-powered or hybrid electric vehicles with battery electric vehicles before the end of the vehicle’s useful lifespan achieved at least some overall reduction in carbon emissions.

Plug-in hybrid electric vehicles are a notable exception. While standard hybrid electric vehicles use an electric motor to capture and reuse energy from the gas-powered engine each time the vehicle slows down, plug-in hybrid electric vehicles have small batteries that can be charged from the electric grid, providing some all-electric driving range. As a result, they’re efficient enough that replacing them early with battery electric models could actually result in increased emissions in some cases. Similarly, extremely low-mileage internal combustion engine vehicles — driven annually less than 7,054km for cars, 6,837km for SUVs, or 10,794km for trucks — are not worth replacing, from a carbon emissions standpoint.

The energy mix that powers your local electricity grid also affects whether retiring a gas-powered vehicle early makes sense. In areas with power grids that are exceptionally reliant on coal or other high-polluting fossil fuels, there’s less of an emissions reduction benefit to driving electric. That makes it harder to offset the emissions cost of producing a new battery electric vehicle.

For example, if you own a traditional hybrid electric vehicle with class-leading efficiency, you’d want to think twice about replacing it early if your local electricity grid is in the bottom 33% for efficiency among total U.S. energy generation. To find out if that’s the case, check whether your local grid has a CO2 emissions rate exceeding 970 lbs/MWh.

For the majority of the U.S., though, there are consistent benefits to early retirement of even the most fuel-efficient gas-powered cars. And for the most common internal combustion engine vehicle models sold in the U.S., replacing your car early offers carbon emissions reduction even on the dirtiest power grids.

Implications for policymakers

Overall, the study’s results show that helping drivers transition from internal combustion engine vehicles to battery electric vehicles as quickly as possible is crucial for fighting climate change.

Many states, including California, have vehicle “scrap-and-replace” programs that offer financial incentives to make trading out vehicles more cost-effective. Increasing the amount of funding available through such programs could help put EV ownership within financial reach for more people. That’s especially true when those subsidies can be stacked alongside rebates for purchasing EVs.

The paper’s findings also demonstrate the potential benefits of expanding eligibility for scrap-and-replace programs to a wider range of internal combustion engine cars, beyond just the highest-emitting vehicles. The case for a broader approach could become even stronger in the coming years. As renewable energy grows to provide a larger share of U.S. electricity generation, the carbon emissions benefits of driving an EV will grow accordingly. And development of a strong EV battery recycling industry could significantly offset the initial carbon emissions associated with producing new EVs.

The sooner we can facilitate these transitions, the better protected our communities will be from the impacts of climate change, researchers say.

“The rate of climate change is accelerating, so the rate of climate action needs to accelerate too,” Campbell said. “If states want to put more money into programs that encourage people who are on the fence about EVs to make that leap toward a newer, cleaner, more cost efficient car to own and operate, our results show that certainly makes sense from an emissions reduction point of view.”

text:
The study also found that relatively small, inexpensive interventions can have significant effects

Canada’s clean energy transition is creating thousands of new jobs, but structural barriers are preventing many qualified workers from entering the sector, according to new research from the Trellis Foundation and the University of Victoria.

The study draws on the experiences of 119 applicants to the Trellis Foundation’s bursary program, which supports women pursuing careers in the clean energy transition. Rather than identifying a lack of interest in clean energy careers, the research concludes that financial hardship, credential recognition, workplace culture, and traditional hiring practices are limiting participation at a time when demand for skilled workers continues to grow.

Rebecca Black, executive director of the Trellis Foundation, said the research was designed to better understand why people who want to work in the clean energy sector are struggling to find pathways into those careers.

“We have all these students looking for jobs in the sector, and there seems to be a disconnect,” Black said. “We wanted to understand what those disconnects are between the companies and utilities that are hiring and the people who want to work in the sector.”

The findings suggest the issue is not a shortage of interest or talent. Instead, researchers identified systemic barriers affecting women and people with intersecting identities, including newcomers to Canada, Indigenous people, racialized Canadians, LGBTQ+ individuals, and young workers. Financial insecurity, difficulties obtaining recognition for international credentials, exclusionary workplace cultures, and traditional education and hiring pathways all contribute to the problem.

Black said employers also have opportunities to broaden recruitment by reconsidering conventional hiring practices. Lengthy lists of required qualifications, for example, may discourage otherwise capable applicants from applying, particularly women.

The report recommends expanding mentorship programs, recognizing transferable skills alongside formal credentials, supporting more flexible education pathways, and treating bursaries and mentorship as essential workforce infrastructure rather than optional initiatives.

The findings come as Canada’s energy sector prepares for significant growth in electricity demand driven by electrification, renewable energy development, grid expansion, battery storage, and building decarbonization. At the same time, a growing number of experienced workers are approaching retirement, increasing pressure on employers to recruit and retain skilled employees.

Black said the discussion should be viewed primarily as an economic and workforce issue rather than a political debate over diversity initiatives.

“When we have gaps, we need to look at who can fill them,” she said. “There are a lot of people who can fill them, just not necessarily through the transition that has traditionally happened into the sector.”

The study also found that relatively small interventions can have significant effects. A modest bursary can help students remain in school instead of taking on additional work, while mentorship and networking opportunities provide valuable connections between students and employers.

Black said the Trellis Foundation is already building mentorship programs and working with industry partners to test more inclusive approaches to workforce development.

She hopes the organization’s work will eventually become unnecessary.

“The best outcome of something like the Trellis Fund is that we see the systemic change that we need,” she said. “These pilot projects wouldn’t need to happen anymore because we’ve seen scaled-up versions of inclusive policies that allow these sectors to attract and retain the people they need.”

Canada’s clean energy transition will require more than new technologies and infrastructure, Black said. It will also require building a workforce capable of delivering them.

text:
By Nora Eckert

DETROIT, Aug 6 (Reuters) – Ford Motor said on Thursday that its upcoming midsize electric pickup truck would be priced starting at about $28,000 ​and named Fathom, as the Michigan automaker ‌looks to offer an affordable model in a market full of pricey EVs.

• Ford has approached development and manufacturing of this vehicle from the ground up, assembling a specialized team in California aimed ‌at ​competing with rivals like Tesla and ⁠China’s BYD.

• The automaker ⁠has established a new assembly-tree manufacturing process at its Louisville Assembly Plant.

• Three lines, for the front, rear and structural battery and seating, will run ​simultaneously and join at the end instead of having one traditional, long conveyor belt. The new system ⁠is meant to improve efficiency ⁠and reduce costs.

• Ford reset its EV ​strategy after a $19.5 billion writedown late last year, in which ​it axed several planned models as well as ‌its larger, more expensive Lightning electric pickup truck.

• Fathom is part of a limited group of vehicles, gasoline-powered, hybrids and EVs included, that are available under $30,000. Data ⁠from car-shopping website Edmunds, updated through May 2026, shows 36 models are available for under a starting price of $30,000 in ⁠the U.S.

• Fathom ‌would become one of Ford’s least ⁠expensive models, rivaling its Maverick pickup, which ​starts ‌at just below $30,000, according to Edmunds.

• Pre-orders ​for Fathom ⁠will open in early 2027, with customer deliveries beginning in autumn 2027. The sub-$30,000 pickup truck is expected to be the first of a family of models based on Ford’s new EV platform.

(Reporting by Nora Eckert; Editing ​by Jamie Freed)

description:

But for power engineering students, they become interesting challenges to solve and the foundation for meaningful careers.

Now power engineering is back on top.
text:
Engineers are crucial to the electric grid, but it worked so well for so long that it became a victim of its own success– many engineering students started to see it as boring and looked elsewhere for careers they perceived as more exciting.

All that is starting to change, and Clemson University is using that momentum to recruit students and prepare the grid workforce of the future.

Factors that include rising energy demand from data centers, electrification of the manufacturing sector and extreme weather are putting unprecedented stress on the grid. At the same time, utilities are facing a wave of workforce retirements.

Clearly, those are problems for society. But for power engineering students, they become interesting challenges to solve and the foundation for meaningful careers.

For the Clemson faculty members who teach those students, it is an opportunity to foster a passion for power engineering in the next-generation workforce.

Ramtin Hadidi, an associate professor of electrical and computer engineering, said he is seeing an uptick in interest in the grid among students.

“There was a period of time when this was not a popular topic,” Hadidi said. “Students said, ‘Oh, power, everybody knows how it works. There’s nothing to research about that.’ It was not an enticing topic. Computers and the internet were enticing. Now power engineering is back on top. Students like to know more about it and work in this field.”

The next generation of power engineers will need more than a traditional electrical engineering background.

Clemson faculty members said that while strong fundamentals in power systems will continue to be critical, students will also need to understand power electronics, computing, communications, controls, artificial intelligence and the practical realities of keeping electricity reliable.

That is why Clemson is combining classroom instruction with hands-on labs, industry-connected projects and facilities such as the Duke Energy eGRID, where students can see how real grid equipment behaves under real-world conditions.

It’s a combination that has attracted top students, including a Fulbright Scholar.

“You have to teach fundamentals at the right level but also make it interesting,” said Johan Enslin, a professor of electrical and computer engineering. “I don’t think you should just give them differential equations until it’s over their heads. I think it’s important to make it fun for them in class.”

Kevin Tomsovic, the Duke Energy Endowed Chair in Smart Grid Technology, said power engineering gives students a wide range of problems to solve, from helping data centers manage their electricity use to keeping the full grid working together.

title: Vineland, N.J. data center makes case for on-site power generation during 6-hour hearing
description:
Representatives for a hyperscale artificial intelligence data center in Vineland, New Jersey, on Wednesday defended a proposal to house liquefied natural gas and utilize fuel cell technology to power the 300-megawatt facility.
During a six-hour hearing before the city’s planning board, DataOne pleaded their case for the project’s second phase: a new proposal to use Bloom Energy fuel cells to power the site.
The fuel cells use a chemical reaction to convert natural gas into electricity.
While the new energy plan is projected to emit fewer pollutants than the natural gas engines, it would increase the amount of water required to cool the data center.
However, that water generation was only possible through the use of diesel or natural gas engines proposed in the original plan.
text:
This story is part of the WHYY News Climate Desk, bringing you news and solutions for our changing region.

From the Poconos to the Jersey Shore to the mouth of the Delaware Bay, what do you want to know about climate change? What would you like us to cover? Get in touch.

Representatives for a hyperscale artificial intelligence data center in Vineland, New Jersey, on Wednesday defended a proposal to house liquefied natural gas and utilize fuel cell technology to power the 300-megawatt facility.

The project, with the first phase already approved and under construction, is being developed by DataOne for the Nebius Group to support AI infrastructure as part of a $17 billion deal with Microsoft.

During a six-hour hearing before the city’s planning board, DataOne pleaded their case for the project’s second phase: a new proposal to use Bloom Energy fuel cells to power the site. If approved, it would be Bloom Energy’s largest single-site fuel cell project to date. Currently, the company’s largest fuel cell project is an 80-megawatt installation in South Korea.

DataOne’s attorney Michael Fralinger said the fuel cells, which do not utilize combustion, release fewer carbon emissions than traditional power generation. The fuel cells use a chemical reaction to convert natural gas into electricity. Fralinger also said on-site generation takes strain off the electrical grid and won’t impact ratepayers’ bills.

“This particular project has been deliberately designed and structured so that its energy requirements are not subsidized by existing electric or natural gas customers,” Fralinger said at the planning board hearing, which included six hours of witness testimony and cross examination. “All of the financial risk for this project is being borne by the project.”

The planning board, after ending the hearing at midnight, must reconvene to allow for additional comment and decide whether to approve the plan. Members of the public were not afforded the chance to speak during the lengthy and detail-oriented meeting, and many walked out as it neared the midnight hour.

“People in the room felt that he was going at a certain pace and focusing on extraneous details to basically run out the clock and to get it to a point where people were just like, ‘This is so boring, I don’t want to be here anymore,’” said Zac Landicini, who lives about 3 miles from the data center and has been advocating against its development.

The acceleration of power-hungry artificial intelligence has boosted demand for data centers. President Donald Trump’s administration last year announced plans to accelerate AI development with limited regulatory oversight.

DataOne said its facility will benefit Vineland by hiring more than 200 permanent, full-time workers, and by becoming one of the largest taxpayers in the city. The city’s mayor and City Council president have voiced support for the project, and have approved a tax exemption for the company as part of a five-year plan.

Residents have voiced concerns about the potential impact on air quality and water supplies, which in some areas of the country have been threatened. Some residents have also complained about whining metallic construction noises, leading to a class-action lawsuit that claims construction and operational noise will impact property values.

Much of the meeting was focused on DataOne’s plans to generate the majority of its energy on site, utilizing natural gas accessed through an already-existing gas pipeline that runs from the facility. The proposal would also make way for a 1.5-million gallon LNG storage tank on site in the event access to the natural gas pipeline is interrupted.

Eric Reaman, president and CEO of Cashman Preload Cryogenics, which is the manufacturer of the tank, said LNG cannot ignite inside the tank without coming in contact with a source of ignition. He also said there’s no oxygen inside the tank necessary to trigger a fire or explosion. Reaman said the tank is built with fire resistant concrete, and equipped with leak and heat detection monitors as well as an automatic shut-off system in case of emergency.

DataOne’s application previously proposed the use of 32 high-efficiency natural gas engines, of which five would be utilized for back-up generation, as well as six diesel generators for emergency power. During the hearing, Fralinger said DataOne scrapped the plan to use engines because of public outcry over potential air emissions.

The company is now seeking approval to use Bloom Energy fuel cells, which turn natural gas into electricity through an electrochemical reaction without releasing high amounts of air pollutants like nitrous oxides and sulfur dioxides. During the hearing, Marisa Blackshire, Bloom Energy’s vice president of environment and regulatory law, said the technology is quieter than a hair dryer and has such a low emission profile it’s exempted from New Jersey’s air permit requirements.

“The nature of the electricity generation being that it comes from a noncombustion reaction dictates that we have very low criteria pollutant emissions,” she said.

However, during cross-examination, Blackshire confirmed that the facility in Vineland would still emit about 2.19 billion pounds of climate-warming CO2 a year.

While the new energy plan is projected to emit fewer pollutants than the natural gas engines, it would increase the amount of water required to cool the data center.

Hyperscale data centers can consume up to 5 million gallons of drinking water per day to cool the facilities and their servers to prevent overheating. In some areas, that has drained residents’ well water supplies.

Previously, DataOne said the facility wouldn’t consume water from the region’s aquifer because it would use waste heat to generate its own water supply by utilizing thermal energy to extract moisture from the air. However, that water generation was only possible through the use of diesel or natural gas engines proposed in the original plan.

Instead, the new plan would use more than 400 fans to cool the data center, and during particularly hot days, a misting spray would be utilized to further cool the system. Though DataOne will use a closed-loop system that reuses water, the water from the misting spray would evaporate. An engineer testified that the project would require about 8 million gallons of water a year drawn from the city’s water supply. The proposed Bloom units would also require an undetermined amount of water on start-up, which would be reused.

name: Indiana Environment
title: The problem with going solar in Indiana
authors: Gabriel Bosslet, Matthew Will, Danielle McGrath, Sean Mobley
description:
The average Indiana home uses ~900 kilowatt-hours of energy per month.
Indiana high court sides with utilities on solar power, ending benefits for small owners To cover 100% of those energy needs, a family would need an 8-kilowatt solar system, which costs around $25,000 to install.
This greatly changes the financial math for solar energy in Indiana.
Rather than reducing the previous $152 monthly energy bill for a solar owner to $17, this net metering boondoggle means that the average solar owner in Indiana still pays $85 monthly.
Those savings become profits for Indiana electric utilities and their (mostly) out-of-state shareholders.
text:
Over the past year, I have been noodling over the possibility of installing solar panels on my roof. This simple curiosity eventually turned into action — I got several quotes for what solar installation might cost. It was at that point that I discovered a 2017 Indiana state law that makes installing solar financially difficult for individual homeowners but quite profitable for electric companies.

I like the idea of being more self-sufficient. I like the fact that, once installed, solar panels provide pretty much free energy for my home that is healthier for our planet. And solar technology has become much better and more affordable over time. As climate author Bill McKibben put it on a podcast: “Sometime earlier this decade, we passed some invisible line where it became cheaper to produce energy from the sun and the wind than from setting stuff on fire.”

While it has become less expensive, installing a solar harvesting system is not cheap in the short term; especially after federal lawmakers abruptly eliminated the 30% residential tax credit at the end of last year. I would have to pay a lot up front for the ability to harvest free photons that would otherwise just warm up the shingles on my roof. Under fair economic conditions, that upfront cost pays for itself over time through drastically lower monthly power bills, eventually earning back every dollar spent and saving money for years to come.

Let’s look at what this should look like for an average Hoosier household.

The average Indiana home uses ~900 kilowatt-hours of energy per month. At an average cost of $0.15 per kWh, that equates to an average electricity bill of $135 per month (plus a $17 monthly customer fee, totaling $152 monthly) .

Indiana high court sides with utilities on solar power, ending benefits for small owners

To cover 100% of those energy needs, a family would need an 8-kilowatt solar system, which costs around $25,000 to install.

With fair energy policy, this system would essentially eliminate a family’s electricity charges, leaving them with only the mandatory monthly fee to the electric company required to be connected to the grid. That would drop their $152 monthly energy bill to $17.

At this savings rate, the payoff horizon is 15.4 years. Assuming a 30-year solar panel lifespan, a solar household would save around $23,650 in energy bills over the last 14.6 years of the system. All while releasing zero carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.

While that is how it should happen, a 2017 state law ensures that is not how it works in Indiana. Here’s why.

On a sunny afternoon in July, a home solar array typically makes far more power than the house needs, sending the extra electricity back to the neighborhood power lines. At night, when the sun is shining in Australia instead of Indiana, the family has to pull electricity back off the grid to keep the lights on.

Think of the power grid like a bank account: with a solar system you make energy “deposits” during the day, and make energy “withdrawals” at night. The system that tracks these deposits and withdrawals is called “net metering”.

In most states, if you deposit 20 kWh of power during the afternoon (as is usual on a typical sunny day), you get a full 1-to-1 credit to withdraw those same 20 kWh later that night. While states like Florida, Ohio, and Iowa protect 1-to-1 net metering as a matter of property rights and energy freedom, Indiana’s Senate Enrolled Act 309 created an artificial government price control that penalizes Hoosier families for investing in their own homes.

Passed in 2017, the law allows electric companies to harvest those same 20 kWh of afternoon power from you and immediately sell them to your neighbors for $3.00 (the full $0.15/kWh retail price), while crediting you just $0.70 (the discounted $0.035/kWh wholesale rate). When you pull that same power back out of the grid that night, they charge you $3.00 once again. That leaves the homeowner getting back less than 25% of the energy value they deposited just hours earlier.

This greatly changes the financial math for solar energy in Indiana. Rather than reducing the previous $152 monthly energy bill for a solar owner to $17, this net metering boondoggle means that the average solar owner in Indiana still pays $85 monthly. That pushes the payoff horizon to over 31 years, which exceeds the lifespan of the panels entirely. Instead of saving tens of thousands of dollars, Hoosier families actually end up taking a $900 net loss on their investment.

The $23,650 of potential savings that SEA 309 takes from solar households does not disappear into thin air. Those savings become profits for Indiana electric utilities and their (mostly) out-of-state shareholders. Funded out of the pockets of Hoosiers. It’s time for the General Assembly to repeal SEA 309, restore fair 1-to-1 net metering, and give Hoosier families the right to benefit from their own private property investments.

title: RWE relinquishes North Coast offshore wind lease, part of $1.22 billion Trump admin deal
description:

This is yet another example of how off the rails the Trump Administration has gone.
text:
On Thursday, renewable energy company RWE announced that it entered into a $1.22 billion agreement with the Trump administration to relinquish its offshore wind leases. RWE is one of two companies, alongside Vineyard Offshore, that hold wind leases off California’s North Coast through its RWE U.S. Offshore subsidiary.

According to a press release published by RWE Thursday morning, the company’s settlement with the U.S. Department of Interior will “resolve claims against the U.S. government and relinquish its offshore wind leases off the coasts of New York, California and Louisiana.”

“RWE U.S. Offshore secured these leases from the U.S. government with a long-term commitment to develop offshore wind capacity in American waters and invested more than $1 billion toward the leases and the development of these projects,” RWE’s release reads. “These leases provided legal rights to develop offshore projects and represented years of planning, investment, and partnership with federal agencies.

“After careful consideration, it was determined there is no path forward to permit these projects in the U.S. for the foreseeable future. The settlement resolves RWE U.S. Offshore’s legal claims and provides $1.22 billion in settlement funds. The company determined that this resolution best serves the interests of its stakeholders and allows it to direct resources toward energy projects that can be advanced with certainty.”

The news did not come as a shock.

“Today’s news is disappointing but not surprising,” Environmental Protection Information Center Executive Director Tom Wheeler told the Times-Standard via an emailed statement Thursday morning. “The Trump Administration has used its full weight to hamper offshore wind development. Elsewhere, other offshore wind companies have already caved to the pressure. The winners today are the fossil fuel industry and the losers are Humboldt County and the planet. But tomorrow is a new day. The Trump Administration will end. And the promise of offshore wind remains: clean, reliable energy built locally by well-paying blue-collar jobs. The Trump Administration can delay, but it cannot suppress the future.”

RWE’s press release says that the agreement will allow the company to “redeploy its capital to accelerate value-accretive opportunities that deliver reliable and affordable energy.” That “redeployment” is described as including “$900 million to acquire an indirect 16% stake in the Louisiana LNG Project” — a large-scale natural gas development that has been criticized as a major source of greenhouse gas pollution — and other natural gas projects throughout the U.S.

“While RWE’s shareholders get their bag, the rest of us get the finger. We the people are paying for this buyout, and what we get in return is more expensive energy, backwards climate policy and greater harm to our communities,” Assemblymember Chris Rogers told the Times-Standard via email Thursday morning. “The Trump Administration is again using taxpayer dollars to settle personal vendettas and line the pockets of his friends and donors by protecting oil profiteers from the competition of clean, affordable and renewable energy.

‘Every American should be enraged.’

U.S. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-San Rafael), ranking Democratic member of the U.S. House of Representatives’ Committee on Natural Resources, released a statement Thursday morning just before noon, calling the DOI and RWE’s agreement a “fake settlement” and saying that “the deals are deeply corrupt and illegal” and “when the accountability comes, and I promise you accountability is coming, everyone involved in them will answer for it.”

“The most corrupt, lawless administration in American history is once again flouting the law and attempting to use over $1 billion in taxpayer dollars to kill off clean energy projects slated to create thousands of good jobs and lower electricity bills for Californians,” Huffman said. “Trump is strongarming companies into taking these illegal deals and abandoning offshore wind projects that would put huge amounts of cheap electricity on the grid and lower electricity prices. Instead, he is pressuring them to invest not only in dirty fossil fuel projects, but in LNG export facilities that push domestic energy prices even higher at a time when American families are reeling from skyrocketing costs caused by his reckless war of choice in Iran.

“One of the projects illegally canceled in this fake settlement is off the coast of Humboldt County in my district. The benefits of that project were tremendous — revitalizing the economy of a rural community, creating thousands of quality jobs and lowering utility bills for families all across California. Like a mob boss, Trump tightened the screws on RWE and, shamefully, the company capitulated and went along with this sham deal that robs the American people and makes a mockery of RWE’s stated commitments to clean energy. When these illegal, fake settlements are reversed by the courts and/or future congressional action — and they will be — RWE and others who participate in these charades will own every bit of the shame they deserve.”

Huffman said that the total cost to the taxpayers for paying companies to abandon offshore leases already ads up to “the tune of about $4 billion” noting that such settlements have thus far employed funding intended for the payout of federal lawsuits and settlements.

“Trump is using the Judgment Fund as a slush fund to pay for it. This is the same pot of taxpayer money Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche tried to use for his so-called ‘Anti-Weaponization Fund’ to pay off convicted J6 felons,” Huffman said. “Once again, we see this administration’s priorities laid bare: treating a fund that exists to resolve valid claims and liabilities as a massive personal slush fund Trump can use to reward criminals, kill off clean energy projects and do virtually anything else that serves his personal and political interests.”

Spokesperson Anthony Martinez from Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office provided the Times-Standard with the following statement: “The pattern is impossible to ignore. After getting beaten in court again and again, Trump has stopped trying to win on the merits and continues to make backroom deals to kill clean energy projects — a gift to his fossil fuel industry donors at the expense of America’s economic security.

“While China and other global competitors race to dominate the technologies that will power the future, California is building a modern grid, energy independence and an energy future that Trump is too small to understand.”

“This action by the Trump Administration is utter BS,” Sen. Mike McGuire (D-Healdsburg) said in an emailed statement delivered around 1 p.m. “The overall California RWE wind project would have advanced clean, reliable wind energy — enough to power 5 million homes — and created good rural jobs for the North Coast. Seemingly ripped from a script of VEEP, Trump is now forcing RWE’s hand to reinvest in the same fossil fuels which delivered the climate crisis to our door. This is yet another example of how off the rails the Trump Administration has gone. Total buffoonery.”

The Interior Department provided a statement from Secretary of the Interior and Chairman of the National Energy Dominance Council Doug Burgum Thursday afternoon.

“Americans deserve an energy system built on common sense, not one dependent on costly subsidies or technologies that can’t meet our country’s current demand,” said Burgum. “We welcome RWE’s agreement and voluntary investment in projects that strengthen our nation’s energy security, provide dependable baseload power, and help keep electricity affordable for hardworking Americans today while supporting our country’s long-term energy future.”

Robert Schaulis can be reached at 707-441-0585.
