name: EVs
title: How the EV transition is reshaping cost models for international automotive OEMs
description:
The result is a shift from traditional automotive cost models toward more dynamic, region-specific approaches that account for a growing range of variables.
Battery materials, steel, aluminium, energy, logistics, tariffs and compliance costs now play a direct role in vehicle profitability.
EV demand is reshaping investment decisions The EV transition continues to advance, but not uniformly across regions.
Battery materials are now a core margin driver The most significant change in automotive cost structures is the rise of battery materials as a major profitability factor.
A new approach to automotive cost management The EV transition is transforming automotive cost models in fundamental ways.
text:
Key takeaways:

Battery materials like lithium, nickel, and cobalt have become central to vehicle margins, influenced by fluctuating prices and chemistry choices.

Regionalization and trade policies introduce localized supply challenges and tariff impacts, complicating sourcing decisions.

OEMs increasingly adopt data-driven procurement strategies incorporating market intelligence and carbon compliance to navigate complex cost and regulatory landscapes.

The early EV growth story centered on scaling battery production, securing raw material supply and accelerating model launches. Today, however, demand patterns, battery raw material volatility, trade policy and carbon regulation are making manufacturers rethink how they manage profitability.

The result is a shift from traditional automotive cost models toward more dynamic, region-specific approaches that account for a growing range of variables.

Battery materials, steel, aluminium, energy, logistics, tariffs and compliance costs now play a direct role in vehicle profitability. Managing those factors effectively has become critical for OEMs to maintain margins throughout the EV transition.

EV demand is reshaping investment decisions

The EV transition continues to advance, but not uniformly across regions. In Europe, battery-electric vehicles (BEVs) captured around 20% market share during the first five months of 2026, while hybrid vehicles remained the largest powertrain category. At the same time, growth remains concentrated in Western European markets, highlighting significant regional differences in adoption rates.

This fragmentation is changing how OEMs forecast demand and allocate capital.

Rather than relying on a single global EV growth trajectory, manufacturers increasingly need to plan by geography, powertrain mix, battery chemistry and vehicle segment. A premium European BEV, a North American hybrid strategy and an entry-level Asian EV each carry different raw material and cost exposures.

North America illustrates how market conditions can alter investment plans.

Honda recently suspended aspects of its North American EV strategy, citing uncertainty over EV business viability and shifting its focus toward hybrid and internal combustion engine vehicles. The company’s decision underscores how automakers are reassessing whether planned EV investments align with actual market demand.

Battery materials are now a core margin driver

The most significant change in automotive cost structures is the rise of battery materials as a major profitability factor.

While OEMs have long managed exposure to steel and aluminium, electrification has introduced additional dependence on lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, manganese and other battery materials. These are highly sensitive to supply-chain constraints, refining capacity and rapidly evolving market dynamics.

Lithium demonstrates how dramatically market conditions can shift. Fastmarkets reported that lithium hydroxide prices exceeded $80 per kg in late 2022 before falling to around $8 per kg by 2025 as supply expanded and demand growth underperformed earlier expectations.

While lower lithium prices have supported OEM margins in the short term, they also create uncertainty around future supply investment. Prolonged low prices often can delay new projects, increasing the risk of tighter supply if EV demand accelerates again. As a result, procurement teams must monitor not only current pricing but longer-term supply fundamentals.

Battery chemistry choices are also becoming a cost-management tool. The growing adoption of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, which generally rely on lithium carbonate rather than lithium hydroxide, has altered previous assumptions about raw material demand.

For many automakers, chemistry selection now involves balancing performance, affordability and commodity price exposure.

Want to learn more about what is happening at the cutting-edge of critical minerals and battery raw materials? Listen to our Fast Forward podcast series for insight, debate and news from the major players.

Localization introduces new automotive cost challenges

Government policies such as the USMCA and the Inflation Reduction Act have encouraged OEMs to localize sourcing and manufacturing across North America. While domestic supply chains can reduce logistics risks, they do not eliminate commodity exposure.

In many cases, localization creates new challenges, including tighter regional supply, local price premiums and greater exposure to domestic policy changes.

Fastmarkets analysis notes that steel and aluminium markets are becoming increasingly fragmented as tariffs, supply restrictions and regional regulations reshape pricing dynamics.

Honda reported significant profit losses linked to tariffs while also facing Section 232 steel duties, automobile tariffs and anti-dumping measures.

For international OEMs, this means sourcing decisions can no longer be based solely on headline commodity prices. Tariffs, incentives, logistics costs, policy stability and supply availability must all be incorporated into cost models when evaluating production locations and supplier networks.

Carbon and compliance costs are gaining importance

Alongside material costs, carbon and compliance considerations are becoming increasingly important in automotive procurement strategies. European OEMs must now manage battery material costs while also addressing a more complex regulatory environment and rising sustainability expectations.

Carbon-related pricing mechanisms are also beginning to influence trade flows and sourcing decisions. While regulatory impacts vary by region, automotive manufacturers increasingly need visibility into the emissions profile of materials alongside their financial cost.

This is particularly relevant for steel and aluminium, where decarbonization efforts can significantly influence pricing and supplier selection.

As a result, many OEMs are moving toward cost frameworks that evaluate commodities based on both financial and carbon performance rather than price alone.

Automotive procurement is becoming data-driven

Greater cost volatility is driving a shift toward more sophisticated procurement and risk-management strategies. OEMs increasingly require independent benchmarks, market forecasts and exposure analysis to support sourcing decisions and supplier negotiations.

Fastmarkets’ lithium risk-management framework illustrates this trend. By using Cash Flow at Risk (CFaR) methodologies, companies can quantify the financial impact of potential commodity price movements and establish predefined hedging triggers when exposure exceeds acceptable limits.

The broader battery materials industry is also evolving. Discussions at the Fastmarkets Global Lithium, Battery and Critical Materials Conference highlighted how battery raw materials are now influenced not only by EV demand but also by growth in energy storage, AI infrastructure and national security initiatives.

These new demand drivers increase competition for future supply and reinforce the importance of long-term supply planning.

A new approach to automotive cost management

The EV transition is transforming automotive cost models in fundamental ways.

First, battery materials have become central to vehicle profitability.

Second, trade policy and localization strategies are fragmenting global sourcing economics.

Third, volatility is forcing procurement, finance and strategy teams to rely on shared market intelligence and risk-management frameworks rather than static annual budgets.

For international OEMs, the challenge is no longer simply scaling EV production. It is doing so profitably while navigating volatile commodity markets, shifting policy frameworks and evolving consumer demand.

The manufacturers best positioned for success will be those that combine cost visibility, procurement agility and robust market intelligence to make faster, more informed decisions in an increasingly complex automotive landscape.

The global Advanced Energy Storage Systems Market size estimated at USD 16164.04 million in 2026 and is projected to reach USD 24649.12 million by 2035, growing at a CAGR of 4.8% from 2026 to 2035.

The global Advanced Energy Storage Systems Market is becoming a critical component of the modern energy ecosystem as governments, utilities, industries, and consumers increasingly focus on renewable energy integration, grid stability, and electrification. Advanced energy storage systems enable efficient storage of electricity generated from renewable sources such as solar and wind, improving energy reliability and reducing dependence on traditional fossil fuel-based power generation.

The rapid expansion of renewable energy capacity has significantly increased the requirement for efficient energy storage technologies. Global renewable energy installations surpassed 4,000 GW of cumulative capacity, creating strong demand for battery storage, thermal storage, mechanical storage, and hybrid energy solutions. Energy storage systems help address renewable energy intermittency by balancing electricity supply and demand throughout different time periods.

Lithium-ion battery technology remains the dominant technology within the advanced energy storage sector due to its high energy density, longer lifecycle, and declining manufacturing costs. Lithium-ion batteries account for more than 90% of new battery energy storage deployments globally, particularly for utility-scale projects, electric vehicles, and commercial applications.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

1. What are Advanced Energy Storage Systems Market companies?

Advanced Energy Storage Systems Market companies are organizations involved in developing, manufacturing, and deploying technologies that store electrical energy for future use. These companies provide battery systems, grid storage solutions, thermal storage technologies, and energy management platforms for utilities, industries, businesses, and consumers.

2. Which companies are leading the global Advanced Energy Storage Systems Market?

Major companies operating in this market include LG Chem, ABB, BYD Company, Toshiba Corporation, NGK Insulators, Exide Technologies, GS Yuasa Corporation, Samsung SDI, EnerSys, Hitachi, General Electric Company, and AES Energy Storage.

3. Why are advanced energy storage systems important?

Advanced energy storage systems help manage electricity demand, support renewable energy integration, improve grid stability, and provide backup power during outages. These systems are essential for creating reliable and flexible energy networks.

4. Which technology dominates the Advanced Energy Storage Systems Market?

Lithium-ion battery technology currently dominates the market due to its high energy density, efficiency, long lifecycle, and wide adoption in electric vehicles, renewable energy projects, and commercial storage applications.

5. What industries use advanced energy storage systems?

Industries using advanced energy storage systems include renewable energy, automotive, utilities, telecommunications, manufacturing, data centers, commercial buildings, aerospace, and industrial infrastructure.

6. How do energy storage systems support renewable energy?

Energy storage systems store excess electricity generated from renewable sources such as solar and wind power. The stored energy can be released when renewable generation decreases, helping maintain consistent electricity supply.

7. What factors are driving the growth of advanced energy storage companies?

Major growth factors include increasing renewable energy installations, electric vehicle adoption, grid modernization programs, government clean energy initiatives, and rising demand for reliable backup power solutions.

8. What challenges affect the Advanced Energy Storage Systems Market?

Key challenges include battery material availability, manufacturing costs, recycling requirements, safety concerns, supply chain limitations, and the need for improved long-duration storage technologies.

9. What role does artificial intelligence play in energy storage systems?

Artificial intelligence helps optimize battery performance, predict energy demand, improve maintenance scheduling, monitor system health, and increase operational efficiency through advanced energy management platforms.

10. What is the future outlook for Advanced Energy Storage Systems Market companies?

The future outlook remains highly positive as global energy systems shift toward renewable generation, electrification, and decentralized power networks. Companies investing in advanced battery technologies, sustainable manufacturing, and intelligent energy solutions are expected to play a major role in the future energy landscape.

FIRST ON FOX: Senate Republicans are launching a multi-front effort targeting the legal framework they say allows California to exert outsized influence over vehicle and equipment emissions standards beyond its borders, creating economic and consumer consequences.

Republicans argue California has become the nation's de facto emissions regulator — as manufacturers rarely create separate product lines for the Golden State and instead are inclined to build to California’s standards, creating implicit national requirements.

Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wyo. — a top member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee (EPW) — is leading the effort alongside Sens. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., Jon Husted, R-Ohio, and Pete Ricketts, R-Neb. They argue EPA waivers granted to California during the Obama and Biden administrations under the Clean Air Act have turned narrow environmental exceptions into de facto climate regulation, advancing the state's sweeping climate agenda.

"California's climate zealots have run roughshod over the rest of the country for too long," Lummis told Fox News Digital.

CALIFORNIA SUES TRUMP EPA OVER MOVE TO SUBJECT STATE VEHICLE EMISSIONS WAIVERS TO CONGRESSIONAL REVIEW

"Under Governor Newsom, Sacramento has decided it can dictate what Wyoming families drive and what equipment our small businesses use. That ends today."

Last year, lawmakers successfully rescinded three Biden-era EPA waivers allowing California to create emissions standards for trucks, cars and buses that they said gave the state outsized regulatory control. Thursday’s package goes a step further by targeting earlier EPA decisions they say laid the legal foundation for those now-rescinded regulations.

Each resolution uses the Congressional Review Act (CRA) to nullify a different EPA waiver. The CRA gives Congress the power to check agencies' executive power.

NEWSOM, WALZ URGE CONGRESS TO BLOCK ANTI-CLIMATE BILL IN THEIR ‘WOKE’ CRUSADE

Because the CRA bars agencies from issuing rules that are "substantially the same" without new authorization from Congress, Republicans argue overturning the waivers would prevent future administrations from simply reinstating them — which targets the legal foundation of such carveouts.

Collectively, the package targets California's authority over gas-powered lawn equipment, passenger vehicle emissions standards, the Advanced Clean Cars program and the original 2009 EPA waiver allowing Sacramento to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from automobiles.

In the 1960s, the Clean Air Act gave California a narrow carve-out to seek EPA waivers for emissions rules that could be stricter than federal standards — but critics say the exemption, originally intended to address severe Los Angeles smog, has been weaponized to force manufacturing changes that reverberate across the country.

Andrew Bray, an executive with the National Association of Landscape Professionals, whose members rely on small off-road engines affected by the waivers, said he supports a responsible transition to lower-emission equipment — but underlined that it must come from "practical innovation" and not government mandates.

TRUMP’S REINDUSTRIALIZATION AGENDA FACES ITS BIGGEST HURDLE — AMERICANS

"This resolution is a critical step in securing the flexibility businesses need while technology continues to advance," Bray said. Michael Lee of the Golf Course Superintendents Association of America added that the legislative process, not state-specific fiats with "nationwide consequences," is the way to address the situation.

The four lawmakers leading the fight said in a release that California regulators have "abandoned any pretense of addressing local air quality and turned the waiver process into a backdoor for imposing a radical climate agenda on the entire country… without a single vote in Congress."

Lummis' resolution would rescind a 2025 waiver granted just before President Donald Trump took office that she said allowed California to phase out gas-powered small engines such as chainsaws and leaf blowers.

In doing so, manufacturers would no longer be inclined to transition to electric or zero-emission models.

TRUMP'S EPA CHIEF PUSHES BACK ON CLIMATE SKEPTICS BEING LABELED 'SCIENCE DENIERS'

Lummis' resolution targets a 2025 EPA waiver that allowed California to move toward phasing out new gas-powered small engines such as chainsaws, leaf blowers and lawn mowers. Supporters say repealing the waiver would remove regulatory pressure encouraging manufacturers to transition those products toward zero-emission technology.

Husted’s resolution targets a 2022 EPA waiver that restored California’s authority to continue its Advanced Clean Cars program.

"Ohioans shouldn’t be forced to follow California’s lead when it comes to policies that make everyday life more expensive and less convenient," he told Fox News Digital on Thursday.

Ricketts said the situation is proof that the Obama-Biden era of "overregulation and red tape" continues to cost Nebraskans and Americans writ large millions of dollars, citing his state's massive agricultural industry as an example of regulatory reverberations from Sacramento.

EUROPE'S 'GREEN IDEOLOGY' CLIMATE AGENDA RISKS CRUSHING ITS INDUSTRY, ENVIRONMENT MINISTER WARNS

"They used California policies as a backdoor EV mandate and even tried to control how we cut our grass," he said. His CRA resolution targets an Obama-era waiver originally authorizing the clean car program, while Schmitt seeks repeal of a waiver granted just months after President George W. Bush left office that allows California to enforce greenhouse gas emissions standards for new passenger vehicles beginning with the 2009 model year.

Schmitt said the waivers allow Sacramento to "continue to punish" manufacturers around the country and affect consumer choice and costs through their "climate alarmist rules."

Together, Republicans say the four resolutions represent Congress' broadest effort yet to unshackle states and manufacturers from California's emissions framework by targeting not only individual regulations but the EPA decisions they argue made those regulations possible.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Opponents are expected to counter that the effort would undermine California's longstanding authority under the Clean Air Act to adopt stricter environmental standards.

text:
Carbon capture technology can reduce carbon in the atmosphere by storing it underground or using it to make products like concrete or jet fuel.

The 45Q tax credit was created to incentivize development of this technology. But some taxpayers have difficulty claiming it. Those who use captured carbon to make products face the biggest hurdles—long delays for approval and a high rejection rate, for example.

No agency is tasked with measuring results and the law didn't set clear goals, so it's hard to know if the 45Q tax credit is working.

We made recommendations to Congress and agencies to improve oversight and administration of the tax credit.

Industrial carbon capture and storage facility with tall metal towers, and pipes.

What GAO Found

The Carbon Oxide Sequestration Credit (45Q) is a tax credit provided for certain carbon oxides that are captured at emission sources or directly from the air and either stored underground or used to produce products. The credit has been amended multiple times, including by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), which added new credit features. More recently, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act created parity in credit values across uses of captured carbon. As of March 2026, there were 33 carbon capture facilities in the U.S., with additional facilities planned. The number of 45Q credit claims more than tripled from 2019 to 2023, according to IRS data.

The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has taken several actions to administer the 45Q credit and mitigate potential noncompliance. However, taxpayers using carbon to produce products face compliance burdens, delays, and uncertainty in claiming the credit. GAO identified areas in the approval process for carbon utilization where IRS and the Department of Energy (DOE) could potentially minimize compliance burden and improve certainty for taxpayers. Pursuing such opportunities—for example, streamlining certain processes, or clarifying acceptable datasets that can be used to calculate carbon displaced—could improve the process and help minimize delays for both agencies and taxpayers.

Multiple potential goals, the lack of a designated agency to evaluate the effectiveness of the credit, and data limitations complicate Congress’s ability to understand the performance of the 45Q credit. Even so, periodic reviews of tax expenditures are crucial for informed oversight. GAO has previously recommended various actions Congress and agencies could take to improve oversight for other tax expenditures, such as identifying what should be analyzed and by whom. In this report, GAO identified key questions for Congress to consider directing agencies to analyze to help determine the performance of the credit. These key questions are: (1) how well the credit is working to achieve its goals, (2) how efficiently the credit is performing and (3) how the credit compares to other policy tools.

Why GAO Did This Study

The 45Q credit was created in 2008 to incentivize the development of carbon capture technology and reduce carbon emissions. Carbon capture involves complex and novel technology, and the 45Q credit could result in potentially substantial revenue expenditures.

The IRA includes a provision for GAO to review the distribution and use of IRA funds. This report assesses (1) IRS’s administration of the 45Q credit, and (2) the challenges in evaluating the effectiveness of the credit. GAO reviewed agency policies and procedures and interviewed officials from IRS, DOE, and the Environmental Protection Agency. GAO also interviewed selected external stakeholders knowledgeable about the 45Q credit, representing advocacy, research, and industry. GAO also conducted two site visits to carbon capture sites in Houston, Texas.

text:
Illinois is one step closer to building its first new nuclear reactors in nearly 40 years.

Though the state leads the nation in nuclear energy generation, a recently lifted moratorium on new nuclear power plant construction means the race is on to bring new plants online — a task that can take years.

As Illinois looks for the right sites to build, several communities have already said “yes” to new plants.

Planning for these new reactors is happening in a different context from the last time they were built in the state in the 1970s and ‘80s. Reactor technology has advanced, but so has wind and solar power. And with energy demands rising quickly, construction time and costs are sure to play a big part in the trajectory of nuclear power.

A Winding Path to New Plants

This is just the latest step in the state’s long history with nuclear technology.

University of Chicago scientists built the world’s first nuclear reactor under the stands of the school’s football field in 1942. After World War II, the federal government opened Argonne National Laboratory to continue research into civilian uses for nuclear power.

Today, Illinois leads the nation in generating nuclear energy, with 11 plants pumping out half of the state’s total electricity. But of these existing plants, the last one came online in 1988.

A statewide moratorium on new construction lasted from the late 1980s until this January, when it was lifted as part of an energy omnibus bill. Gov. JB Pritzker wasted little time getting the ball rolling on new projects.

“The economic opportunity of building new, clean power is enormous,” Pritzker said in his February budget address, announcing an executive order intended to speed up the construction of new nuclear facilities.

“We can take years off of the development and launch of new base load energy production,” Pritzker said.

Read More:

These 9 Illinois Communities Say They’re Interested in New Nuclear Facilities

What Does Pritzker’s Nuclear Energy Executive Order Do in Illinois?

Pritzker Signs Major Energy Reform Bill Amid Projected Shortages

The order directed state agencies to create a framework for the evaluation, financing and safety regulation of new nuclear power plants. Importantly, the order also directed those agencies to request information from communities interested in hosting a new facility.

Now, the responses are in. Nine communities, plus the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, submitted initial comments.

Many came from communities that host existing nuclear plants, like Grundy County. In addition to the Dresden Generating Station within the county lines, the LaSalle Generating Station is a 40-minute drive to the west, and the Braidwood Generating Station is about 25 minutes south.

“We have a comfort with nuclear, we have the workforce for nuclear, we have the safety mechanisms in place,” said Nancy Norton, president of the Grundy County Economic Development Council.

“And frankly, (we have) the infrastructure and transmission to get power out to the customers,” Grundy said.

Then there are places like Peoria County, which is navigating a new energy landscape after the closure of a coal-fired power plant in 2022.

“Where we separate ourselves is we’ve been very supportive and agnostic of all the alternative energy sources,” said Scott Sorrel, the Peoria County administrator.

Peoria County is one of the state leaders in approving utility-scale solar power projects and is planning two utility-scale wind power projects, according to Sorrel.

“At this point in time, we’re not closing a door to nuclear, but making sure that door stays open,” Sorrel said. “And if the opportunity presents itself, to walk through that door.”

Time and Money Shape the Clean Energy Transition

Nuclear power is considered “clean” energy, since it does not emit the greenhouse gases that cause climate change. It can also output energy around the clock. But the role it can play in the transition away from fossil fuels is still a matter of debate.

The two most recent nuclear plants to come online in the United States, at the Vogtle Generating Plant in Georgia, opened seven years behind schedule and $17 billion over budget.

With energy demand rapidly rising, environmental advocates point to the relatively cheap and fast deployment of renewable sources like solar and wind projects.

While nuclear power still provides Illinois with about half of its electricity, the share provided by renewables has tripled in the past decade — growing to 16% in 2025, according to the Illinois Power Agency.

That’s at least the current status of nuclear power in Illinois, generated at large facilities with the familiar hourglass-shaped cooling towers. But Norton and Sorrel both acknowledged that the technology is changing, and the next generation of reactors could look and operate differently.

Advancing Reactor Designs

One place to look for what modern nuclear reactors might accomplish is the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. There, the university is working in partnership with the company NANO Nuclear Energy to build a prototype of a “microreactor” on campus.

While this would produce around 1% of the energy made by traditional large reactors, James Walker, the NANO Nuclear Energy CEO, said the advantage is in how it can be built and operated.

“All the components will be shipped to site as a modular system, assembled there, and begin to immediately output power,” Walker said.

So far, no commercial small modular reactors (SMRs) have been completed in the United States, and the industry is split between dozens of different designs. The NANO Nuclear reactor, which would fit on a 2-acre plot of land adjacent to an existing power plant, is the first of its size to be submitted for federal approval from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

But even though the designs are new, Walker said the technology isn’t the main bottleneck for quickly deploying reactors like the University of Illinois project.

“It’s having all of the components to be able to mass manufacture the reactors, that’s going to be the challenge,” Walker said.

And since new reactors of any size haven’t been built in decades, one remaining question is where the workforce and expertise might come from.

For Norton, the answer is right down the street.

“We have the construction workers that have been maintaining these nuclear plants,” Norton said.

“In our region, we probably have a couple thousand employees who understand how nuclear reactions and nuclear reactors work,” Norton said. “So I don’t know that to scale up would be that difficult for us.”

Capitol News Illinois contributed to this report.

text:

For more than half a century, the R.E. Ginna Nuclear Power Plant has quietly generated carbon-free electricity along the southern shore of Lake Ontario, producing enough power for more than 400,000 homes. Its lone reactor is the smallest operating commercial nuclear unit in the United States, yet it consistently ranks among the nation’s most reliable, operating with a capacity factor above 99 percent.

Now, New York wants to build something far bigger.

Gov. Kathy Hochul last year directed the New York Power Authority to begin developing at least one new advanced nuclear power plant in Upstate New York while charting a course toward what she calls a statewide “nuclear reliability backbone” totaling 8.4 gigawatts of nuclear generation. That vision includes New York’s existing reactors, a planned 1-gigawatt advanced nuclear facility and another 4 gigawatts of future development—a buildout unlike anything attempted in the U.S. in decades.

Among the possible locations for the proposed 1-gigawatt advanced nuclear facility: Wayne County, home to the Ginna plant, and a site only a few miles from downtown Rochester.

State officials argue the investment in nuclear energy is essential. Artificial intelligence, semiconductor manufacturing, electrification and economic development are driving electricity demand upward just as New York struggles to meet its ambitious climate goals.

But before a single reactor is built, New York faces a question that could determine whether the governor’s vision ever becomes reality: Who pays for it?

The state’s own financial modeling estimates that making a 5-gigawatt advanced nuclear buildout commercially viable could require between $15.4 billion and $23.9 billion in public support, depending on how the projects are developed. Separate construction cost estimates suggest the full price tag could approach $45 billion.

Those figures have transformed what might otherwise have been a debate over energy policy into one of the state’s most consequential political fights—drawing labor unions, economic development officials and local governments eager for investment into conflict with environmental organizations that see nuclear as an extraordinarily expensive gamble at the very moment New York is retreating from portions of its landmark climate law.

Whether New York’s next generation of nuclear plants ever gets built may depend as much on politics and public acceptance as engineering.

The financial reality of 5 new gigawatts

When the Department of Public Service and the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority released the 2026 New York Advanced Nuclear Policy Options Paper in June, the document offered the clearest picture yet of the financial challenge ahead.

Its conclusions were sobering.

Private investors remain reluctant to finance nuclear construction because of the industry’s long history of delays and cost overruns. Wholesale electricity markets alone cannot generate enough revenue to make new reactors economically viable. Before construction even begins, developers would likely require hundreds of millions of dollars simply to reach a final investment decision.

The report concludes that substantial public intervention will almost certainly be necessary.

Among the options under consideration:

■ Cost-overrun guarantees, allowing the state, federal government, reactor developers and engineering firms to share the financial risk of construction delays and budget overruns.

■ Advanced Nuclear Zero Emission Credits,a proposed subsidy modeled after New York’s Zero Emission Credit program for existing nuclear plants. The paper also contemplates allowing large technology companies operating energy-intensive data centers to voluntarily purchase those credits or negotiate direct power purchase agreements.

■ Public ownership and construction grants, including direct state equity investments designed to reduce financing costs.

■ Federal financing through the U.S. Department of Energy, which could cover as much as 80 percent of construction costs through long-term, low-interest loans.

The report also acknowledges another difficult question: What exactly should New York build?

State officials are weighing traditional large light-water reactors against a new generation of small modular reactors, or SMRs, that promise lower upfront costs and greater siting flexibility but remain largely unproven commercially.

Rather than issuing a traditional request for proposals based primarily on price, the paper recommends an open-book negotiation process that would allow developers and the state to jointly evaluate financial risk before selecting a technology.

Why New York Is betting on nuclear again

The state’s renewed embrace of nuclear represents one of the most dramatic shifts in New York energy policy in a generation.

Standing at the Robert Moses Niagara Power Plant in June 2025, Hochul announced that New York would pursue construction of a new advanced nuclear facility in the upstate region—the first major state-backed nuclear project proposed anywhere in the country in more than 15 years.

The announcement came as electricity forecasts were changing dramatically.

Massive semiconductor manufacturing projects such as Micron’s planned campus outside Syracuse, rapid expansion of AI infrastructure and broader electrification efforts have all fueled expectations that electricity demand could rise significantly over the coming decades. State officials increasingly argue that renewable energy alone cannot provide enough around-the-clock generation to maintain reliability.

As of 2024, nearly half of New York’s in-state electricity generation came from zero-emission sources, with 21% from nuclear generation and 26% from renewable sources: hydroelectric, solar, and wind. Combustion generation—which uses natural gas, oil, biofuels, or solid waste as fuel—produced 53% of in-state bulk electricity. Coal is no longer used for electricity generation in New York.

In her 2026 State of the State address in January, Hochul expanded her vision for nuclear’s future in New York.

“I’ve decided to raise the bar to 5 gigawatts,” she told lawmakers. “That’s more nuclear energy than has been built anywhere in the United States in the last 30 years.”

The governor framed nuclear not as a replacement for renewable energy but as the dependable backbone needed to support it—a source of emissions-free electricity capable of operating regardless of weather conditions.

This view is mirrored by Kristy Hartman, senior director of state policy and external affairs at the Washington, D.C.-based Nuclear Energy Institute, which promotes the use and growth of nuclear energy. She notes that the surge in interest is a nationwide phenomenon.

“New York is a leader in this space,” Hartman says. “There are a lot of states coming up with innovative policy and regulatory concepts to support the future of nuclear. We’ve seen a complete change in that landscape. Last year, 350 bills were introduced across state legislatures across the country. We’re halfway through the year this year and we’re on track for that number again.”

That argument has resonated across much of Upstate New York, where communities already hosting nuclear facilities see an opportunity to build on decades of experience while attracting billions of dollars in new investment.

Others, however, see something entirely different.

To critics, New York is preparing to spend tens of billions of dollars on technology they believe remains too expensive, too slow to deploy and burdened by an unresolved radioactive waste problem.

An expensive mistake?

Few have emerged as more outspoken critics than Tim Judson, executive director of the Maryland-based Nuclear Information and Resource Service, an information and advocacy organization that supports efforts for a nuclear-free planet and a sustainable energy future.

“It’s hard to see what the upsides would be to the governor’s plan,” Judson says. “Nuclear power is extremely expensive. It takes a really long time to build nuclear plants. The technologies, some of the ones they’re considering, are, at best, nascent but certainly unproven. We have a lot more effective ways to provide energy, including renewable energy, which the governor seems to be undermining.”

Judson argues the state’s newly released policy paper should become the focus of public scrutiny rather than simply the governor’s announcement.

“The Public Service Commission opened up a public comment period for people to weigh in on this,” he says. “It includes a study or a report that the PSC staff and NYSERDA produced, laying out their proposed options. All of which are really terrible.”

For Judson, the financial modeling itself raises serious questions about whether the projects can ever become affordable for ratepayers.

While critics emphasize high upfront costs, proponents argue these figures fail to capture the long-term value of nuclear assets.

“It is expensive to build nuclear,” Hartman says. “But what sets us apart, and I don’t think we have a great way to value this, is that you’re building energy assets for your kids and grandkids. There is no energy source where you’re building it out for 80 or 100 years. When we spread those costs over the life cycle of a nuclear power plant, it’s actually pretty low.”

Others see broader implications.

Ethan Gormley, legislative coordinator for Citizen Action of New York, argues the debate cannot be separated from New Yorkers’ growing concerns about utility bills.

“Nuclear energy is one of the, if not the, most expensive forms of energy out there,” Gormley says.

He notes that the governor’s proposal comes as households continue to struggle with rising utility costs.

“More nuclear is just going to create higher bills for a lot of people who are already struggling to keep the lights on,” he contends.

Gormley frequently points to Georgia’s Plant Vogtle expansion—the nation’s largest recent nuclear construction project—as a warning. Cost overruns totaling roughly $7.6 billion ultimately resulted in higher monthly electric bills for customers, in addition to years of construction surcharges.

“A lot of people are either unaware of Gov. Hochul’s reckless pursuit of new nuclear power or they’re not sure how it’s going to affect them yet,” he says.

For his organization, the strategy is straightforward: Raise public awareness before New York selects host communities.

Communities’ response

As state officials refine the financial framework, another question is beginning to dominate the conversation: Where, exactly, should New York build its next nuclear plant?

The state Power Authority has not selected a site, but its requests for information last fall drew responses from 23 nuclear developers and eight communities interested in hosting the state’s first advanced reactor.

For some upstate communities, the proposal represents a once-in-a-generation economic opportunity. For others, it has become a flashpoint.

Support for the governor’s goal is also coming from advocacy groups. Scott Cicora, co-executive director of Nuclear New York, says his group felt validated by the state’s move.

“We were ecstatic,” Cicora says. “We formed in 2019 primarily to oppose the closing of Indian Point (near Peekskill). We obviously failed there. But we’ve been working on public outreach and educating legislators around nuclear and trying to demystify all of the things that have happened with the messaging in the past.”

Wayne County looks to build on Ginna’s legacy

Few communities are more familiar with nuclear power than Wayne County.

For more than 50 years, the Ginna nuclear facility has operated along Lake Ontario, providing hundreds of high-paying jobs while serving as one of the country’s most reliable generating stations. Constellation Energy is already seeking to extend Ginna’s operating license to 80 years, reinforcing the company’s long-term commitment to the site. That would extend the current license, which runs through 2029, another 20 years to 2049. The company is one of the developers that responded to the Power Authority’s RFI.

Wayne County Administrator Mark Humbert believes that history gives the county a distinct advantage if New York decides to expand nuclear generation.

“We’ve built a lot of infrastructure, community support, and essential services related to nuclear being in our neighborhood,” Humbert says. “For instance, we do annual drills with the plant. There is already good transmission capacity throughout the region of the state from the plant. So, it already exists.”

Rather than starting from scratch, Humbert sees existing nuclear communities as logical places to grow.

Cicora agrees, identifying Wayne and Oswego counties as the most practical options.

“Wayne County and Oswego County are the low-hanging fruit,” Cicora says. “They have the land. And actually before the governor’s announcement, all of the town supervisors in Wayne County had already weighed in about wanting new nuclear. The fact that there is community support, that’s huge for both Wayne County and Oswego County.”

The emergency planning systems are already in place. Transmission infrastructure already exists. Residents understand the industry because they’ve lived alongside it for decades.

For local officials, the conversation is about more than electricity. It is about jobs, tax revenue and long-term economic stability.

Oswego makes its case

The same argument is being made 60 miles to the east.

Oswego County already hosts three operating reactors at the Nine Mile Point and James A. FitzPatrick nuclear plants, making it one of the country’s largest concentrations of nuclear generation.

State Assembly Minority Leader Will Barclay, whose district includes Oswego County, has called Hochul’s nuclear initiative “a positive step forward,” arguing the region has both the workforce and public acceptance necessary to accommodate future development.

Communities that have lived with nuclear power for decades generally see less uncertainty than places being introduced to the technology for the first time.

That dynamic could shape the state’s eventual siting decisions.

Eastman Business Park becomes a lightning rod

No potential site has generated more controversy than Rochester’s Eastman Business Park.

Among the eight community responses submitted to the Power Authority was one from RED-Rochester, the nonprofit utility operator serving the sprawling industrial campus just three miles from downtown Rochester.

The submission immediately drew criticism from anti-nuclear advocates, who argue the park’s proximity to residential neighborhoods makes it an inappropriate location for a reactor.

“It’s opened up the opportunity for crazy ideas like what RED-Rochester is proposing—to put a nuclear power plant in an urban neighborhood three miles from downtown Rochester,” Judson says.

“This has been illegal for the past 60 years in the U.S., to put a nuclear power plant in a densely populated area,” he adds. “But the nuclear industry has been pushing this crazy idea that these new designs for small reactors are so small and inherently safe that the radiation, even in an accident, wouldn’t get beyond the site boundary. This is just all fundamentally untrue.”

When asked about those criticisms, RED-Rochester declined an interview, saying the process remains too preliminary.

“At this early stage, we do not believe there are sufficient project-specific details available to warrant an interview,” Paul Tyno, RED-Rochester’s director of client and market development, wrote in an email.

Instead, the organization emphasized that its participation has been limited to responding to NYPA’s request for information and a subsequent informational meeting.

“Our submission reflects the capabilities of Eastman Business Park as an industrial energy and infrastructure platform, not a defined project,” the statement said. “There is no specific project, site design, development plan, or siting decision associated with Eastman Business Park at this time.”

The organization also stressed that Eastman Kodak Co. is not part of the submission and that nuclear represents only one of several possible decarbonization technologies being evaluated for the campus.

That distinction matters.

An RFI is not a construction proposal, nor does it commit a community to hosting a reactor.

Rather, it is an early planning exercise designed to help NYPA understand which communities believe they possess the infrastructure, workforce and local interest necessary to support future development.

Still, the Rochester response illustrates how quickly the governor’s proposal has moved from an abstract statewide policy discussion to a locally focused issue. Even before a site has been selected, communities are already debating whether they want to become New York’s next nuclear hometown.

Kate Kressmann-Kehoe, New York state lead for Mothers for Nuclear, offers a nuanced take on the potential for new sites like the Eastman location.

“I think different things require different responses,” Kressmann-Kehoe says. “We’re at the very, very early stages of everything. To me, I am a geology major, I am a filmmaker. I am not a structural engineer, I’m not a nuclear engineer. Putting more nuclear in Wayne County where there is already nuclear, that seems relatively straightforward. Looking at new sites that may require new technologies is a process. It may be a great fit, it may not be. It’s something that you need to deliberately go through the site assessments and look at the technology.

“It could be a great source of stable, emissions-free power for the city,” Kressmann-Kehoe adds. “But we could be like, ‘No, this isn’t a good idea.’”

Labor sees thousands of jobs

If environmental organizations have become the loudest critics of Hochul’s plan, organized labor has emerged as one of its strongest supporters.

Construction unions view advanced nuclear not simply as another energy project but as one of the largest potential public works programs in decades.

Vincent Albanese, director of policy and public affairs for the New York State Laborers’ Organizing Fund, says the labor movement has been preparing for precisely this moment.

“There are just thousands of jobs that would be created in the construction of new units, whether they be smaller SMRs or larger-scale units,” Albanese says.

The support extends beyond rhetoric.

Albanese says the Laborers’ union and Constellation Energy now co-chair the Future Energy Alliance, a coalition formed specifically to advocate for new nuclear development in New York.

The organization has also begun preparing workers for projects that may still be years away.

Using a portion of the governor’s recently announced $40 million NextGen Nuclear New York workforce initiative, apprenticeship programs are beginning to incorporate nuclear-specific training and certifications intended to ensure qualified workers are available if projects move forward.

Albanese rejects the notion that labor’s support for nuclear comes at the expense of renewable energy.

“We’re very supportive of renewables,” he says. “That’s creating a tremendous amount of jobs at the moment.”

The challenge, he argues, is scale.

Electricity demand is growing rapidly enough that no single resource can meet it alone.

“Our electricity demand is increasing,” Albanese says. “Combining all of these sources still is a challenge for us to meet that demand.”

That “all-of-the-above” philosophy increasingly reflects the position of many business and economic development organizations across Upstate New York.

Greater Rochester Enterprise president and CEO Matt Hurlbutt says his organization remains neutral on where a future reactor should be located, but he believes the broader need for additional generation is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

The region’s industrial expansion, housing development and economic growth all depend on one thing, he said: reliable electricity.

“The ability to get and think out of the box and to help things move forward as quickly as possible—and importantly, as safely as possible, and making sure we’re affordable, efficient—is something we’re working collaboratively with other partners to support,” Hurlbutt says.

For proponents, that is the central argument.

Whether the answer ultimately comes from conventional reactors, small modular reactors or another technology altogether, they believe New York cannot achieve its economic ambitions without significantly expanding reliable, around-the-clock power generation.

For opponents, however, that premise remains deeply flawed. To them, the question is not whether New York needs more electricity. It is whether nuclear power is the right—and affordable—way to produce it.

A climate law under pressure

For critics like Citizen Action’s Gormley, the debate over nuclear power cannot be separated from a broader shift in New York’s climate policy.

The state’s 2019 Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act established some of the nation’s most ambitious emissions-reduction goals, requiring an 85 percent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 while setting interim benchmarks for 2030 and 2040.

Meeting those targets, however, has proven far more difficult than lawmakers anticipated.

This spring, as part of negotiations over the fiscal year 2027 state budget, Hochul secured changes that pushed back implementation of key emissions-reduction regulations, including the long-delayed cap-and-invest program, until the end of 2028—four years later than originally contemplated. Lawmakers also approved a change in how the state calculates methane emissions, shifting from a 20-year to a 100-year measurement window.

The governor has defended those changes as necessary to balance climate goals with affordability and economic realities.

Environmental organizations see them differently.

More than 200 organizations signed a letter this spring urging Hochul to abandon both the proposed nuclear expansion and the changes to the state’s climate law, arguing that the two policies represent a retreat from New York’s commitment to rapidly deploy renewable energy.

To Gormley, the two issues are inseparable.

Whatever promise advanced nuclear may hold decades from now, he argues, it does little to address today’s affordability crisis.

“If anything,” he says, “it’s going to make it worse.”

Judson raises another concern that has followed the nuclear industry for generations.

Even if the economics eventually work, he argues, New York still has no permanent solution for the radioactive waste already being produced by its existing reactors.

“The cost issue is the one that’s going to affect everybody across the state,” Judson says. “But the reality is that we don’t have a solution for nuclear waste.”

Industry representatives argue, however, that the waste issue is frequently misunderstood.

“There just isn’t that much nuclear waste used fuel,” Hartman contends. “And I think that’s a misnomer. If your entire life was powered by clean nuclear energy, all of that waste would fit in a soda can. All of the used fuel that has been created by the existing nuclear reactors in the U.S. would fit in an Amazon warehouse or a Walmart or any of those types of big box store buildings.

“Of course, we’d like to see a permanent repository and a plan,” she adds. “But in the meantime as the government works through all these options, there is a lot of momentum and excitement. The nuclear industry is very safe. The used fuel is stored on-site. It can be stored indefinitely.”

For his part, Judson points to the closure of Indian Point in 2021 as an example. Although the Hudson Valley plant stopped generating electricity, its spent nuclear fuel remains stored on site because the U.S. still lacks a permanent federal repository.

“There is this crazy logical fallacy at play,” Judson says. “Essentially what they’re saying is that we can figure out how to keep nuclear waste out of the environment for a million years, but we can’t figure out how to keep the lights on.”

Supporters of nuclear power acknowledge those concerns but argue the alternative carries its own risks. Nationally, the industry points to decades of safe on-site storage of spent fuel in steel-and-concrete casks and is pressing the federal government to open a consolidated interim storage site as a bridge to a permanent underground repository, a position the Nuclear Energy Institute has outlined as its preferred path forward.

Without substantial new sources of reliable, around-the-clock electricity, they say, New York could struggle to accommodate the very industries state leaders have spent years recruiting. Semiconductor manufacturing, AI infrastructure and widespread electrification all depend on a grid capable of producing massive amounts of power regardless of weather conditions.

For them, the debate is less about choosing between nuclear and renewable energy than ensuring there is enough electricity to support both economic growth and the state’s long-term climate ambitions.

The $45 billion question

The fight over New York’s nuclear future has never really been about whether reactors can produce electricity. They already do.

For more than five decades, plants like Ginna, Nine Mile Point and FitzPatrick have generated carbon-free power while employing thousands of New Yorkers. The harder question is whether the next generation of reactors can be built on time, within budget, and at a cost taxpayers and ratepayers are willing to accept.

The state’s own policy paper offers no easy answers. It acknowledges that new nuclear construction is unlikely to proceed without significant public support. It recognizes that private investors remain wary after decades of cost overruns and abandoned projects. And it outlines a menu of subsidies, financing mechanisms and risk-sharing agreements that could require billions of dollars in public participation before a single watt of electricity reaches the grid.

For supporters, those costs represent a necessary investment in New York’s economic future and electric reliability.

For opponents, they are evidence that the state is preparing to spend tens of billions of dollars pursuing a technology that remains slower and more expensive than other clean-energy alternatives.

The next several months may begin to determine which vision prevails.

The public comment period on the Advanced Nuclear Policy Options Paper remains open through Aug. 10, after which the Department of Public Service and NYSERDA are expected to develop a formal white paper recommending specific policy actions to the Public Service Commission. At the same time, NYPA continues reviewing responses from reactor developers and communities interested in hosting the state’s first advanced nuclear project, with additional announcements expected later this year.

The decisions that follow will shape far more than where New York builds its next power plant.

They will determine how the state intends to power an increasingly electrified economy, how much the public is willing to spend to achieve that goal and whether one of the most ambitious nuclear expansions proposed in a generation ever moves beyond the drawing board.

Will Cleveland is a Rochester Beacon contributing writer.

text:
Lineage Logistics faced residents and public officials Wednesday during an air quality hearing focused on persistent odors from its fire-damaged cold storage facility. NBC4 Investigates has learned that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency sent a letter to Lineage demanding answers about a potential hazardous substance release.

The hearing marked the first time Lineage representatives had appeared before the general public since a town hall held shortly after the June 17 fire.

Residents of Boyle Heights, East Los Angeles and nearby communities told the South Coast Air Quality Management District that odors from the facility have made daily life unbearable.

“This is not a humane way for anyone to live,” one resident said.

“Whenever we step outside, it reeks,” another resident said. “I feel a sensation to throw up. That’s how bad it is.”

More than 90 people, including Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, signed up to speak at the hearing.

“It’s unlike anything I’ve ever experienced,” Bass said.

The air district has received nearly 4,000 odor complaints related to the facility, where meat and fish have been decomposing since the fire. The agency has issued Lineage 24 notices of violation since July 12, though no financial penalties have been imposed.

Wednesday’s hearing centered on whether the district should issue an abatement order requiring Lineage to take additional steps to reduce odors during the cleanup.

NBC4 Investigates also learned that the EPA sent a letter to the facility’s general manager requesting information about the fire and its aftermath.

“The EPA is aware of a potential hazardous substance release event at the Lineage Logistics-Big Bear facility in Los Angeles, California, on or around June 17-20, 2026,” the agency wrote.

The letter did not identify the hazardous substance under investigation.

Lineage previously acknowledged that ammonia was present at the facility during the fire but said the chemical was successfully removed from the property. The company said readings have shown no detectable concentrations of ammonia since the fire began.

However, Jill Johnston, an environmental scientist at the University of California, Irvine, said her analysis of air district data collected from late July through early August found elevated ammonia levels near the facility.

“It’s not stating that they’re exceeding regulatory standards, but they are much higher than we would expect,” Johnston said. “In other research, these concentrations have been linked with adverse health effects.”

Johnston also analyzed air samples collected near the facility by trained community scientists. She said the results showed ammonia levels above typical background concentrations in Los Angeles.

Lineage released a time-lapse video of its cleanup and said it has removed about 80% of the food waste from the warehouse. The company estimates the cleanup will cost between $80 million and $100 million.

The company has wrapped portions of the building in tarps, sprayed deodorizers and placed traps in an effort to control odors and pests. Residents, however, said the problems continue.

Lineage’s response to the EPA investigation was not immediately available.

The air quality hearing is scheduled to continue Thursday.

text:
CHARLOTTESVILLE, VA (CVILLE RIGHT NOW) – Gov. Abigail Spanberger will intervene at the State Corporation Commission (SCC) level about the proposed $67 billion merger between Virginia-based Dominion Energy and Florida-based NextEra, according to a Thursday morning release from the Governor’s Office.

Spanberger is expected to push for certain assurances from Dominion as it goes before the State Corporation Commission for approval of the deal.

A Dominion spokesperson told Cville Right Now on Thursday morning the company was working on a response to the Governor’s announcement.

The Governor, according to the announcement, will hold an afternoon virtual media briefing on her action, which the release said is “the first time a Governor of Virginia has taken such an action at the State Corporation Commission (SCC).”

The announcement referenced a new Washington Post op-ed with some of her reasoning.

“The Governor outlined the three non-negotiable priorities that will guide her involvement as the SCC conducts its review: delivering more affordable energy bills for Virginia families and small businesses, protecting Virginia’s utility workforce, and accelerating Virginia’s progress toward producing affordable, reliable, local, and clean power into the future,” according to the announcement.

“We welcome the Governor’s participation in the regulatory process and agree with her priorities of affordability, protecting Virginia jobs and supporting the Commonwealth’s energy future,” Dominion Energy Chair, President and CEO Robert M. Blue told Cville Right Now in a statement. “Those priorities are at the core of this proposal. The transaction includes $1.78 billion in NextEra shareholder-funded bill credits for Virginia customers, as well as long-term benefits from greater purchasing power and lower borrowing costs. It also includes strong employment protections and career opportunities for Virginia employees, as well as commitments to maintain a significant Virginia presence, headquarters and local leadership. The proposal will leverage NextEra Energy’s expertise as the world’s leading clean energy developer to help meet Virginia’s growing energy needs.

“As the Governor noted, the SCC is the appropriate forum to evaluate this transaction and balance the interests of the Commonwealth, and we are confident its established, fact-based review will demonstrate the benefits this proposal offers Virginia,”

The merger will create the world’s largest regulated electric utility business, serving approximately 10 million customer accounts across Virginia, Florida, North Carolina and South Carolina.

The company will be more than 80% regulated and own 110 gigawatts of generation across a variety of energy sources.

The merger comes in the midst of a historic demand for energy. Virginia is far from an exception, as its large amount of data centers, particularly in Northern Virginia, has heavily contributed to a stark increase in demand.

Dominion spokesperson Tim Eberly told Cville Right Now on Tuesday the company was anticipating energy demand in Virginia to double over the next 20 years, with the company planning to add 33 new gigawatts of new power generation over the next two decades in response.

Dominion CEO Robert Blue, who will stay with the newly merged company as President and CEO of Regulated Utilities and join its Board of Directors, said the merger “brings together two strong operating platforms and creates an even stronger energy partner for Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Florida, with the scale and balance sheet to deliver the generation, transmission and grid investments our customers and economies need.”

Blue added the company is committed to retaining its teams in NextEra’s current headquarters of Juno Beach, Florida, and Dominion’s headquarters of Richmond. Both will serve as the new company’s dual headquarters, and the company is also keeping Dominion Energy South Carolina’s team and operational headquarters in Cayce.

CHARLOTTESVILLE, VA (CVILLE RIGHT NOW) – Multiple people were injured in a shooting incident near the entrance to 5th St. Station early Thursday morning, according to a Charlottesville Police Department social media post.

Just before 3 a.m., CPD announced that it had responded to a report of gunshots in the area of 5th St. SW and 5th St. Station Parkway, and found “several individuals have been injured.”

CPD said the public should expect a large police presence in the area.

No other information is available at this time.

title: Before approving $4.1B in new gas plants, Louisiana regulators should compare all options
description:
Why this matters Louisiana is experiencing one of the fastest periods of projected electricity demand growth in its history, driven by major industrial development.
The question is whether building two large gas plants now is the smartest way to deliver it.
Main reasons for concern First, Entergy has not demonstrated that Louisiana needs two new gas plants of this size.
Rather than asking which combination of resources would best meet future demand, Entergy largely compared different gas plant proposals with one another.
Better document and validate future electricity demand.
text:
Louisiana families and businesses deserve an electric system that is reliable, affordable and prepared for a rapidly changing future. They also deserve confidence that when utilities ask customers to pay billions of dollars for new power plants, those investments truly represent the best available option.

That is the central issue before the Louisiana Public Service Commission as it considers Entergy Louisiana’s request to build two new gas-fired power plants, Waterford 6 and Westlake, at an estimated cost of $4.1 billion. If approved, the projects could add nearly $15 a month to the average residential customer’s electric bill, with those costs ultimately recovered through customer rates.

In testimony filed on behalf of Environmental Defense Fund with the Louisiana Public Service Commission, energy planning expert Dr. Maria Roumpani concludes that Entergy has not demonstrated these plants are the lowest-cost, lowest-risk option for customers and that regulators should require a more rigorous evaluation before committing ratepayers to decades of costs.

Why this matters

Louisiana is experiencing one of the fastest periods of projected electricity demand growth in its history, driven by major industrial development. Meeting that demand will require significant investment, but regulators must ensure utilities invest in resources that are the lowest-cost, lowest-risk option and continue to deliver value for customers if conditions change, including load forecasts, commodity prices or policy constraints. The Commission must also evaluate these proposed plants in the context of Louisiana’s broader electricity system and the additional infrastructure and generation being planned to support future industrial growth, including data centers.

No one disputes that Louisiana needs reliable electricity to support a growing economy. The question is whether building two large gas plants now is the smartest way to deliver it. Once customers begin paying for these facilities, they could be responsible for their costs for decades, making today’s decisions critical for the future of customer bills, fuel reliance and grid reliability.

Main reasons for concern

First, Entergy has not demonstrated that Louisiana needs two new gas plants of this size. The testimony finds that the company’s demand forecasts rely heavily on projected large industrial customers without adequately accounting for uncertainty, changing customer plans or the possibility that some projects never materialize. For example, if one or more of the largest proposed industrial projects are delayed, reduced in scope or never built, one of the proposed generators may no longer be needed, yet customers could still be on the hook for its costs. The company also has not committed to retirement dates for aging power plants or completed analyses showing these new facilities are the best replacement option.

Second, Entergy did not adequately evaluate whether more incremental, cost-effective solutions could meet Louisiana’s growing electricity needs. Rather than asking which combination of resources would best meet future demand, Entergy largely compared different gas plant proposals with one another. That means alternatives like energy efficiency, demand response, solar power, battery storage, transmission upgrades and customer-owned energy resources were never fully evaluated alongside the new proposed fossil fuel plants.

Third, the economic case is weaker than it appears. Entergy’s economic analysis relies on assumptions that have not been sufficiently supported. The testimony finds that the projected benefits depend on assumptions about costs and future demand that may not hold. A modest increase in project costs or a likely shortfall in projected load growth could erase the projected savings altogether, leaving customers to bear the costs without receiving the promised benefits.

Finally, the proposal shifts substantial risk onto customers. If construction costs increase, fuel prices rise, or anticipated industrial demand fails to materialize, Louisiana ratepayers could remain responsible for paying for infrastructure they may not need. They would also face decades of exposure to natural gas price volatility because fuel costs are passed directly through on electric bills. Louisianans have already seen what those price swings can mean. Between October 2025 and February 2026, higher natural gas prices added about $16 to the monthly bill of a household using 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity.

A smarter path to affordable growth

As Louisiana plans for future electricity demand, EDF recommends evaluating more incremental, cost-effective solutions before committing customers to major new gas generation. That broader portfolio includes energy efficiency, demand response, customer-owned resources like rooftop solar and battery storage, transmission improvements, grid-enhancing technologies, and incremental utility-scale solar and battery storage. Together, these resources can improve reliability, meet growing demand and reduce the need for costly new power plants.

Together, these resources can improve reliability, meet growing demand and reduce the need for costly, customer-funded gas investments. With important regional transmission studies already underway, it’s worth waiting for more information and evaluating additional technologies that could improve reliability while reducing costs before committing customers to major new generating facilities.

What we recommend

EDF recommends that the Commission deny certification of both plants at this time. Before reconsidering the proposal, the Commission should require Entergy to:

Conduct a competitive all-source procurement.

Better document and validate future electricity demand.

Commit to retirement plans for existing generating units.

Demonstrate stronger use of energy efficiency and demand response through the Commission’s Proactive Utility Energy Needs process.

Evaluate transmission solutions and grid-enhancing technologies.

Analyze how customers would be affected if projected industrial growth does not occur.

Cap recoverable construction costs if any project ultimately moves forward.

Building the right grid for Louisianans

Louisiana’s economy is changing rapidly, and the electric grid must evolve with it. But planning for growth should not mean assuming that expensive investments automatically deliver better outcomes. Before asking customers to pay billions of dollars for new infrastructure, regulators should require utilities to demonstrate that those investments are the most cost-effective way to meet the state’s growing energy needs.

The Commission has an opportunity to require utilities to compare competing solutions, evaluate customer risks and pursue the most cost-effective path forward. With billions of customer dollars at stake, regulators should insist on a thorough evaluation of all viable alternatives before asking Louisianans to pay for decades to come.

text:
The Ford Fathom will be Ford Motor Co.'s first vehicle built on its new Universal Electric Vehicle Platform — a midsize truck that'll start at $28,350 plus $1,595 destination and come with a standard-range battery.

It's not a heritage name like Bronco or Maverick from deep in the 123-year-old Dearborn automaker's archives. But perhaps that's the point: Ford is doing something different with this all-electric truck. Executives say it needs to because it's struggled to win mass consumer acceptance of its first-generation EVs, and because Chinese automakers are expanding globally and rapidly with subsidized, low-cost electrified models customers want.

"That owner's motivations," Kay Hart, general manager of Model e, Ford's EV division, said in a blog post about the target buyer of the Fathom, "look a little different from the traditional truck customer's, and defining them guided every decision on the first vehicle built on our Universal EV Platform. Which meant the name had to do more than sound good. It had to capture a mindset, shifting the focus from specs to a spirit of adaptability."

Customers can sign up for Fathom updates, though pre-orders won't open until early next year. First deliveries are expected later in 2027. Timing for a true reveal hasn't been shared, though customers already have spotted camouflaged pre-production models on the roads.

Naming the vehicle was a nine-month process, Hart said. The company evaluated archived names: Galaxie, Taurus and Ranchero. Each, Hart said, came with a specific implication that might not fit with the new electric truck.

Two Ford copywriters separately brought Fathom forward among hundreds of other options. The naming team asked engineers to pick their favorites. One engineer who fit the vehicle's customer profile chose the winner before every meeting.

"Long before it meant depth, fathom described the span of a person's outstretched arms, roughly six feet," Hart said. "Sailors borrowed that span to measure water they couldn't see the bottom of. And eventually the word came to mean something else entirely: to understand a thing completely.

"A name about measuring what you can't see, that grew into a word about understanding," she continued. "For a truck that started with years of trying to understand a specific customer, that was the whole brief in six letters."

Executives have described the five-seater, midsize truck as similar in size to the Maverick, but having more passenger room than the latest Toyota RAV4, the most popular SUV in the United States. Ford has said it will have a 0-60 mph time on the truck to be as fast as the Mustang EcoBoost with more downforce. Like the Tesla Cybertruck, a 48-volt system will replace the traditional 12-volt battery that operates in-vehicle electronics.

Executives have said the pickup will support drivers who need 300 miles of range, similar to the EVs it already has offered but with a third of the battery cells. That, however, is not what the standard-range battery will offer, spokesperson Emma Bergg said. Fathom will have bidirectional power capability that can charge a home without a generator, though the company declined to share for what length of time. The full-size, first-gen electric F-150 Lightning could power a house for up to six days, according to the company.

Every Fathom will be capable of BlueCruise, launching with Ford’s Level 2+ hands-free highway driving assistant. The company has said the UEV platform also will support its launch of Level 3 eyes-off-the-road driving in 2028. Plus, a high-resolution touchscreen will have Apple Maps embedded, though consumers still will be able to use Android Auto and Apple CarPlay should they desire. The vehicle will have a digital key.

The truck will be a test for Ford. EV demand has missed expectations as consumers remain wary of their range, cost, speed to charge, and reliability. Mustang Mach-E's U.S. sales are down 50% through July. The elimination of federal tax credits hasn’t helped.

But global regulators are pushing for zero-emission vehicle adoption, and Chinese companies are expanding around the world with subsidized, affordable electrified vehicles. Ford CEO Jim Farley has called them an "existential threat."

The UEV is a simplified underpinning developed by Ford's California-based EV hardware and software "skunkworks" team, a group launched in 2022 at a tenth of the size of what Ford typically would hire for this kind of work. The intentional separation of the group was done for the sake of innovation outside of the legacy, bureaucratic system, executives have said.

Ford is investing $2 billion into Louisville Assembly for the UEV and is abandoning the traditional moving assembly line developed by founder Henry Ford in 1913. The new tree-shaped manufacturing design brings together three sub-assemblies and reduces parts by 20%. It will be Ford's most automated assembly plant, and the investment secures 2,200 hourly jobs at Louisville Assembly.

Large, single-piece aluminum unicastings replace dozens of smaller parts so the front and rear of the vehicle can be assembled separately. They then combine with the structural battery, which is assembled independently with seats, consoles and carpeting.

The midsize truck will use batteries from the $3 billion BlueOval Battery Park Michigan in Marshall that began pre-production manufacturing earlier this year. It's producing lithium-iron-phosphate batteries, which don't use cobalt or nickel, making them less expensive than traditional EV batteries. They also are less likely to catch fire, though they also are less energy dense. The technology is licensed from China's Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. Ford expects to be the first manufacturer of LFP batteries for automobiles in the United States.

"We wanted to choose a name," Hart said, "to give the vehicle personality, a soul, and make it a character in our customer’s life."
