name: American Energy
title: Building at the Speed of AI: Data Centers, Expedited Permitting, and Who Bears the Burden
authors: Harvard Law Review, Elizabeth Jordan, Alex Zhao, Elena Chachko
description:
“xAI is scaling at an immeasurable pace—we are building our third massive data center in the greater Memphis area….
Environmental Impacts The AI data center buildout produces four core environmental burdens: noise, water consumption, land use, and air pollution.
Second Trump Administration In July 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14,318, Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure.
The AI Action Plan goes further, recommending expanded use of FAST-41 for all eligible data center and data center energy projects.
When those procedures are weakened in the name of speed, the buildout of AI data centers does more than transform the grid.
text:
“xAI is scaling at an immeasurable pace—we are building our third massive data center in the greater Memphis area…. This is insane execution speed by xAI and the state of Mississippi. We are grateful to Governor Reeves for his support of building xAI at warp speed.”—Elon Musk, xAI CEO

“Breathing has become more difficult than it should ever be. This is not an inconvenience—this is a health crisis inside my own home…. No parents should have to watch their child struggle to breathe and wonder if the air around them is the cause.”—Chestela Farmer, Southaven resident

In August 2025, xAI—Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company—began installing gas turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, to help power its Colossus II data center across the state line in Tennessee. These turbines were installed without permits to construct or operate and without public notice to the surrounding community, which is approximately 40% Black. Nearby residents compared the noise to “roaring jet engines” that made sleep impossible. For one asthmatic resident, the pollution became so severe that she was forced to leave the home that had been in her family for generations. The turbines emit nitrogen oxides, fine particulate matter, and formaldehyde into a county that already received an “F” for ozone from the American Lung Association. A health-impact study estimated annual public health damages of $30–44 million across North Mississippi and West Tennessee. Nevertheless, the Mississippi Environmental Quality Permit Board recently approved xAI’s request to install forty-one permanent gas turbines in Southaven, replacing the twenty-seven temporary turbines. The NAACP and NAACP Mississippi State Conference later sued xAI and its subsidiary over the twenty-seven temporary turbines, alleging violations of the Clean Air Act, 42 U.S.C. § 7604.

Southaven is part of a broader pattern. The United States is in the midst of a rapid AI data center buildout, driven by surging demand for computing power and by competition to secure land, electricity, and grid access on compressed timelines. Where grid capacity cannot be delivered quickly enough, developers have turned to on-site combustion generation as a stopgap. At the same time, the federal government has increasingly treated AI infrastructure as a national economic and strategic priority and has pursued a permitting agenda to speed up the review and approval of data centers and their associated energy systems. Some legal tools used to fast-track AI infrastructure predate the second Trump Administration; others have been redirected or expanded for the present moment. Their cumulative effect is to shorten the period in which projects are publicly scrutinized and to reduce the occasions on which environmental review occurs before construction begins. Southaven illustrates how AI infrastructure development can proceed on accelerated timelines while environmental burdens fall on nearby communities with little meaningful opportunity for input.

This Essay argues that the convergence of AI data center expansion and federal permitting acceleration is producing a governance gap—a mismatch between the national push to build AI infrastructure quickly and the weakening of the procedures through which affected communities can identify, contest, and mitigate its local burdens. The benefits of speed are framed in national terms: U.S. leadership in the AI sector, economic growth, and strategic advantage. The burdens, by contrast, are often experienced locally in the form of increased water consumption, land use, noise, and air pollution. When environmental review is narrowed or accelerated, those burdens do not disappear. They become less visible before construction begins and are more easily shifted onto the communities with the least power to resist them.

Part I describes the AI data center boom and its environmental footprint, including the scale and speed of the buildout, and the environmental and environmental justice implications of current siting patterns. Part II analyzes the legal tools the second Trump Administration has deployed to accelerate the construction of AI infrastructure. Part III examines Savannah River Site as a case study of what that agenda looks like on federal land already shaped by industrial contamination.

I. The AI Data Center Boom and Its Environmental Footprint

A. Scale, Speed, and Siting

A data center is a physical facility that houses the servers, storage systems, and network equipment needed to process and transmit large volumes of data. For much of the internet era, data centers were electricity-intensive but manageable: A conventional server rack typically used roughly 5–15 kilowatts (kW) of power while operating. AI-focused configurations demand power at a different order of magnitude because training and running large models rely on graphics processing units operating near full capacity for extended periods, increasing both electricity and cooling needs. NVIDIA, whose chips power much of modern AI computing, has projected that its next-generation system could require roughly 600 kW per rack by 2027, an energy demand comparable to that of 500 homes. Global projections estimate data center electricity demand could rise by about 50% by 2027 and as much as 165% by 2030, relative to 2023 levels. In terms of electricity consumption and on-site generation needs, an AI data center increasingly resembles an industrial plant more than the technology infrastructure that preceded it. And anticipated growth in energy demands is already reshaping investment and construction. By the end of 2024, computing capacity under construction in North America reached a record 6,350 megawatts, more than double the prior year’s figure.

Speed is as important as scale. The central obstacle to data center development is often not capital or land, but “time to power”: the interval between selecting a site and the delivery of electricity at the required scale. Data centers can often be built within 18 to 24 months, while the high-voltage transmission upgrades needed to deliver electricity at that scale may take 7–10 years to plan, approve, and construct. As a result, developers facing an “urgent need for speed to market” have increasingly deployed on-site combustion turbines as “bridging solution[s] ” while awaiting permanent grid connections.

That solution imposes local costs. On-site combustion concentrates hazardous air pollutants near the facility, transforming what might otherwise be diffuse emissions into a localized air-quality problem. And the geography of the buildout is not accidental. Siting decisions involve a multi-factor calculation, including land costs, zoning, water access, available electrical capacity, and the speed with which power can be delivered. Large industrial parcels are more readily available in areas with lower land values and where prior industrial use has already shaped surrounding development. Faster approvals tend to correlate with jurisdictions willing to offer incentives and prioritize rapid construction. Northern Virginia illustrates the cumulative effects of clustering: It accounts for roughly one quarter of U.S. operational data center capacity, and its data centers are projected to consume nearly 50% of all electricity produced in the state by 2030. Data centers thus do not simply go where land is cheap, but where power can be secured quickly and delay is least likely—producing siting patterns with predictably unequal distributional consequences.

B. Environmental Impacts

The AI data center buildout produces four core environmental burdens: noise, water consumption, land use, and air pollution.

Noise is often the most immediate burden experienced by nearby residents. Smaller diesel generators can reach roughly 85 decibels—levels associated with hearing damage over sustained exposure—and larger industrial units can approach 100 decibels, comparable to a continuous motorcycle engine or jackhammer. Residents near clustered data centers in Loudoun County, Virginia, have described sleep disruption, headaches, and a persistent decline in quality of life.

Data centers’ water demands also create immediate local impacts. About one-fifth of U.S. data centers rely on water from stressed watersheds, creating competition over scarce municipal resources. High-density computing generates heat that must be continuously removed, and many facilities rely on cooling towers that consume water through both evaporation and “blowdown,” the flushing needed to remove mineral scale. Beyond on-site cooling, data centers also drive upstream water consumption at the thermoelectric power plants that supply their electricity, which are already among the largest users of freshwater in the United States. The Congressional Research Service estimates that a 100-megawatt data center could directly consume water at a rate equivalent to roughly 2,600 households—or as many as 6,500 households once indirect upstream consumption is included.

Land conversion is the next visible burden, as AI computing is pushing facilities toward larger campus-style developments. The average data center campus in 2024 covered approximately 224 acres, a 144% increase from two years earlier. Land conversion at that scale brings familiar industrial consequences, including increased runoff and loss of land otherwise available for farming, housing, or habitat.

The air quality consequences of data center buildout operate both upstream and locally. An analysis of 2,132 U.S. data centers estimated that 56% of data center electricity came from fossil fuels, which create emissions at the grid level. And on-site combustion turbines emit nitrogen oxides, particulate matter, and other hazardous air pollutants linked to asthma, respiratory and cardiovascular disease, and cancer. Research on Northern Virginia data centers found that cumulative neighborhood exposure to hazardous air pollutants near some clusters was already comparable to, and in some cases exceeded, exposure from a major oil- and natural-gas-fired power plant. Data center demand has also prolonged the operation of coal plants that might otherwise have retired, leaving nearby communities exposed to continued pollution.

C. Environmental Justice

Pollution often follows the “path of least political resistance,” and the AI data center buildout is no exception. The siting calculus described above favors locations where land is inexpensive, infrastructure can be delivered quickly, and political resistance is least likely to delay construction. Environmental justice scholarship has long explained why those criteria correlate with race and income: Property values are often depressed near existing or anticipated industrial uses; local governments compete for tax base and investment; and communities with fewer resources face higher barriers to sustained participation in zoning and permitting processes.

Data center expansion is reproducing that pattern at scale. One review of roughly 700 data centers found that nearly half are located in census tracts with above-median environmental burdens. Many are also located in tracts with above-median social vulnerability indicators, including poverty and lower educational attainment. A separate study by the Environmental Data and Governance Initiative found that communities of color disproportionately live within one mile of EPA-regulated data centers and are exposed to levels of nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter above the national median. Those findings suggest that data centers are deepening broader patterns of inequality that environmental justice law has long struggled to confront.

The distributional problem is compounded by the mismatch between the benefits cited to justify these projects and the burdens they impose. Data centers can generate substantial short-term construction activity and, in some jurisdictions, significant tax revenue. But permanent employment is often modest relative to a facility’s footprint and resource demand—even the largest facilities may employ fewer than 150 permanent workers, and sometimes as few as 25. Tax revenues accrue to the host jurisdiction, while the environmental impacts can extend beyond municipal boundaries to neighboring communities that receive no comparable fiscal benefit and often have little voice in the siting process. The result is a familiar pattern in environmental justice conflicts: Localized and durable burdens are justified by economic gains that are more attenuated, unevenly distributed, and often overstated.

These dynamics have not gone uncontested. Civil rights groups have increasingly identified AI data centers as “one of the nation’s fastest-expanding environmental justice threats,” and the NAACP developed a community toolkit for residents confronting proposed facilities. These are also the kinds of inequities that federal environmental justice policy was designed to surface. Executive Order 12,898, signed by President Clinton in 1994, directed federal agencies to embed environmental justice within their missions by identifying health or environmental harms that fall disproportionately on minority and low-income communities. Under the second Trump Administration, that framework has been significantly weakened. Executive Order 14,173 rescinded Executive Order 12,898; the EPA has dismantled or restructured core environmental justice functions, including the Office of Environmental Justice; and EJScreen, the EPA’s primary environmental justice mapping tool, was taken offline. Those rollbacks remove both the legal directives and analytical tools that agencies and affected communities relied on to identify environmental burdens at the front end of permitting decisions.

This problem is further amplified by the rapid AI infrastructure buildout and broader administrative efforts to streamline the review processes through which disparate impacts might otherwise be identified. Part II turns to that expedited permitting architecture.

II. Permitting Acceleration Under the Second Trump Administration

The second Trump Administration’s data center permitting agenda emerged from an existing bipartisan framework for accelerating federal infrastructure review. The Administration applies that framework to AI infrastructure development and narrows the occasions for project-specific environmental review before construction begins.

Although many data centers are permitted principally under state and local land-use law, federal law is implicated whenever a project depends on federally regulated energy infrastructure, including certain generation facilities, transmission lines, interstate pipelines, or projects sited on federal lands or waters. The campuses themselves must also comply with federal environmental statutes, and federal action may trigger review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). Given the scale of new power generation required to serve the AI buildout, the federal nexus reaches a growing share of the buildout’s most consequential environmental decisions.

A. Bipartisan Origins

The second Trump Administration inherited a bipartisan permitting-acceleration framework. FAST-41, enacted in 2015 as Title 41 of the Fixing America’s Surface Transportation Act, created the Federal Permitting Improvement Steering Council and the Permitting Dashboard to make federal infrastructure review more coordinated, deadline-driven, and transparent. Importantly, FAST-41 was designed as procedural reform, not substantive deregulation: Its purpose was to reduce duplication, improve interagency coordination, and impose greater discipline on the timing of federal review, while leaving underlying environmental statutes in place.

Congress later strengthened and expanded that framework. In 2021, the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act—one of the Biden Administration’s signature legislative achievements—made the Permitting Council permanent. In 2022, Congress expanded FAST-41 eligibility to six additional technology-related sectors, including semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and high-performance computing. By the time the second Trump Administration began promoting rapid data center buildout, the basic machinery for accelerated review was already in place.

What changed was the object and rationale of acceleration. The Biden Administration deployed these tools primarily to support a green energy transition and broader infrastructure delivery, while preserving public participation through workshops, meetings, and opportunities for written comment. The bipartisan framework was presented as a way to reconcile speed with transparency, not as a mechanism to strip away environmental review.

The second Trump Administration, however, retained that streamlining toolkit and redirected it toward a different substantive objective: the rapid buildout of AI data centers and the energy infrastructure required to serve them.

B. Second Trump Administration

In July 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14,318, Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure. Issued alongside Winning the Race, which the Administration billed as an “AI action plan,” the order declares it federal policy to facilitate the “rapid and efficient buildout” of data centers and the “infrastructure that powers them.” Crucially, the order treats a data center not as a stand-alone building, but rather as part of an integrated system, including transmission lines, natural gas pipelines, substations, switchgear, and other energy equipment. That framing places the full physical apparatus of the AI buildout within the same acceleration agenda.

The order works through three mechanisms. First, it removes more projects from NEPA review altogether. It expands the use of categorical exclusions under NEPA, which allow agencies to bypass NEPA analysis for categories of actions that typically have little or no substantial environmental impacts. It also narrows what counts as a “major Federal action” triggering NEPA review by presuming that federal financial assistance of less than 50% of total project costs does not constitute substantial federal control. The cumulative effect is to shrink the number of AI projects that receive project-specific NEPA review. These mechanisms also operate in a NEPA environment already challenged by separate Trump Administration action rolling back the federal regulations that once governed NEPA implementation across agencies.

Second, the order redirects AI infrastructure toward federal land. It directs the Departments of the Interior and Energy to identify suitable sites for data center development and associated power generation. The Department of Energy quickly identified four sites: Idaho National Laboratory, Oak Ridge Reservation, Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant, and Savannah River Site. The order pairs that siting initiative with more programmatic review mechanisms—including programmatic Endangered Species Act consultation and a directive that the Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works review existing nationwide permits under Clean Water Act section 404 and Rivers and Harbors Act section 10—moving review from individualized, site-specific processes toward more generalized forms of approval.

Finally, the order channels qualifying projects through FAST-41. It authorizes the Permitting Council to designate qualifying projects as transparency projects and publish them on the Permitting Dashboard with expedited review schedules. The AI Action Plan goes further, recommending expanded use of FAST-41 for all eligible data center and data center energy projects. The order also directs the EPA to develop or modify regulations under the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act, and other statutes to expedite permitting. Together, these measures do not just accelerate timelines; they move qualifying projects into broader authorization pathways with less dependence on project-by-project review.

C. Effects of Expedited Permitting

Taken together, the Administration’s expedited permitting program changes the point at which environmental harms become visible. NEPA requires agencies to identify environmental effects before federal commitments harden, and public participation gives affected communities notice, access to information, an opportunity to supply local evidence, and a basis for seeking mitigation. Disclosure itself can alter outcomes even without litigation, because agencies and developers with more complete information may revise siting decisions, adopt mitigation measures, or modify project design before construction begins.

A permitting regime that relies more heavily on exclusions, programmatic review, and generalized approvals makes cumulative environmental burdens harder to scrutinize on a project-specific basis. That dynamic is particularly consequential for AI infrastructure, because the parts of the buildout where federal review applies are also the parts that generate heavy environmental burdens. The federal nexus often attaches to associated generation, transmission, pipelines, federal lands, and other supporting infrastructure rather than to the data center shell alone. As Part I described, those are also the parts of the buildout likely to produce cumulative regional impacts, including added air emissions, water demand, noise, land conversion, and intensified industrial use. Thus, when review is shortened, generalized, or bypassed, environmental burdens are less likely to surface at a stage when they can still influence siting, design, or permit conditions.

The distributive consequences are equally significant. The benefits of accelerated permitting are framed at the national level, in terms of industrial policy, AI leadership, and rapid infrastructure deployment. But the burdens are borne locally, by the communities that host the supporting energy infrastructure, absorb the pollution and water demand, or live near federal industrial lands newly opened to redevelopment. As a result, expedited permitting narrows the time available for those communities to identify harms, demand disclosure, and press for project-specific mitigation.

III. Case Study: Savannah River

The Savannah River Site is a 310-square-mile Department of Energy reservation spanning Aiken, Barnwell, and Allendale Counties in South Carolina, created in the early 1950s for tritium and plutonium production. The EPA placed the site on the National Priorities List1 of contaminated sites in 1989, and it continues to identify radioactive contaminants, including cesium-137, in the sediment and groundwater. The Savannah River borders the site on the west, so additional industrial activity carries consequences not only for conditions inside the reservation but also for surrounding and downstream communities, especially where new construction may disturb contaminated soil, groundwater, or active cleanup areas.

The federal government has nevertheless moved to position Savannah River as part of the national AI buildout. DOE has solicited proposals to build AI infrastructure on DOE lands, citing their access to power, secure locations, support for permitting, and “supportive communities,” and named Savannah River one of four sites to move forward with private-sector AI data center and energy generation projects.

Acceleration works at Savannah River by moving the most consequential land-use decision upstream. DOE first determined the site to be suitable for rapid AI development; the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) then identified 10 tracts totaling 3,103 acres and issued a request for proposals to private-sector partners interested in leasing the land. By the time project-specific review begins, the federal government will have already selected the site, defined the available acreage, and opened the land to competitive private proposals. The practical effect is to harden the siting decision before the public can test, in any concrete way, whether a new AI campus and its associated energy infrastructure belong on a still-contaminated federal reservation.

That concern is not abstract. In 2024, the U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina held that DOE and NNSA had violated NEPA by failing to properly consider alternatives before proceeding with their plan to produce plutonium pits at Savannah River Site. The court concluded that the agencies’ plans had changed sufficiently to require renewed analysis of alternatives, including site alternatives that NNSA had not considered. The resulting settlement enjoined certain construction activities and the introduction of any nuclear materials at Savannah River until completion of a nationwide programmatic environmental impact statement. Against that backdrop, the AI data center solicitation places a new industrial project on the same reservation where a court had just found that more environmental review was required, not less.

Thus, a contaminated site still undergoing cleanup and recently the subject of NEPA litigation has been designated for AI development through a process that prioritizes site selection and commercial solicitation over project-specific analysis. The consequence is not just administrative speed; it is a narrower opportunity for affected communities to insist that existing burdens be counted before new ones are added.

The surrounding communities make the environmental justice stakes concrete. Allendale County is approximately 71% Black with a poverty rate above 30%; Barnwell County is approximately 43% Black; and Aiken County is approximately 25% Black. New industrial development at Savannah River would compound broader patterns in which communities of color and low-income communities disproportionately bear pollution, contamination, and exclusion from meaningful participation in land-use decisions. The plaintiffs in the recent Savannah River NEPA litigation likewise included the Gullah/Geechee Sea Island Coalition, underscoring that the communities affected by federal land-use decisions at the site extend beyond those living immediately adjacent to the reservation.

Conclusion

The problem this Essay identifies is ultimately one of governance. As AI infrastructure expands, the law is increasingly being used to accelerate projects before affected communities have a meaningful chance to understand, contest, or shape them. Environmental law matters not because it guarantees a particular outcome, but because it preserves the procedures through which harms are made visible, tradeoffs are examined, and decision-makers are forced to reckon with local consequences. When those procedures are weakened in the name of speed, the buildout of AI data centers does more than transform the grid. It reveals a deeper choice about whose environments are treated as expendable in the race to build the future.

Charlotte City Council is preparing to consider new regulations governing e-bikes and similar vehicles after concerns from police and city leaders about how some of the vehicles are classified and used.

At the City Council Transportation Committee meeting Monday, CMPD Capt. Jeremiah Blow said many vehicles commonly referred to as e-bikes are more accurately described as motorcycles.

“They're referred to as e-bikes, but they're motorcycles,” Blow said. “There's no pedals, there's no part of it that's a bicycle.”

Blow cited a recent incident involving a young rider.

“Two weekends ago, we got a 12-year-old at 1 a.m. on one of these,” he said. “We called his parents and they're like, 'He's just on his e-bike.'”

City Council member Dante Anderson, who chairs the Transportation Committee, said he wants staff to develop recommendations for potential ordinance changes.

“I'd love for us to have a proposal around what our potential modifications of an ordinance would look like, including those definitions of a motorbike and other vehicles,” Anderson said.

No proposed ordinance changes were discussed during the meeting.

name: Texas American Energy
title: Data centers use lots of water and power, but Texas officials don't know exactly how much
authors: Kailey Hunt, Katy McAfee, Leigh Walden, www.houstonpublicmedia.org, kailey-hunt-kut, katy-mcafee-kut, leigh-walden-kut
description:
Data centers need a lot of power to operate, and, depending on how they’re cooled, a lot of water too.
A recent poll by Gallup News found that seven in 10 Americans oppose local construction of AI data centers.
After nearly eight hours of public comment, the council voted to deny the request for rezoning — effectively blocking the data center.
Most data centers either use air or water, but Cook said because it’s so hot in Texas, water is the preferred method.
Connecting to the grid Texas has had more success at figuring out how much electricity data centers use.
text:
The high transmission line that bisects Torrie Martin’s ranch hums subtly. Occasionally the frequency changes to a droning buzz that ends in a pop.

“ You can actually hear the power plant right now,” Martin said. “It’s been pretty loud the last few years.”

The Vistra Hays Power Plant is directly across the street from Martin’s property. It generates around 990 megawatts of power, enough to power 250,000 homes. This facility is considerably larger than Austin’s biggest power plant — Sand Hill Energy Center — which generates 595 megawatts.

The proximity to the power station makes Martin’s neighborhood a desirable place to build data centers.

Data centers need a lot of power to operate, and, depending on how they’re cooled, a lot of water too. As more and more data center developers submit proposals to build in Texas, questions about how they’ll impact Texas’ grid and contribute to drought conditions across the state are widespread.

So much so, that Gov. Greg Abbott effectively ordered a pause on all data center projects looking to connect to the grid until officials get a better grasp on the amount of resources they will use.

For Martin, these concerns aren’t just hypothetical. A year ago, a developer approached the city of San Marcos with a request to build a data center behind her ranch. She and many other residents of the city opposed it.

“ I love San Marcos,” Martin said. “This is my home, and so I’m just standing up for it.”

Martin grew up on the ranch in Hays County where she now tends to a herd of horses. She said, in this rural part of the county, power and water outages aren’t uncommon.

“We do have brownouts kind of regularly and we get our water shut off at least twice a month, usually [for] two or three hours, sometimes more,” Martin said.

A brownout is a reduction in power availability. It can cause lights to flicker and appliances like washing machines or microwaves to run sluggishly or make weird noises. Repetitive brownouts put extra strain on machines and can shorten their lifespan.

Martin attributes these outages to new development happening in her neighborhood. She thinks the county is failing to keep up with road maintenance and keeping development in check.

“ [The county’s] unable to give us water and power now,” Martin said, staring at the site of the proposed data center. “How are [they] gonna keep up with this?”

Water use and utility costs are often major concerns when a new data center is proposed. A recent poll by Gallup News found that seven in 10 Americans oppose local construction of AI data centers. Half of those opposed cited water and power use as their primary reason.

In February, the San Marcos City Council voted on a request for rezoning the property behind Martin’s ranch. Approving the request would have cleared the way for the data center developer eyeing the land.

Hundreds of people attended the meeting, which stretched into the early hours of the next day. Speakers were overwhelmingly opposed to the idea of data center development in the area.

After nearly eight hours of public comment, the council voted to deny the request for rezoning — effectively blocking the data center.

At the meeting, speakers shared their worries about power costs, loss of green spaces and the increased use of artificial intelligence in society.

But the most prominent concern for residents was about water.

The San Marcos River is a huge part of the town’s identity, and some speakers wanted to know how the council was going to protect it. But it can be hard for local governments to know just how much water a data center will use.

Margaret Cook, the vice president of water and community resilience for the Houston Advanced Research Center, said there is an answer to how much water data centers are using.

Just not a satisfying one.

“The clear answer to the general question is it depends,” she said.

Cook said it depends primarily on two things: how big a data center is and what cooling technology it uses.

Small-to-mid-sized data centers don’t necessarily have to use more water than a large subdivision or golf course. All the data centers in Texas today use less than 1% of the state’s water. For reference, Texas’ manufacturing industry uses 7%.

That’s rapidly changing as tech companies invest in AI data centers, which require more space, power and water to operate. Cook said by 2030, data centers could collectively consume anywhere between 29 and 161 billion gallons of water a year — accounting for 0.5% to nearly 3% of the state’s total water use.

But Cook said these are rough estimates. How much water a data center actually consumes depends on what system it uses to cool its servers. Most data centers either use air or water, but Cook said because it’s so hot in Texas, water is the preferred method.

“Water is much more efficient at cooling than air is,” Cook said. “That’s why on a hot day you’d probably rather jump in a pool than stand under a tree and try to get the airflow.”

Many data centers rely on what’s called evaporative cooling — a process that uses water to absorb heat from the servers.

Cook said evaporative cooling can be an energy efficient way of cooling a data center.

But even though some of the water can be reused, new water is needed regularly to replace the water that evaporates. Closed loop systems are better, but even those come with trade-offs, Cook said.

In a closed loop, a coolant gets moved through a data center, pulling heat off of servers. As the fluid moves through the system, it gets hotter and hotter — and something else needs to cool it back down.

“Use your body as an example: you can’t cool down unless something takes heat off of you,” Cook said. “So you’re going to sweat, and ... the air is going to pull the sweat off of you ... and then your skin and your blood cool down, and that’s a closed loop system.”

Just like how your body cools itself, some data centers use an air chiller to cool down that fluid, which can limit a data center’s overall water usage to things like landscaping and flushing toilets.

Some data centers use water to cool down that fluid. Cook said in that case, a closed loop system can “still be very water intensive.” According to estimates from her team, data centers that use water to chill that coolant fluid could use up to half a billion gallons a year.

Not even state regulators know for certain how much water most data centers are using — and they have tried asking.

Earlier this year, the Public Utility Commission of Texas sent out a survey to collect information about water and energy usage among data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities. Less than a third of the state’s 341 data centers responded to the survey.

Connecting to the grid

Texas has had more success at figuring out how much electricity data centers use.

There are 248 known data centers planned for the state, according to an analysis from The Texas Tribune. They are reported to use anywhere from 5 megawatts to 11,000 megawatts of power when operating at full capacity, according to the same analysis.

For reference, 1 megawatt is equivalent to the amount of electricity it takes to power 200 homes.

The state’s power grid operator, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), has historically made it easy for new data centers to get up and running as long as the grid has enough electricity available. It would evaluate projects on an individual case-by-case basis as requests for electricity came in.

But doing that has become increasingly difficult as more and more developers look to build data centers and connect to the state’s grid.

As of April, ERCOT had requests for more than 400,000 megawatts of electricity from the grid. Nearly 89% of those requests came from data center developers, according to the organization.

“All of that is definitely not going to come online, but the question is, well, how much of it will?” Brian Korgel, the director of the Energy Institute at University of Texas at Austin, said.

That uncertainty is a cause for concern for some people.

ERCOT, which is overseen by the PUC and the Texas Legislature, knows it needs to expand the state’s power grid to account for all these new connection requests. But it doesn’t know by how much, especially considering that large power users, such as data centers, often pop up in clusters.

“You’re not just going to add one new data center here, you’re probably going to add five or six in that location,” Korgel said. “So [ERCOT is] moving to a new way of reviewing those projects. They’re calling it a ‘batch process’ where they will review like a cluster of proposed data centers in a geographical region.”

ERCOT approved this “batch process” in June and stopped evaluating requests on a project by project basis.

“Texas is experiencing an energy transformation unlike anything we have seen before,” ERCOT President and CEO Pablo Vegas said at the time.

“This new process represents a fundamental shift in how ERCOT manages the significant growth of large load interconnection, providing a structured, transparent path forward that protects reliability for Texans while supporting the state’s continued economic growth.”

That same month Gov. Greg Abbott directed ERCOT and the PUC to require data centers to fully fund the costs of the electric infrastructure they need to operate, so as not to pass on the costs to homeowners.

The PUC responded to the governor in July, saying it was working on enforcing this requirement. It also put together a list of suggestions for state lawmakers to tackle during their next legislative session, which starts in January. One suggestion is to require data centers to register with the PUC so the state has accurate information about their electricity and water use.

In August, Abbott also directed the agencies to audit all data centers advancing through ERCOT’s interconnection process to make sure they are complying with the requirement. No data center project was to move forward until the audit was completed, he said.

Ultimately, however, Korgel said he believes people should be less concerned about the reliability of the state’s power grid and more concerned about whether or not communities are willing to welcome so many data centers to the state.

“It’s not really ‘can the grid — is the grid going to break’ or whatever. Because ERCOT and the utilities are not going to let the grid break,” he said. “What’s going to happen is that data centers won’t get built and things like that. So the big question is ‘can Texas keep up with this economic development or promise of economic development?”

What does this mean for the average customer?

Besides grid concerns, people are worried about how data centers might further drive up electricity costs.

“Retail electric prices have gone up 20 to 25% since 2020. In Texas alone, they’ve gone up 29%,” Alison Silverstein, a former state and federal energy regulator, said.

Aging infrastructure, supply chain issues and high demand projects — like data centers — are all contributing to increased energy costs. High demand projects require more high-voltage transmission lines and power plants to operate.

”Those cost increases within ERCOT for transmission are assigned across every retail customer in Texas, so there is no escaping those,” Silverstein said.

Some developers have started including power generation as part of their data center proposals. Silverstein explained that won’t necessarily bring costs down.

“Even if they are buying and building all these energy resources…inside the fence of the facility… they are still increasing costs for everybody,” Silverstein said.

Demand for equipment like gas turbines and transformers has gone up since 2022. The wait time to receive a new turbine can be up to seven years, according to an analysis from S&P Global.

The short supply has resulted in steep competition for these resources, but Silverstein said data centers are mostly “cost indifferent,” meaning they can spend more and out-bid competitors. Which also means sellers can bump up the price.

This cost indifference extends past equipment.

“ Data centers are paying way more than you or I or a local utility could to hire electricians and plumbers and carpenters,” Silverstein said. “[That] affects everything we do in our community in terms of building and fixing stuff.”

text:
The Critical Minerals (CM) Accelerator is a £25 million grant funding scheme, aimed at unlocking the commercialisation of innovation through the scaling up of innovative solutions for critical minerals, spanning extraction, processing and recycling and building on the UK’s strengths.

Funding will support projects across the UK for all minerals on the UK 2024 Criticality Assessment published as well as Critical Minerals technical annex by 2035. Successful projects should increase the security of supply of minerals, boost resilience, create jobs and growth. The CM Accelerator is part of the £50 million UK Critical Mineral Programme.

The CM Accelerator is focused on companies and projects at technology readiness levels (TRL) 6 to 8 which are close to commercialisation and that face significant barriers in proving unit economics and de-risking their processes. Projects supported will be at the pilot to pre-commercial or demonstrator to commercialisation stage of development.

The £25 million CM Accelerator grant scheme will support multiple projects through a competitive process. Our expectation is that all approved grants will sit within a range of £150,000 to £3 million. All projects funded under this scheme are expected to be delivered by March 2030.

What the Critical Minerals Accelerator will do

The overarching objective of the CM Accelerator is to support research and development innovation (typically projects at minimum technology readiness level 6 to 8) in extraction, midstream processing and recycling (which currently do not qualify or are unable to attract support from public finance institutions and private finance) to increase validation, commercialisation prospects and scale up in the UK. This objective is underpinned by 3 strategic priorities:

Driving economic growth

support high-value manufacturing and growth-driving sectors, including clean energy, advanced manufacturing, and defence

support job creation, skills development, and regional economic growth

catalyse private sector investment and expansion across UK critical minerals value chains

2․ Strengthening economic security

reduce vulnerabilities associated with concentrated global supply chains

build sovereign capability in a strategically critical sector

improve resilience against supply disruptions and external economic pressures

3․ Building domestic resilience

reduce reliance on overseas supply chains for critical minerals

develop domestic capability across critical minerals value chains

establish a sustainable ecosystem, spanning production, skills and innovation

promote a circular materials economy by enabling recycling, recovery, and reuse of critical minerals across products’ lifecycles

Funding available

The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) will provide up to £25 million to a range of projects that best meet the Programme’s objectives. The funded projects must take place in the UK and deliver grant-funded activity by 31 March 2030.

Applicants should request only the minimum amount of funding required to deliver their proposal and will need to demonstrate value for money as part of the assessment process.

Who can apply

The lead applicant must be a UK registered business with operations based in the UK and be committed to developing innovation and follow-on commercial activity within the UK.

Charities, not-for-profits, universities/academic institutions, research and technology organisations (RTOs) and public sector organisations may be included in the project team but not lead a project.

How to apply

Application stage

The competition will begin with an 8 week application window. After this, BIST will shortlist applicants ahead of the interview stage.

The purpose of the application stage is to identify applicants who demonstrate a credible and relevant proposal aligned with the objectives of the Critical Minerals Accelerator. It will ensure that only those applicants with a sufficiently strong strategic fit, capability, and delivery potential are invited to progress to an interview.

You can submit your application on the Grants Hub.

Interview stage

This stage is only open to applicants successful at application stage.

The interview stage is designed to test:

the quality of the management team

the credibility of delivery plans

strategic fit to the scheme

the depth of commercial understanding.

application stage opens – 5 August 2026

application stage closes – 30 September 2026

notification of application stage outcome – October 2026

interview stage – October/November 2026

funding decision – November/December 2026

grant funding period ends – 31 March 2030

How this fits within the Critical Minerals Programme

In 2025, the UK government published Vision 2035: Critical Minerals Strategy, building on the ambitions set out in the UK’s Modern Industrial Strategy. Together, these strategies recognise the essential role that critical minerals play in enabling growth across key sectors of the economy, including clean energy, advanced manufacturing, and defence.

The Critical Minerals Strategy sets out a long-term vision to strengthen the UK’s access to these materials, in the context of increasing global demand, supply chain concentration, and geopolitical risk. A central ambition of the strategy is to grow a resilient domestic supply chain, supporting both economic growth and economic security.

Help and guidance

More information about the competition can be found in the Critical Minerals Accelerator scheme guidance document.

description:

Even Tesla’s most affordable EV, the Model 3 (RWD), costs $36,990, while the actual take-home cost is slightly higher.

text:
This is not the first time I’ve watched European or Chinese car shoppers, for that matter, get a chance to buy genuinely affordable EVs. Meanwhile, American buyers keep hearing and talking about higher starting prices and fewer features on the entry-level trim.

Geely’s new compact electric hatchback costs 19,490 EUR in Belgium, or roughly $22,490, and is yet another example of the same. While the entry price is only available for a limited time, I’m talking about the overall package the automaker is offering.

So what exactly did Geely launch?

This Geely E2 is sold in China as the Geely Xingyuan, and for those catching up, it was the country’s best-selling car in all of 2025. After moving 465,000 units that year, it’s already leading sales again through the first half of 2026.

Recommended Videos

And while you already know the price, you deserve to know what all the Geely E2 offers in Europe. The list includes a 35 kWh battery pack on the base Pro trim, which provides a claimed WLTP range of 156 miles. Buyers also get seven airbags, a 14.6-inch infotainment screen, a 375-liter trunk, and a 70-liter frunk.

There’s a bigger 47 kWh battery pack as well, which stretches the claimed range up to 214 miles. As seen in the pictures, the EV carries a minimal yet functional look, with sleek headlights up front, regular door handles and stylized rims on the side, and a simple rear profile with only the useful elements in place.

Inside, it has enough space to comfortably seat four people. You could drive it to your office or drop off your kids at college, while saving thousands of dollars that otherwise go into getting a more expensive everyday EV. However, Geely has no plans to launch the E2 in the US.

Meanwhile, what does $22,000 actually buy you in America?

Nothing that even comes close. America’s cheapest EV right now is the revived Chevrolet Bolt at $28,995, followed by the Nissan Leaf around $31,535 and the Hyundai Kona Electric at $34,470. Even Tesla’s most affordable EV, the Model 3 (RWD), costs $36,990, while the actual take-home cost is slightly higher.

The lone outlier is Slate, the Bezos-backed startup that sells a bare-bones electric pickup for $24,950. It’s cheap, no doubt about that. But I can’t recommend it to everyone because it strips out nearly every feature you’d expect to be standard on a car in 2026, including power windows, powered seats, a factory paint job, or a center console, for that matter (Forget the center infotainment screen).

You see? The sub-$25,000 EV market in the US is essentially an empty showroom with no mass models or cars whatsoever, while other markets like China, due to growing competition among automakers, are flooding the segment with feature-packed models.

Weren’t Ford and Volkswagen working on affordable EVs?

It’s not like all automakers in the US are ignoring the gap entirely. Ford is working on prototypes of a $30,000 midsize EV pickup, based on its new Universal EV Platform. The company is using megacasting and domestically made LFP batteries to hit that price, though the car might not arrive until next year.

Similarly, Volkswagen’s sub-$27,000 ID.2 hatchback has been stuck since 2023, though the company is still aiming for production in 2026. You see? Both automakers want a slice of the affordable EV market, but nobody actually has a model that’s ready to hit the road.

I also covered the IEA’s Global EV Outlook 2026 report in June, which highlighted how EV adoption is ramping up everywhere across the world, courtesy of falling prices, but in the US.

In fact, recent policy changes, such as the elimination of tax credits and the 100% import duties on Chinese EVs, keep Americans from buying affordable, everyday-use EVs that save the gasoline bill while being easy on the environment. You’ve to keep paying a premium that European and Chinese buyers aren’t paying anymore.

This year, the ARDC celebrates 30 years of automotive development and testing, as a satellite of the Stellantis North American tech center across the Detroit River in Auburn Hills, Michigan.
All About Extending Range, Reducing Cost For the new battery center, it's certainly handy to have the Dodge Charger Daytona EV assembled nearby at Stellantis' Windsor plant.
text:
Of Detroit's three automakers, Stellantis North America has been the laggard in delivering compelling battery-electric vehicles to the US market, well behind General Motors but also trailing Ford. And the company's recent history sort of explains why: In January 2021, well after the Chevrolet Bolt EV arrived and about the time Ford launched the Mustang Mach-E, Stellantis was born from the merger of French Groupe PSA and Fiat Chrysler Automobiles.

So while GM and Ford (and pretty much every automaker on the planet) were pivoting quickly to EVs while nervously watching Tesla's explosive growth from the Model 3 and Model Y, Stellantis was dealing with the growing pains of just trying to consolidate global operations, accommodate several different languages, and understand how more than a dozen automotive brands could actually fit together.

This week, Stellantis is making up for lost time, celebrating the opening of a new Battery Technology Center in Windsor, Ontario, to focus well beyond BEVs to include hybrids and plug-in hybrids, in keeping with Stellantis' multi-powertrain strategy to give consumers their propulsion system of choice, including internal-combustion Hemi V8s. The new tech center helps Stellantis line up better with Toyota, the king of hybrids. And it can't come too soon.

Why Stellantis Needs Battery Tech Hub

"The freedom of choice is what we've been communicating, and we're well-prepared for it," Micky Bly, senior vice president of Global Propulsion Systems Engineering for Stellantis, told employees gathered inside for a celebration of the new tech center today. And in a few words, Bly pretty much summarized Stellantis' approach to the EV market.

"We never dove all the way in. We never stayed all the way out. And this facility is helping us continue that growth within Stellantis."

–Micky Bly, Stellantis Senior Vice President-Global Propulsion Systems Engineering

It was Bly who pushed for the $2.8 billion investment, announced in May 2022, to build the battery tech center as an extension of Stellantis's Automotive Research and Development Center in Windsor. This year, the ARDC celebrates 30 years of automotive development and testing, as a satellite of the Stellantis North American tech center across the Detroit River in Auburn Hills, Michigan.

Some 800 engineers and technicians work at ARDC with a full chassis dynamometer, four-post chassis shaker, virtual reality simulator, and testing for everything from extreme weather to brake and seat durability.

All About Extending Range, Reducing Cost

For the new battery center, it's certainly handy to have the Dodge Charger Daytona EV assembled nearby at Stellantis' Windsor plant. The tech center, working in tandem with a companion Stellantis facility in Turin that opened in 2023, has 35 technicians and engineers (with perhaps room for 20 more in the future) for extensively testing the charging and discharging cycles for high-voltage lithium-ion batteries, gathering data, and analyzing how they perform as a way to predict their behavior in certain conditions.

Testing can be done independently or as part of a battery pack, to determine if it will be compatible with a particular chassis. The facility isn't focused on developing new battery chemistry but instead on helping extend driving range and reducing cost. The center houses 35 walk-in climatic cells for testing up to 63 battery packs, as well as 11 reach-in cells for testing up to 132 cells. That's 11 test chambers, and each one can support up to 12 battery cells. Testing temperatures within the chambers can swing from -40° F to 176° F.

'This is the future of Stellantis'

Bly recalls a much different market that was leaning more aggressively toward BEVs five years ago, as Stellantis was considering whether to build the new tech center.

"We had great need at the time for electrification, and we needed it in North America... and America started to ramp up its electrification," Bly said. While saying next that "none of that has changed," well, the cancellation of federal tax credits and several EV programs, including Ram's full-size pickup, says otherwise. But he's convinced a multi-energy approach is best.

"We continue to see electrification activities grow within the North American region, whether it's BEVs, hybrids, or plug-in range extenders along the way."

–Micky Bly

Stellantis Canada CEO and President Trevor Longley says the auto industry is "obviously... at an inflection point" as automakers pursue various propulsion systems, autonomous vehicles, new safety technologies, and software-defined vehicles. For Stellantis, the ARDC and new BTC will be "one of our core facilities around the world" to take the automaker forward. "This is the future of Stellantis. This is the future of our vehicles being built right here."

title: Putting more roofs to work - Ministers
description:
The Albanese Government is helping businesses, farms and community organisations cut energy costs and strengthen Australia’s energy security by slashing the cost of installing medium-sized solar systems by around 20 per cent.
This reform will unlock more rooftop solar for the missing middle – helping more businesses take up solar and shield their energy bills from volatile global energy markets.
Lower energy costs will improve productivity and competitiveness across manufacturing, agriculture, retail, transport and logistics, with benefits flowing through to households using those goods and services.
It means more regional and remote areas will have access to clean, reliable and affordable solar energy – with community groups, schools, hospitals, farms and businesses able to secure the discount.
“We're putting more rooftops to work and helping businesses, farms and community organisations cut energy costs by slashing the cost of installing medium-sized solar systems by around 20 per cent.
text:
The Albanese Government is helping businesses, farms and community organisations cut energy costs and strengthen Australia’s energy security by slashing the cost of installing medium-sized solar systems by around 20 per cent.

The Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (SRES) will be expanded from 100 kW to 1 MW, allowing businesses, farms and community facilities to install solar systems up to ten times larger, better matching their energy needs and unlocking the potential of large commercial rooftops.

According to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, while Australia’s residential solar is sitting at 22 gigawatts, businesses have only installed around 5.6 gigawatts, with most of this being rooftop solar systems below 100 kW in size.

This reform will unlock more rooftop solar for the missing middle – helping more businesses take up solar and shield their energy bills from volatile global energy markets. Lower energy costs will improve productivity and competitiveness across manufacturing, agriculture, retail, transport and logistics, with benefits flowing through to households using those goods and services.

And more energy generated where it’s used is good for the grid too – reducing the need for expensive networks and smoothing out demand peaks for all energy users.

It means more regional and remote areas will have access to clean, reliable and affordable solar energy – with community groups, schools, hospitals, farms and businesses able to secure the discount.

We will also improve network connection processes for mid-scale solar projects through targeted rule change requests and enhancements to the existing framework.

Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen said the expansion would help businesses and communities realise the same benefits from solar that millions of Australian households already are.

“We're putting more rooftops to work and helping businesses, farms and community organisations cut energy costs by slashing the cost of installing medium-sized solar systems by around 20 per cent.

“One in three Australian homes have rooftop solar, but larger energy users have been locked out because the existing solar rebate only supports systems up to 100 kW.

“We're fixing that by expanding support to systems up to 1 MW, unlocking the potential of commercial rooftops and helping businesses cut power bills, invest in growth and create jobs.

“This will help manufacturers, farmers, retailers, logistics centres, schools, hospitals and community organisations reduce energy costs – and it uses an existing, proven scheme meaning no new bureaucracy or red tape.”

“More rooftop solar means lower energy costs, a stronger economy and faster progress towards an energy system powered by Australian renewable energy.”

The expanded SRES is expected to commence from 1 October 2026, subject to the necessary regulations being in place.

BACKGROUND – POLICY DETAIL

The discount will be delivered through expanding the existing Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (SRES) – the successful and safe program that has been providing discounts for solar upgrades since 2011 and more than 490,0000 Cheaper Home Batteries program installation since 2025.

The expansion of the SRES is expected to be budget neutral and will add to Australia’s renewable energy, which is putting downward pressure on wholesale prices, with those prices down 47% in the most recent quarter.

Each installation generates certificates which are then traded on the open market. The SRES is administered by the Clean Energy Regulator. The federal scheme is separate from state-run rebates.

The SRES has always had a small compliance cost for retailers and that is designed to continue to reduce each year to 2030.

The incremental compliance costs from adding these types of systems is expected to be very small, in the order of $1 to $2 a year.

Expanding the SRES to include solar installations up to 1 MW in size will lower the upfront installation costs for commercial, industrial and agricultural buildings by around 20 per cent.

Based on a mid-scale solar PV system installations the estimated discount is about $68,000 off a 250 kW system - enough to support a reasonably large commercial operation or $136,000 off a 500 kW system, which could power a small manufacturing site.

A 250kW solar PV installation on a medium sized enterprise, like a retailer, could produce around 345 MWhs of electricity a year, saving around $50,000 of electricity costs each year.

A large 850kW solar PV installation, which would be more suited to an industrial energy user, could produce around 1,173 MWhs of electricity a year, saving around $175,000 of electricity costs each year.

title: Louisiana utility plan for Meta data centre draws scrutiny over gas buildout, ETChemicals
description:
Louisiana’s push to attract large-scale artificial intelligence infrastructure is now colliding with a familiar utility worry: who pays, and who bears the pollution.
The groups say the filings leave key details about projected electricity demand, future rates and the number of jobs the data centre may create outside public view.
If the infrastructure is approved and the assumptions behind the project prove too optimistic, Entergy customers could end up financing a costly buildout for one of the world’s most valuable technology companies.
In a statement provided to Fox 8, communication manager Brandon Scardigli said Meta alone is expected to generate about $2.6 billion in savings for Entergy Louisiana customers over the next two decades.
Critics see the possibility of a long-lived gas buildout, opaque cost allocations and environmental damage that could outlast the economic headlines.
text: Louisiana’s push to attract large-scale artificial intelligence infrastructure is now colliding with a familiar utility worry: who pays, and who bears the pollution. As Entergy Louisiana advances a plan tied to Meta’s proposed AI data centre in north Louisiana, consumer and environmental groups are urging regulators to slow the process and examine the long-term cost to households, according to Fox 8.Regulatory review intensifies The proposal is now before the Louisiana Public Service Commission, which oversees utility decisions in the state. The central question is whether Entergy should be allowed to build multiple new gas-fired plants to serve the power needs associated with the Meta project, or whether the deal shifts too much risk on to ordinary customers.EarthJustice, the Alliance for Affordable Energy and the Union of Concerned Scientists have all raised objections, arguing that the public has not been given enough information to assess the scale of the project. Their criticism is not limited to the plants themselves. The groups say the filings leave key details about projected electricity demand, future rates and the number of jobs the data centre may create outside public view. Christie Hicks, an attorney with EarthJustice, said gas turbines bring a familiar set of emissions problems, including smog-forming nitrogen oxides, fine particulate matter and chemicals such as formaldehyde. Susan Miller, a senior attorney at EarthJustice, also accused Meta of withholding information that would help the public understand how much power the facility is expected to use and what economic benefits it would actually deliver.Why the bill debate matters The concern from the coalition is straightforward. If the infrastructure is approved and the assumptions behind the project prove too optimistic, Entergy customers could end up financing a costly buildout for one of the world’s most valuable technology companies. That fear has become a recurring theme in utility regulation across the US as data centres multiply and electricity demand grows faster than planners expected.Logan Burke, executive director of the Alliance for Affordable Energy, told Fox 8 that the pace of the proceeding leaves little room for meaningful public scrutiny. In her view, the matter is moving with too much urgency for regulators to determine whether the arrangement is truly in Louisiana’s interest. She also argued that the process is being shaped to reveal too little, too late.Paul Arbaje, senior analyst at the Union of Concerned Scientists, said the level of secrecy in the filings makes it impossible to pin down a precise estimate of what Entergy ratepayers might ultimately owe. That uncertainty, he suggested, is itself a warning sign when public utility customers are being asked to support a project of this scale.Entergy says savings will outweigh the risksEntergy Louisiana pushed back strongly, saying the Meta project will lower customer bills compared with what they would otherwise have been. In a statement provided to Fox 8, communication manager Brandon Scardigli said Meta alone is expected to generate about $2.6 billion in savings for Entergy Louisiana customers over the next two decades. The utility also said it is reviewing testimony filed by all parties, including the LPSC staff, which Entergy said supports moving forward with the plants if customer safeguards are in place. The company said it would respond within the deadlines set by the commission and insisted that claims of withheld information are false. According to Entergy, representatives for the organisations raising concerns have access to relevant information and have already used it in testimony before the commission. The utility said it will keep working with regulators to make sure the projects protect customers while also modernising the grid.What happens next The dispute now shifts back to the Louisiana Public Service Commission, where the decision will have implications far beyond one data centre. If approved, the project could become a template for how utilities across the South finance the electricity demands of artificial intelligence. If regulators impose tighter safeguards or slow the timetable, it may signal greater caution as states race to court cloud and AI investment. For Louisiana, the stakes are unusually high. Supporters see a chance to secure jobs, investment and grid upgrades. Critics see the possibility of a long-lived gas buildout, opaque cost allocations and environmental damage that could outlast the economic headlines. The commission’s next steps will determine which of those visions carries more weight.
