text:
The global automotive battery market could reach $84.1 billion in 2026 and grow to $132.3 billion by 2033. The forecast represents a compound annual growth rate of 6.7%.

Electric vehicle adoption is a primary growth driver. Investments in battery manufacturing and government clean-transportation policies also support expansion. Lithium-ion batteries have become central to the automotive industry’s transition toward electrification. They offer higher energy density, longer driving ranges and improved charging performance.

Automotive Battery Market Gains From EV Adoption

Global electric-car sales reached nearly 14 million units in 2023. That total represented about 18% of new passenger vehicle sales. Industry projections indicated annual sales would exceed 20 million units by 2025.

Each additional electrified vehicle increases demand for advanced battery packs. These vehicles include BEVs, PHEVs, HEVs and FCEVs. Government incentives continue to encourage adoption in China, Europe and North America. Measures include subsidies, tax incentives, emissions regulations and charging infrastructure investments.

Passenger vehicles could generate about 56.8% of automotive battery revenue in 2026, while BEVs could account for nearly 34.9% of propulsion-related battery revenue.

Automakers are expanding their EV portfolios across multiple price segments. This expansion increases battery procurement requirements. Manufacturers are also introducing higher-capacity battery packs. These packs support longer ranges and shorter charging times through advanced battery management systems. Commercial fleets are also moving toward electrification. Applications include buses, delivery vans and logistics vehicles.

Operators are adopting these vehicles to meet stricter emissions standards. These developments support long-term battery demand and manufacturing investment.

Gigafactory Investment Expands Capacity

Battery manufacturers continue investing in large production facilities. These gigafactories support rising EV output and improve economies of scale. Lithium-ion batteries account for approximately 68.5% of global automotive battery revenue. Their advantages include high energy density, longer lifecycles and declining manufacturing costs.

Improvements in LFP, NMC and NCA chemistries support longer vehicle ranges. They also improve safety and charging performance.

Global EV battery usage reached approximately 686.7 GWh during the first 10 months of 2024. The increase reflected year-over-year growth in EV production.

Battery manufacturers are investing in high-energy-density cells and solid-state battery research. They are also developing battery management software and manufacturing automation. These investments aim to improve efficiency and reduce production costs.

Large production facilities can also strengthen regional supply chains. Local manufacturing reduces dependence on imported batteries.

Governments are introducing local-content requirements and industrial policies. Manufacturers are responding with new capacity across Europe, North America and Asia Pacific.

CATL Plans Hungary Battery Gigafactory

CATL is investing $8.4 billion in a battery gigafactory in Debrecen, Hungary. The plant will have a planned annual production capacity of 100 GWh. Construction began in 2022.

Completion should take 64 months.

The project ranks among Europe’s largest planned battery manufacturing investments and aims to expand the region’s EV battery production capacity. CATL said the plant will manufacture battery cells and modules for European automakers. The project will support growing regional EV demand.

The investment expands CATL’s European manufacturing footprint. It complements the company’s existing battery production facility in Germany. CATL said localized production will improve its ability to serve European customers.

Europe continues to attract battery manufacturing investment. Governments and automakers are working to strengthen regional supply chains.

These efforts also aim to reduce dependence on imported batteries.

Reuters identified the Debrecen project among several planned European battery factories. The investments continue despite a more challenging regional EV market.

BEVs Lead Propulsion Segment

BEVs remain the largest propulsion segment in the automotive battery market. They could generate approximately 34.9% of global revenue. Higher EV sales and demand for larger battery capacities support growth. Government incentives for zero-emission vehicles also contribute.

FCEVs could record the fastest growth among propulsion types. The segment is expected to expand at a 16.4% CAGR through 2033. Hydrogen-powered buses, trucks and commercial fleets are gaining momentum.

Toyota and Hyundai continue to expand fuel-cell vehicle programs. They are also pursuing partnerships for hydrogen infrastructure development.

BEVs are expected to retain their leading position. They benefit from an established charging network and broad consumer adoption.

Fuel-cell commercialization could increase demand for batteries used in hybrid fuel-cell systems.

Asia Pacific Leads Regional Revenue

Asia Pacific accounts for approximately 51% of automotive battery revenue.

China supports the region’s position through EV manufacturing and battery production. The country also leads in critical mineral processing. China generates nearly $23.9 billion in automotive battery revenue. Domestic EV demand and manufacturers such as CATL and BYD support the total.

Japan and South Korea contribute advanced battery technologies. India is expanding domestic cell production through government-backed localization programs.

Europe is identified as the fastest-growing regional market. It is projected to expand at approximately 6.5% annually through 2033.

Carbon regulations and internal combustion engine phase-out targets support regional growth. Gigafactory investments are also expanding across Germany, Hungary and Spain.

Battery recycling and localized EV supply chains support Europe’s long-term competitiveness. North America represents approximately 18.7% of global automotive battery revenue.

Regional growth is supported by expanding EV production and Inflation Reduction Act incentives. Battery manufacturing investments are also increasing across the United States and Canada.

Localization and cross-border supply-chain integration are strengthening regional production capacity.

Battery Manufacturers Expand Production

Leading manufacturers include CATL, BYD, LG Energy Solution, Panasonic Holdings, Samsung SDI and SK On. Other participants include CALB, Gotion High-Tech, EVE Energy and AESC Group.

CATL is expanding through gigafactory investments and battery recycling initiatives. It is also developing advanced LFP battery technologies. The company said it continues strengthening partnerships with global automakers.

LG Energy Solution is expanding localized production through automotive joint ventures. Its investments include projects across North America.

BYD combines battery manufacturing with electric vehicle production. The company is also expanding Blade Battery deployment in domestic and international markets.

Panasonic continues investing in high-energy-density battery technology. It is also expanding manufacturing and long-term supply agreements with EV manufacturers.

Automotive Battery Market Highlights

The market is projected to grow from $84.1 billion in 2026 to $132.3 billion by 2033. The forecast represents a 6.7% CAGR.

Asia Pacific is expected to retain approximately 51% of global revenue. Europe is projected to grow at about 6.5% annually through 2033.

BEVs are expected to represent approximately 34.9% of propulsion revenue in 2026. FCEVs are projected to record a 16.4% CAGR between 2026 and 2033.

name: American Energy
title: Imagine a refrigerator that only works 40% of the time. That's Washington's energy policy
description:
Utilities are responding by extending the life of existing power plants, investing in transmission, and planning billions of dollars in new generation.
In 2024, former President Joe Biden’s Environmental Protection Agency finalized a rule that places strict limits on greenhouse gas emissions from coal and natural gas power plants.
They must retire critical power plants early and severely limit how often new power plants operate.
The rule is especially consequential for new natural gas plants, which are critical for meeting growing electricity demand while maintaining reliability.
And the grid cannot expand with a rule on the books that forces new power plants to operate only 40% of the time.
text:
Utilities are responding by extending the life of existing power plants, investing in transmission, and planning billions of dollars in new generation. But at the very moment we need to move faster, federal policy is slowing us down.

In 2024, former President Joe Biden’s Environmental Protection Agency finalized a rule that places strict limits on greenhouse gas emissions from coal and natural gas power plants. These limits cannot be met with commercially available technology. Despite that, the rule remains the law of the land.

The rule is both legally flawed and technologically unworkable, and it puts utilities in an irreconcilable position. They must retire critical power plants early and severely limit how often new power plants operate. Neither action makes sense in the face of the reliability challenge at hand.

The rule is especially consequential for new natural gas plants, which are critical for meeting growing electricity demand while maintaining reliability. Unless those plants deploy technologies that aren’t even available, they are restricted to operating just 40% of the time.

Think about that in simple terms. If federal regulations required a new refrigerator to operate only 40% of the time, consumers would be forced to either buy additional refrigerators or accept spoiled food. The same logic applies to the electric grid under this rule: Limiting how often new power plants can run means consumers will ultimately pay for more power plants than they otherwise need.

None of this is theoretical. America’s electric cooperatives are making permitting and investment decisions right now that will determine whether there is enough electricity at the end of this decade.

Electric cooperatives are actively planning to bring more than 20 gigawatts of new natural gas generation online at a total cost of nearly $29 billion. That’s enough to power 17 million American homes. But so long as the 2024 rule remains on the books, most of those plants won’t be allowed to operate more than 40% of the time; some of them, no more than 20%.

Basin Electric Cooperative is planning to spend roughly $4 billion to build Bison Generation Station while facing substantial uncertainty about how the rule’s 40% operating limitation could affect the facility’s long-term economics. Oglethorpe is investing more than $3 billion in its Smarr Combined Cycle facility and faces a similar challenge.

Without repeal of the rule, costs will multiply as utilities are forced to invest in additional generation to compensate for plants that are restricted from operating when needed. At a time when the affordability of electricity is an increasing concern for families and businesses, the last thing we should be doing is asking consumers to pay for more power plants than are needed.

America’s not-for-profit electric cooperatives are owned by the consumers they serve and operate at cost. Every decision is made with an eye toward the impact on the consumer at the end of the line.

The implications here are staggering. America cannot lead in artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, and other energy-intensive industries without a grid that is capable of supporting significant new electricity demand. And the grid cannot expand with a rule on the books that forces new power plants to operate only 40% of the time.

The solution is straightforward. The Biden-era power plant rule must be fully repealed.

President Donald Trump has pledged to restore American energy dominance. He has focused on protecting American families by keeping electricity reliable and affordable in the face of growing data center demand. The continued existence of this Biden-era rule threatens to undermine that effort.

The Trump administration has proposed a partial repeal of the rule, which is a welcome and necessary step. But until a full repeal is completed, the problem persists. Leaving constraints on new natural gas generation in place, even temporarily, will delay investment decisions, increase costs, and prolong uncertainty for utilities planning new generation projects.

WILLIE NELSON IS WRONG. HE’S DECLARING WAR ON THE DATA CENTERS STREAMING HIS MUSIC

America’s electricity needs are growing faster than they have in decades. Meeting that demand requires a pragmatic approach grounded in reliability, affordability, and reality. Policymakers should remove barriers that discourage investment in new generation and grid infrastructure. Repealing the Biden-era power plant rule is an essential first step.

The consequences of getting this wrong will be felt not only in higher electricity bills but also in America’s economic competitiveness and energy security. If we fail to act, we won’t just be behind. We may well be in the dark.

Jim Matheson is CEO of the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association, representing nearly 900 consumer-owned, not-for-profit electric cooperatives that provide power to 42 million people in 48 states. He previously served seven terms as a U.S. representative from Utah.

title: Trump energy chief lied to Congress about canceled clean energy funds, lawmakers allege
description:
“He lied to Congress.” In doing so, they say, Wright violated federal law, which bars individuals from making materially false, fictitious or fraudulent statements or representations to Congress.
But the facts of the situation are clear and undeniable.” The Energy Department denied the allegations.
The grants were for clean energy projects such as new battery plants, electrical grid upgrades, carbon capture initiatives and a $1.2-billion award for California’s nascent hydrogen hub known as ARCHES.
The Energy Department agreed to formal stipulations in exchange for the plaintiffs forgoing the discovery process, which likely would have meant officials would be deposed.

text:
Democratic lawmakers are asking the Justice Department to consider criminal charges against U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, alleging that the nation’s top energy official made false statements to Congress about the termination of $7.6 billion in grants for clean energy projects in blue states, The Times has learned.

Rep. Zoe Lofgren (D-San José) and Rep. Gabe Amo (D-R.I.) say Wright testified falsely during a June 10 hearing before the House Committee on Science, Space and Technology when he stated that the Energy Department did not target states for funding cuts based on their politics. All 16 states that lost money, including California, did not vote for President Trump in the 2024 election.

Then in court documents recently unveiled as part of a California-based lawsuit, attorneys with the Energy Department accepted that the grant cuts announced in October were “based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state, i.e., whether the recipient’s location and/or place of performance was in a Blue State or a non-Blue State.”

“Secretary Wright lied to the Committee with his statements, which sought to prevent us from learning the truth: that the October award terminations were an act of political retaliation, ‘based solely’ on whether recipients were located in Blue States,” wrote Lofgren, ranking minority member on the House Science Committee, and Amo, ranking minority member on the Subcommittee on Environment, in a joint letter to acting Atty. Gen. Todd Blanche dated Tuesday, obtained by The Times. “He lied to Congress.”

In doing so, they say, Wright violated federal law, which bars individuals from making materially false, fictitious or fraudulent statements or representations to Congress. They are requesting the Justice Department review the matter “expeditiously and with the utmost seriousness,” and bring criminal charges against Wright if warranted.

“Referring a Cabinet Secretary for potential prosecution is not a step we take lightly,” the lawmakers wrote. “It is a weighty thing to assert that a Cabinet Secretary lied to Congress. We do not treat that assertion as a trivial matter, and we do not use those words carelessly. But the facts of the situation are clear and undeniable.”

The Energy Department denied the allegations.

“The Secretary’s statements in his testimony are correct,” agency officials said in a statement. “None of the termination decisions were based on political considerations.”

The matter stems from Wright’s comments during the June hearing, when committee members asked about the termination of nearly 300 grants in October. The grants were for clean energy projects such as new battery plants, electrical grid upgrades, carbon capture initiatives and a $1.2-billion award for California’s nascent hydrogen hub known as ARCHES.

“No decisions were made on politics,” Wright said during the hearing. “I keep hearing that charge. It’s bulls—. We’re going to say it a million times. It’s not true.”

Later, Amo asked, “Do you believe the federal grant decisions should be based in any way on how a state’s voters cast their ballots in a presidential election?”

To which Wright replied: “They shouldn’t, and they weren’t.”

Energy Department officials maintain that Wright’s statements were factual. The 284 projects selected for termination were from a larger pool of more than 2,300 projects that the department selected for review earlier in the year, which were located in both red and blue states and not based on political considerations, they said. The Office of Management and Budget then identified the projects announced for termination in October, they said. All but one of these projects were in states that voted for Democrat Kamala Harris.

Lofgren and Amo noted in their letter that the Energy secretary spoke to the Science Committee more than three weeks after department attorneys stipulated to the opposite in court documents signed May 15, 2026. The documents were filed with the court July 15.

In addition to acknowledging that the grant terminations were based on the politics of the grant recipient’s state, the Energy Department also affirmed in the court documents that “neither the inclusions of the ARCHES grant nor any other grants in the October notice tranche was based on any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction, or performance-based factor.”

The lawsuit was brought by a group of faculty members and researchers at UC Berkeley and UC San Francisco, who were among those to lose research grants.

The Energy Department agreed to formal stipulations in exchange for the plaintiffs forgoing the discovery process, which likely would have meant officials would be deposed. Energy Department officials told The Times the admissions were solely to expedite the litigation.

News of the funding cuts first broke in an October post on X from Russell Vought, director of the Office of Management and Budget.

“Nearly $8 billion in Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left’s climate agenda is being canceled,” Vought wrote. “The projects are in the following states: CA, CO, CT, DE, HI, IL, MD, MA, MN, NH, NJ, NM, NY, OR, VT, WA.”

Wright denied political motivations in the weeks and months that followed, telling CNN’s Kaitlan Collins in October that the decisions were “all based on facts.”

He reiterated similar sentiments in congressional hearings before the House Committee on Appropriations, the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the Senate Committee on Appropriations.

Lofgren conceded it’s unlikely that Blanche, a Trump appointee, will take up the case.

“But that doesn’t mean that we shouldn’t proceed,” she said.

Officials with the Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment.

text:
August 5, 2026

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency is proposing regulatory amendments to certain compliance provisions and test procedures related to model year (MY) 2027 and later heavy-duty highway engines. These amendments would include changes to the regulatory useful life periods and the emission-related warranty periods. The EPA also proposes to add clarity to certain regulatory compliance provisions and correct errors in the regulations to support the MYs 2027 and later program for heavy-duty highway engines and vehicles.

Cyrus Western, regional administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency said the recent proposed rule to eliminate Diesel Exhaust Fluid deratements entirely will translate to $12 billion saved by American truckers. He said reversing the Biden-era compliance requirements that are tied to DEF system failures that cause sudden losses of speed is a commonsense solution.

EPA is proposing to completely remove deratements and vehicle speed restrictions for newly manufactured highway engines and vehicles and new non-road engines and equipment, including those used in agriculture. Instead of trucks and tractors lurching to a halt when DEF systems fail, under EPA’s proposal, operators would receive visible and/or audible alerts that allow them to continue operating until they can safely address the problem. EPA is also taking public comment on whether guidance should be developed to allow manufacturers to implement this change for in-use on road and non-road engines and equipment.

SAVING MONEY AND FRUSTRATION

If finalized, the savings could reach up to $6,000 per vehicle on new truck purchases, on top of the increased productivity operators are currently losing when deratements cause sudden speed loss on the road. In addition to savings, he said there have been serious issues stemming from deratements.

“There have been horror stories; it’s not just people who have been inconvenienced,” he said. “There are important functions that haven’t been happening properly. For example, we’ve heard stories of fire trucks that run on a diesel engine with DEF that went into limp mode or got derated because of a faulty code so rather than being able to rush to the scene of a fire, they’re only able to go 5 miles per hour.”

He said similar stories have circulated about ambulances, school buses, and vehicles used in agriculture, making the elimination of the requirements something that helps people do the jobs that make society function.

Troy Lake has been one of the faces of the fight over DEF systems. Lake is a 64-year-old diesel mechanic from Wyoming who spent seven months in federal prison for deleting emissions systems on engines plagued with system failures. Pardoned by President Trump in 2025, Lake’s shop was raided in 2018. He told Cowboy State Daily in a 2025 interview that a more logical solution is needed for expensive emissions repairs that won’t put people out of work. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, Region 8 Administrator Western, and U.S. Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wyo., all worked to secure a pardon for Lake.

“The previous administration and the left in general have weaponized the Clean Air Act to beat up on and go after average, blue collar Americans who are just trying to show up for their job and work hard. We saw these folks who were beat up on using the full force and authority of the federal government and that’s not acceptable. That’s not what the Clean Air Act is for. That’s something the administration and the president immediately recognized and took corrective action to right those wrongs and to ensure that federal authority is being used in a fair and reasonable way.”

He said under the Biden administration, the EPA experienced mission drift, taking the agency away from its mission of ensuring Americans all have clean air, clean water, and a clean environment.

The comment period is currently open

“The rules and regs process have lots of small details to sort through, it’s very litigious,” he said. “But, if we follow it well, what we’re doing is we are making really good, well-crafted rules that have followed the process on the books. One of the top ways that some of these agency laws get tossed out by a judge is they review the administrative record and they review some of the petitions that are getting filed in court against these rules.”

He said to ensure the rule isn’t easily tossed out is to follow the administrative procedures act to the letter. He can’t predict what a future administration will do, but said they are able to exercise control over following the rules.

“We saw the Biden administration on certain rules and regulations take a pretty hasty and sloppy approach and we want to do the exact opposite,” he said. “We want to make sure we’re doing things by the book.”

Submit your comments, identified by Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OAR-2026-0728, at http://www.regulations.gov. The EPA will hold virtual public hearings on July 29, 2026, starting at 9 a.m. ET and on July 30, 2026, starting at 10 a.m. ET. If there is sufficient interest, an additional day of hearings will be held on the subsequent day. Comments must be received on or before Aug. 29, 2026.

Western said the agency will review the comments and if warranted, adjust or make clarifications to the rule.

text:
Transcript

Editor's Note: The following was prepared by a machine algorithm, and may not perfectly reflect the audio file of the interview.

Mike Toffel: John, thank you so much for joining us here on Climate Rising.

John Marshall: It's great to be here, Mike. Thank you for having me.

Mike Toffel: So, why don't we begin with just a brief introduction to what your current role is and a bit about how you got there?

John Marshall: Absolutely. Yeah. I founded and started a nonprofit marketing firm about six years ago, which we sometimes describe as the marketing firm for Planet Earth.

But my career was in management consulting and in marketing and corporate advisory, and I spent the last couple of decades advising senior leaders and CEOs of big companies, the Walmarts, the Bank of Americas, the Comcasts, on their marketing strategies and their brands. And true story, one day, it actually started at Harvard.

One day, my kid, who took a course on climate change, came home and told me I was a useless idiot for selling soap and shampoo. I need to make something of my life. And I was contemplating retirement and then decided, why not take all the skills from the corporate sector and see if we could apply those to selling the product that is the clean energy transition.

So that was the genesis of Potential Energy, and I had a thirty-five-year career in the corporate sector and built a team that had a similar background and also some folks from the nonprofit sector to basically create a marketing firm, with a tax status that's nonprofit, but really servicing the sector that's trying to accomplish this transition.

So that's how it all got started, and we've built a decent-sized business over the course of the last six years and are still pushing away on this hard product to sell, to be honest.

Mike Toffel: Yeah, that's what we're going to talk about. So, two quick follow-ups on that. So why did you organize Potential Energy Coalition as a nonprofit rather than a firm?

John Marshall: It's a great question. First of all, I didn't want to have clients. I'd had three decades of clients, but mostly, all jokes aside I wanted the cause to be the client, and the advantage of and most of our support is from generous foundations and philanthropists who give us general operating support, so we can be very focused on the cause.

I think there are certainly a lot of amazing opportunities in the for-profit sector to move cause-based marketing forward, but I didn't want to have any profit motive behind the messaging. I wanted to have it solely for what's the most effective thing that you can do. And then, in any situation, you're going to have some benefit to a client company that you will also want to achieve.

I wanted to take that out of the equation. We do help companies a great deal, but we do it with the cause at the center rather than the company's goals at the center. Now, those tend to align a high portion of the time. We really wanted it to be a social mission, and we wanted to be able to move money to places that we thought maybe the corporate sector was not tackling.

And that's what the nonprofit sector does. It finds spaces in the world where philanthropic capital can fill a gap. And so, we thought there was a big comms gap that existed. Most of the NGOs in the sector were outstanding at policy and outstanding at science but didn't have marketers in them.

There are very few marketers in this space, and so that was the need that we saw when we started it up.

Mike Toffel: Great. And then my other follow-up is about the focus. So, there are lots of environmental topics, let's just say sticking within the environmental domain, lots of environmental topics that one could imagine need some marketing, whether it be to promote organics, for example, or to phase out some types of pesticides.

Mike Toffel: It could be about transportation, mass transit usage. There are so many. It could be about adaptation. And you focused on energy transition, which I think of as primarily, in the fields of transportation and, like grid-scale electric utilities and sometimes off-grid, what led you to focus on the energy transition portion of the environmental domain?

John Marshall: That's a good question. And we did not start it as an environmental organization. And I don't necessarily even think of us in that category, per se, and we can chat about that a little bit as well.

But the goal wasn't to create a green marketing firm. The goal was to use the power of marketing to reduce carbon emissions, right? And so, the calculus, therefore, was what's the most effective deployment of excellent marketing skills to create the outcomes that we most need?

We quickly decided that we were going to work on policy territories, and as opposed to personal behavior. I think marketing can accomplish all of those, but we saw the path to success as we need, we need systems change as much as we need individual change. And so, we set the firm out to work on the areas that would have a big impact with the right kind of decisions made at a systems level, overall.

What are the areas that can have a big impact on carbon, which tend to fall under a few categories? We need a bunch of cleaner energy, we need to electrify industry, we need to electrify transport, we need to electrify buildings, and we need to gradually start reducing dirty energy.

So, those are kind of the five territories in which we operate, And all of those need a major systems change to happen. So, the second question is, what kind of campaigns can you run that can increase the likelihood of that happening? You can run campaigns that increase demand for clean energy.

You can run campaigns that increase demand for electrification. You can run campaigns that help people understand the cost and the downside of dirty energy. So that tends to be the territory that we occupy. We also realized we were going to be somewhat capital-constrained. I mean, we won't have the size of marketing campaigns that I was running in the corporate sector, and so we needed to pick the acupuncture points where having people see the issue differently could help us achieve a lot of progress.

Mike Toffel: Got it. And, you have lots of choices even within the sphere of energy transition and policy. You could be targeting voters. You could be targeting policymakers. You could be trying to amplify the messages of renewable power or perhaps fighting against traditional, fossil fuel power. How did you then click in one more dimension in detail in figuring out which of these target markets you are going to focus on?

John Marshall: Well, that's a good question. We will always look at what the biggest opportunities are, but what we're good at is understanding humans.

And what I've particularly spent a lot of time on in my career is branding. And so, we focused on the areas where, if we repositioned brand climate change in the minds of citizens, that could help progress policy outcomes. And so, a lot of the effort has been a lot of people talking about rebranding climate change when we started the firm, and a lot of the effort has been how can you put frames in people's minds that are winning frames.

And under the premise that if you have a winning frame, if you have a frame that's unassailably supported, you then have a much higher chance of getting the progress that you need. So, a lot of the thinking is deep analysis of important customer segments that matter a lot, like rural.

You know, rural voters matter a huge amount, for permanent reform, because they've got the land through which the power lines need to go or on which the solar panels or wind farms need to be built. And so, how do you reframe some of that such that the support grows in a way that can achieve progress?

So, it's really a little bit of a core competency-led strategy. What are we great at? We're great at understanding humans. We're great at reframing. Let's bring that skill set into the climate area under the premise that it felt, when we started, to be a little narrow, a little liberal, and maybe a little long-term and a little less relevant.

So, could we make climate something that could naturally get more energy and more support at the citizen level?

Mike Toffel: Got it, and with the idea that citizens themselves can't change the permitting process, but I presume what you're suggesting is that if you get to the citizens, they will create political pressure to, for example, expedite or at least avoid opposing permits.

John Marshall: Right. I would describe it as a necessary but not completely sufficient condition. You need public support, and the public needs power in some of these policy areas. Now, we're a 501 (3), so we focus on education as opposed to sole policy, and we don't focus on elections as a 501[3].

But if you maybe you take gay marriage as an analogy, there was a reframing that happened on LGBTQ rights around freedom to marry and love that had a meaningful impact on public pressure and public support for gay marriage. And so, think of us as providing those kinds of reframes in a way that gives leaders, whether they be political leaders, business leaders, or civic leaders, comfort that they can proceed.

I would say a political leader has 10 or 15 things they could choose to do. They're going to choose the ones that they think keep them in their office, and so helping while we don't do electioneering as a 501[3], helping frame things in a way for both parties or for all parties, it's just a more popular choice to make, and that's what we're good at working at the citizen level to get them to care more about the issue.

Mike Toffel: Great. So now that we understand a bit about your target market and the topics that you’re speaking about, can you tell us a bit about the craft of developing the messages and who the messengers are?

And I think you're using behavioral science as part of that. Love to hear a bit about that as well.

John Marshall: Well, it's a great question, and we've taken an entirely analytical approach to this, which I think makes us an interesting member of the climate ecosystem, because we're not an advocacy organization, as in we have a point of view and we need to communicate that.

So, Potential Energy has done a couple of thousand randomized control tests on different messages like a drug trial. You know, we're exposing some people to a message, and some people don't get a message, and we're trying to understand the lift or the impact on that. And that's a laboratory toolkit that is very comprehensive, and now we can use AI to tease out patterns like we might not have been able to before.

We've also done about 4,000 hours of focus groups, which is just as insightful, sometimes quite painful, like what we think people know is not the same as what we learn. I could tell you some stories about that. And then we have these in-market reads, and so we're always doing tests and controls.

So, we've served and measured about four billion ads, and that gives us a feedback mechanism to see what's moving people. So, we'll test things in a few different dimensions, but the main ones are persuasive impact, and what kind of messengers and messages actually move people.

It gives you some very surprising results. The other one is engagement impact. Like, where can you buy yourself some distribution? Cause the Internet has granted us the ability to find things that other people are willing to spread. So, we'll test both those dimensions, and that will hone us in on some strategic territories around which we can develop powerful messages.

We'll do the same with messengers. So, we'll test the impact of a message coming from a politician versus a corporate leader versus an entrepreneur versus a farmer versus a scientist and try to understand who will have the biggest impact on folks. So that's given us a big body of learning, and a big part of the business is a knowledge business by which we learn all that.

The campaigns spin out a lot of this data, and then we advise leaders, corporate executives, and others, and these are the types of things that connect. And an interesting thing is, we have found that conventional wisdom is often wrong on this. And I can tell you a few ways that we found that, but we came in with a few ideas on what the best messages were that were entirely proven wrong in the first couple of years. And so, we have learned humility in the face of data over the course of time.

Mike Toffel: Well, there's lots to dig into there, so let's unpack this a little bit. So first, let's talk about focus groups. Yeah. So, take us inside a focus group. How do you construct a focus group? How long does it run? Who's there? What are you asking folks? What are you seeking to learn?

John Marshall: Yeah. It's a great question, and there are lots of interesting, new and exciting tools these days. But the standard marketing toolkit is, of deep listening still applies whether you've created a synthetic AI-driven focus group or you're going down to a flood zone in Florida and talking to real people.

But we're trying to listen to drivers in people's lives, their values, their identities, their needs, what they care about, and then relate our issue to those. And so, which is like a slightly different approach. Like I remember the very first frustrating focus group that I did.

I was like, "Oh, we're going to the flood zones of Florida. This is where climate..." Because back then, Florida was well, maybe we'll erase that one. I'll start again. I was about to make a political comment that we can't use. But we decided to go down to the flood zones in Florida and figure out those people who will care a lot about climate change, and we'll learn from them so that we can then position it in a way that others, that others can't.

So, you're always looking for lead users, and so we're like, "Oh, these are our lead users. Our lead users are, are Florida climate flood victims." But when you do focus groups, the smart way to do it is to learn about people and learn about their concerns and then relate your issue to that, rather than say, "I'm here to talk about climate change."

So, in an hour-long focus group, after minute 50, nobody had brought up climate change. We were talking about the things they were most worried about. The shopping was bad, and the traffic was bad. And so eventually somebody mentioned flooding and flood. Okay, we have a little bit of a way in.

But what you're starting with is listening deeply to people's concerns. And I think that's been one of the primary challenges with climate messaging: we've started with our message, our fears, our meaning, climate advocates or climate scientists or climate policy folks, and then try to push it on people rather than starting with their needs and concerns and trying to fit our message in.

And so that's been a major learning for us, and we've learned not to be too climate, is what I say. Like, the advocate who yells, "Climate crisis," or who says, "Climate jobs," or "Climate justice," or "Climate action," or "Climate now," or "Climate can't wait," that feels coming from a place of advocacy and political concern very much.

And what we've learned is that's not the winning place. The winning place is what you are struggling with? And how are pollution and a rise in extreme weather, or the way that energy is generated, affecting your life? That second approach, which is a marketing approach, not an advocacy approach, tends to arrive at slightly different conclusions.

Mike Toffel: Got it. And so then let's switch and talk about sort of the testing, the A/B testing that you described. And that's just for those not familiar with A/B testing; it's basically showing two different versions of a message. Perhaps the messenger has swapped, but everything else is equal.

Or perhaps a few keywords are changed, and everything else is equal, so that you can identify which of these features moves the needle. Is that an accurate representation of what you're up to?

John Marshall: That's exactly right, and you can change anything. I'll give you an example. We had the same text on an ad about a carbon tax, and we changed the imagery from a storm to a pollution smokestack.

And so that was interesting because we'd got more than twice the response from having the pollution smokestack than we did for the storm. And it not only tells you to use this kind of imagery, but it tells you something about somebody's psychology. They're not making the connection between the storm and climate change like you, the advocate, might be.

But they do have concerns about pollution. And so, when you talk, and you don't really say carbon tax, you pay a fee on pollution, and there are all these word choices that you end up making. But you're going to go twice as far with a dollar by putting the smokestack image in than the storm image in.

And now AI lets us do that thousands of times in a millisecond these days. And so that kind of approach finds the message that appeals most to people rather than asserts the message that you care most about.

Mike Toffel: Great. And I think that testing is so interesting that you can do testing on such a scale, at relatively low cost.

I mean, so but the analogy to medicine with drugs, say, drug trials, randomized control trials. There, you observe the patients over time, and whether they are getting better or if there are any adverse events. Here in this world of diffused messaging, how are you mentioning two metrics or two types of metrics?

You talked about persuasion and engagement. How do you measure these outcomes? Are these clicks on a social media campaign or other types of watching videos? How are you measuring this?

John Marshall: Yeah. Well, the internet was built to measure and optimize engagement, and that's all those AI algorithms do.

So that's easy. You need to learn about people more deeply than how they're clicking or their digital footprint. And so, in that case, we do two things. We have the laboratory testing machine where we're asking people questions, and then we have ongoing live panels.

So, we've run a bunch of large-scale campaigns where we're serving hundreds and hundreds of millions of ads, and then we are surveying people in the panels on an ongoing basis. And so, for one campaign, we ended up serving. These are actual people who saw actual ads. And so, in that case, we know the media diet.

We know you've seen X number of impressions a month, and it's been on social media, or it's been through influencers or content creators, or on TV. And we can know exactly what you, as a citizen, have been exposed to, and then we can ask you how you've changed your views, but we can measure how you've changed your behavior as well.

So, we had a five-year panel that we ran for one campaign that gave us a tremendous amount of data about the actual cost of getting someone to act differently, think differently, even down to purchasing behavior and individual behavior to watch and see how the exposure of the messaging changed that.

And so, we now have a big economic database on that, which has just taught us a bunch about things that work and things that don't work.

Mike Toffel: So, the engagement metrics sound like they're more automated in their collection, whether that be click rates or duration of time spent on a video, things like that.

And persuasion is a little harder because there you're asking them basically, what their attitude or what their behaviors are.

John Marshall: And you're asking them what they might have done in the past, so you're creating a record.

But you're doing that by talking to people.

Mike Toffel: How do you avoid concerns about socially desirability response bias, which is a fancy word for saying people are predisposed to tell people what they think they want to hear?

John Marshall: Yeah. Well, that's true.

Mike Toffel: Especially if it makes them feel like a better citizen in some manner.

John Marshall: Yeah. I mean, that's true for the whole polling industry, right? But in general, it's valuable. It's not perfect, but it's valuable. There are ways to do great polls, and there are ways to do polls that aren't quite so good. And so, there is a set of questions that one can ask that are better designed to get to how somebody's really thinking about things.

But we would also do a lot of one-on-one interviews and focus groups as well to sort out the insight toolkit. And so, while I've portrayed this as being a very analytical approach, which it is, we're trying to get to human insight. So just as an example, one of the things in the A/B testing that has come through time and time again through hundreds of these tests is that the jobs message hasn't performed very well.

And so, it was just interesting cause many of our funders come from a place where they would really like to see an economic message because innovation and so forth have been part of how their fortunes were raised. But we find that that message has not performed very well.

So that's interesting analytically. I can win a bet if you put a job message in. I can win three or four bets for sure. One bet is that a job message will probably be lost to other messages. Another is that women will respond much more than men, and so there are three or four of those things that you just learn over time.

Um, so the job's message is interesting. We keep seeing that. So, what did we do? We then spent a lot of time really understanding the why. And you're going to get the way out of talking to people. And so, when you sit in these focus groups, and you tell people the story about the prosperity that's going to come from tackling the climate challenge, first, you see it on their faces, and then they say things like, "I don't think so. I don't think jobs are going up. I think robots are going to get these jobs." And so, people are astute, but the qualitative research really helps to round out a sense of how you do this. So, that gets you to be more nuanced, right? So, it turns out that the job message works well, right, if you're in the county, that's getting the job.

Maybe if you're in the state that might be getting the job, but certainly not if you're in the country or on the planet that's getting the jobs. And then you learn that it's a credibility issue, and then you learn that if you put a politician in that ad, it's going to do a lot worse than the carpenters union, in that county that actually is going to provide the jobs for the clean energy plant, is the one messaging that the jobs are real.

So, you learn the nuance as to how to deliver on that. And it always ends up being, well, it's humans, and it's what's relevant to their lives. And I think, the big miss that we've had on climate is that we've done a lot of conceptual stuff, and the human stuff just beats the conceptual stuff every single time, which is why some of the economic messages are on the low end of the AB testing round robins.

Mike Toffel: That's interesting. Yeah, tell us some more conventional wisdom that is wrong. These are some interesting insights already.

John Marshall: Okay. Yeah. Well, I don't know if this is conventional wisdom anymore, but I can win a bet on this with a test. I would say any message with the words ban, mandate, or limit will lose.

And I can guarantee you, twin- nine to twenty points of increased favorability for any climate solution you have if you avoid any of those particular words. People want more. They don't want less. But the advocacy community historically has been a limiting community. And this is why at the outset I was saying we have tried not to think of ourselves too much as akin to traditional environmental values because a lot of that is reduce, recycling, less banning.

Historically had been a little bit of the movement of no, and I can get you twenty points if you're the movement of yes. So, for example, how do we sell clean energy? We don't sell clean energy by saying it's time to ban fossil fuel energy. We sell clean energy by saying, "We all know we need more energy.

If we're going to get more energy, we might as well get stuff that's more local, more proven, more abundant, and more affordable. Let's put more clean energy in." That, that's a dramatic difference, and so the ban, mandate, limit thing is an automatic winner. I think people realize that now.

I think we've seen this in the data for six years. The abundance movement is gaining traction. That's an empirically justified thing. Net zero relates to that. We have a term at Potential Energy, which is that empty terms make easy targets. No one knows what Net Zero is, so it is easy to make net zero unpopular.

That's happening throughout the world. You see different efforts to say net zero is too expensive or it's too hard. And I would say that the reason from a marketing point of view is that net zero is kind of a crappy brand, first, no one knows what it is, so it's an empty term, and so it can be turned into anything.

A little bit like ESG which we can come back to. Also, a term that people don't understand. It should probably be called no pollution instead of net zero. But secondly, no one wants to go to zero. Like, this is not a place that citizens want to go. They want to go to a more place rather than a less place.

So, my first tagline was, I thought I was so clever, and this was before I started Potential Energy. My first tagline was, "Stop at nothing," because we were all going to get to net zero. And, no one wants to stop, and no one wants to go to nothing. And so, it was totally wrong. It was the worst performing thing that we had done.

Mike Toffel:

Mike Toffel: Yeah, that is super interesting. A great list of examples. Now, I do want to come back to this idea of less or avoidance because we're in a world now, as we think about, I'll just use the language people we just referred to that we critiqued, the four degrees, or three degrees, or two-degree worlds.

There is a tendency to talk about avoiding really problematic climate situations that could lead to problematic influences on climate migration and destruction of cities, and the need to avoid strophic influences on GDP. And if we agree that those are sort of the technical things to address, that doesn't mean that's the language you use to address them, but how do you turn around the avoidance of those problematic outcomes into a positive message?

John Marshall: Yeah. There are a couple of things in this conversation that are interesting, so that the idea of good. Well, one point I want to make about the less stuff is that there is one thing that works with less, which is less pollution.

And we've found that the pollution framing has two benefits. One, it's way less polarized. You have a 37-point gap on climate support, where, between conservatives and progressives in the US, on the phrase climate change, but on carbon pollution or pollution, it's an eight-point gap.

And then secondly, it gives you a massive uptick in solvability. Very few people think you can solve the climate change problem, but a lot of people think you can solve the pollution problem, and it's the same thing. So, the reframe on the cause of it, as opposed to the concept, is a big deal.

So, less pollution is good, and it's a good way to go, and it works well, and I'm not the first to say this. This is Arnold Schwarzenegger's big idea. On the avoidance thing, I think it's a slightly different question. And you commented on positive messaging, and so I want to live on what the data says about positive messaging. This is one of those territories where, when one goes to a conference, the popular thing to say is, "We need less fear, we need more hope.

We need fewer problems, we need more solutions, we need more optimism." And I've dived into this analytically, and I've found that not worthwhile to be a trade-off. I don't know that it's a binary, and I think that loss avoidance is actually a very powerful message. That's different than limitations, right?

Because you can do loss avoidance in a way that things are better rather than things are less. But we have found that without putting the magnitude of what you're potentially going to lose in front of people and only making promises about a gain under the premise that, don't talk about the problem, just talk about the benefits of clean energy, or you can reduce costs, or your cars are going to be quieter, all that kind of stuff.

It helps to have a problem for which you put a solution in place. So, we've actually found that worry messaging, worry is the most effective emotion on this, which is a little problematic for corporate leaders and political leaders because you can't just wander around not proposing solutions. So, you have to accompany it with a solution.

But it's a little bit of a myth that fear doesn't work and hope does. Extreme fear doesn't work because people don't necessarily see it as credible, but activating a worry in people's minds is extremely effective. And so, the question is, what's the worry? If the worry is that the planet's coming to an end, it's not necessarily credible.

If it's a worry that your insurance rates are going up in your home, which is true for 95% of Americans because of climate change, it's effective. And so, this is kind of backed by, what is it, I guess, academic theory, prospect theory, where loss avoidance in experiments has often been proven to be more productive in generating response than gain framing.

That's also true in our message testing. So, we don't subscribe to the solutions only, no problem messaging. We like to say maybe a joke comment that a writer, David Foster Wallace, wrote, marketing is the creation of anxiety, subsequently best relieved by purchase. I mean, it's a bit of a sarcastic remark, but there's some truth in that.

You need to give a reason to buy in marketing to get the sale. And on the energy side, it is helpful to talk about an overheating planet as a strong reason to buy. And so, we don't fall into the school of thought that we should avoid the problem. We should just focus on the solution. The data hasn't borne that out for us.

Mike Toffel: Yeah. I mean, you do think of marketing in common parlance as solving a problem you have, right?

John Marshall: That's right. And the problem with climate is that it's not necessarily a salient problem that people are thinking about on a regular basis. You must activate the salience to drive the demand for a solution, which is basically what one does in selling any product.

But skipping the activation part has proven to be much less productive than finding a good one. And so, our work has been searching for the great reasons to care for and then deliver the solution. It's not just delivering the solution. And we found it to be very elastic. Like, people can move around a lot because you must give them a reason to care.

Mike Toffel: Right. I mean, the challenge of pollution framing, or maybe a benefit, is that it makes you think of the reasons why it's effective because we've had a history of solving pollution problems. Generally, people think of those problems that they've solved as being local and immediate, right?

So, if you're burning dirty coal in your community and it's forming particles that form on your car and on your driveway and on your lawn, you can point to the problem, and you can point to the potential solution if only you put more scrubbers onto that, the smokestack, for example.

And climate challenge has neither of those features. It's a long-time lag between the solution being imposed and when the benefits are realized, and it's also global.

And given the disinformation about climate, especially in the US, the ability to link flooding, for example, to protective measures, say engaging in more renewables, so that we have less fossil fuel.

Therefore, we're not heading to the four degrees; we're heading to the two and a half degrees. That very connection has been so challenged.

John Marshall: Well, there's nothing worse in marketing than a multi-step argument. I mean, as I have a saying, I say all the time to my team, "When you're explaining, you're losing."

And climate is rife with a six-step process, and therefore you should care, but interestingly, you mentioned a couple of things, local and immediate. Most of our messaging is about local and immediate, even though the problem is global and long-term.

And so, this is an interesting, I think, trap that we fall into, those of us who think deeply about is that we feel the need to bring all that forward in our messaging, that it's a global problem and that it's a long-term problem. And that delivers a lot of cognitive messaging that forces somebody through the six-step process.

And once you force them through the six-step process of what's causing it, how do you stop it, and how does it impact your life, all those different things, you yield loss along the way. But you don't have to presume that they need to know all those different things. So, I'll give you an example.

Local messaging beats global messaging every single time. That's another one of the guarantees I've got. And so, you don't have to refer to it as a global problem. You can refer to it as a local pollution problem and still make progress with the policies that you need. People aren't necessarily going down that path, and they think it's a good thing that Michigan has less pollution and less carbon pollution.

And so, you can get there without going through the logic that the scientist or the policymaker would go through. The same is true in the long term, and so we do a whole bunch of stuff on immediacy, because I don't want to have people think long term and then have to say, "But we can solve it now," cause then I've taken them down a pathway where I'm making them overthink.

And so now is a very important word on this, and local is as well. I will say there are a couple of things that the climate community has done, historically, that have the curse of being true, okay? And so, one of them is to keep it in the ground.

Like, first, people don't know what you're talking about. And they're like, "So now how am I going to get my kid in the minivan to school if there's no gas at the gas pump?" And the other one is, the two words that are most likely not to allow us to achieve the massive transformation that we need are massive and transformation, because nobody wants a massive transformation.

And so, what happens is we do all the studying, we do all the thinking, these are all the things we need, and then we must go say them. But when you say massive transformation, we did a poll in 23 countries, about like, "Do you want a step-by-step process? Do you want a massive transformation?"

And in 22 countries, they definitively said, "We want a step-by-step process. We don't want a massive transformation. There's too much change in our lives." The French, for some reason, want a massive transformation, but that's for a deeper study. We can't pick the things that we know and say that's the communication we want to do.

We must pick the things that people care about.

Mike Toffel: Yeah, super interesting. Okay, so we've talked about the messaging, the messenger, the target markets, and the metrics to use. So, the last piece of this puzzle is that there are a million places you could now use your analytical engine and the skillsets that your group has to be deployed. How do you decide where to focus?

John Marshall: Yeah. It's a great question. We're one of the larger, I think, the sort of original climate marketing firm, and we're still relatively small, right? And so, the question is: how do you make a dent in this? So, our business model has two dimensions. One is the stuff we've been talking about.

Get as much knowledge as you possibly can and try to spread that to as many leaders as you can. So, make them more effective climate advocates because they can talk about things that will work for them. And everybody needs benefit from using a message, and so the knowledge business gives corporations a benefit, political and civic leaders a benefit, and cultural leaders a benefit.

It helps them talk about it. And so that's a mechanism by which, if we could have 10X more conversation on the issue cause we've gotten the people who have channels to engage in it, great. So that's business model number one. That's the knowledge business. But the second one is that we run campaigns to get people to care so that we can frame and win issues.

And the question is, if you've got 10,000 campaigns you could run across all these different countries, what would you do? We're trying to find moments in time when framing can create what we would call a flywheel of momentum, and so places where there are ambitious leaders and potentially important policies where we can show up and frame it in strong ways.

And so that's been the search for large opportunities to make advances in carbon pollution in a way that others, that could create some real momentum. So, we're operating in a whole bunch of different states where there's potential progress.

There's a ton of interesting stuff that's happening in states. Virginia just actually passed a clean energy law a couple of weeks ago, which is a good move forward. We've been working in California, Michigan, and Pennsylvania. So, finding these places that we kind of call acupuncture points, where if we frame it well, we can create a sense of a flywheel of progress and get solutions done.

So that's kind of what our business model's been, arming leaders with better messages, so we increase distribution and find places where policy change is a good possibility.

Mike Toffel: So, John, we've been talking about this conceptually, but I wonder if you can bring us inside a particular campaign. If you give us an example of how you decided to focus on that area, and then what you did to ensure that you honed the message, and then what the outcome actually was.

John Marshall: Yeah. Well, let me pick one that has an audience that's perceived as harder, and one of the interesting learnings is that you can move all audiences, right? You were talking about myths earlier. One of the myths is that you can't move conservatives; you can only move liberals. Turns out not to be the case.

We move conservatives in many cases more. And so, one thing that's important for climate success is rural communities and permitting reform, because if we can't build it at the pace, then we're not going to get there. And so the big need right now is for rural communities and farmers to allow transmission lines and be excited about wind farms and solar panels and so forth, and that's in, as much or more in red states as it is in blue states.

So, we did a lot of work to think about how to create support for building energy in rural communities. And when you’re back to the point, I was making about really thinking deeply about relevance and customers, you've got to think about what the values of your audiences are, and a lot of rural communities are much, are much more conservative.

And so, the value that came out of the research was freedom. Like, "Don't tell me what to do." And one of the challenges of the environmental movement is their perception that it's a moralistic lecturing thing where you're telling me what to do. You're imposing your values on me.

So, if you go to a rural community and say, "You should, you must,” "You're not a good person if you don't.” That's the quickest way to get rejection. So, the campaign that we ran in rural communities, which had a dramatic leap in support, was to trust farmers with their land.

Like, go to freedom. And freedom is a conservative value. Freedom's an American value. Freedom's an awesome place for climate messaging. You should have the choice. By the way, that's another bet I'll always win, the freedom messaging usually wins, right? And the ban is like the opposite of the ban messaging.

So, you should have the choice. So, trust farmers with their land, which the farmers, as the spokespeople, had a dramatic uptick in support for permanent farm, which is, "Don't tell us what we can do with our land," which is flipping it on its head a little bit. Another flip on its head is don't ban clean energy, right?

As opposed to which is a more effective argument than banning fossil fuel energy? Just don't ban clean energy, because you're on the side of freedom and you're on the side of abundance. And so that was a campaign that we worked on in Michigan, that was very productive, and it managed to prove out that you can find advocates in places that you might not be looking.

Mike Toffel: Really interesting. You can imagine, like the wind farms, the offshore wind farms that are being banned or stopped in the current administration. I haven't heard people frame that as they're limiting the freedom of choice of energy sources.

John Marshall: Yeah. So, we do these, what we call these up-down charts.

So, you have a percentage of support for a given policy issue, and then you can have a framing that moves. And usually, it's around fifty to fifty-five. You can have a framing that moves down into the thirties. That framing that moves it down into the thirties is usually banning your XYZ, insert gas stove, insert car.

And then the framing that moves it up into the seventies is usually you should have the freedom to do ABC, and so interestingly, the message that we found on electric vehicles, the tempting message on electric vehicles was, "Electric vehicles create good American jobs," which takes support for electric vehicle policy up from fifty-two to fifty-five percent.

But if I say everyone should have the right to drive a clean car, I can get it up to the high sixties. And so, we just find repeatedly that just thinking differently about the abundance and the banning and the freedom and much more move to materiality and away from morality. I think the past message has been about should and musts and moral frames.

And a lot of the case, that's your morals. It may not be my morals. I think freedom framing and a lot of conservative values framing actually work very well.

Mike Toffel: Really interesting. For example, instead of banning gas stoves, it would provide the freedom to breathe clean air in kitchens across America, especially for children. That's right.

John Marshall: Yeah. Well, if you name a toxin, it gets even more productive cause there are other value-based territories that are also interesting, like sanctity and purity. So, health is an interesting area, right? And if pollution is your villain, what's your motivation for it?

It could be that you don't want the pollution that's going to hamper your child's future due to climate change, but it could be that there's an open flame in your home, and that's got toxins in it. And so that leans in maybe differently from. In addition to the freedom one. That leans into a purity and sanctity value that is also. You can see that growing in America right now with the Maha movement and others.

And so there are these cultural trends that are fueled by underlying belief sets that, when you tap into those, you can get people to think a little differently about the issue. And it can't feel too climate. Like, I call climate as an adjective, which is actually, it's a noun.

And so, it feels too climate. It feels like you're bringing an agenda to the conversation as opposed to understanding how I'm thinking, and you're relating it to how I'm thinking.

Mike Toffel: Really interesting. So, let me round out this conversation with some trends. The two big trends that we're seeing are one in the US and one around the world.

In the US, we've seen a change of administration over the past few years, and particularly a change in climate policy, whether it be the cancellation of subsidies for electric vehicles, the cancellation of permits for offshore wind, or a very different set of focus areas. How are you seeing that?

Is that changing the work that you're doing, or is that just simply making it more important? Are there different messages that are used to work that are not working because of just what's in the general culture as a result of these political changes?

John Marshall: Yeah. It's interesting because you've seen pretty big changes in the perceptions of elites, of the political class and the business class, but regular people haven't changed a bit in how they think about this issue.

So, five years ago, sixty-four percent of people in the US were somewhat or highly concerned about climate change, and the number has been sixty-four or sixty-five percent for each of those five years, and so there's a little bit of a risk that those of us who think a lot about the issue or work on the issue perceive that the general public has changed.

It hasn't changed at all. Now what has changed is the amount of message distribution that's happened cause the media coverage of climate has gone down a lot over the last year. And so that's a problem for us because we lose salience if we don't get coverage. But people think about it the same way.

So, a super important thing for those of us who are working on this is to realize that we have a target audience that hasn't changed, and we need to keep at it, and what happens in Washington does not get to your average citizen. They still care about the issue, and so it gets as important to stick with it and to stick with the messages that are empirically just proven to work as opposed to changing strategies.

Mike Toffel: Right. And so, you mentioned AI earlier. I just want to come back to that idea. I mean, two ways off the top of my head that AI might be helping you are in the creation of messages with the tools that create videos in seconds, rather than having to film them with the actual people.

Yeah. And you can create this virtual panel where you're testing your materials not on people, but on virtual people. And I'm sure there's a whole host of other areas. Yeah. So, where are you finding these tools to be helpful? Maybe more helpful than you thought, maybe less helpful than you thought?

John Marshall: Well, and a great thing for your listeners to be thinking about is that if in the marketing sector, AI will be highly disruptive. It's exceptionally good at the things that marketers do: learning, content creation, and targeting. It's not there yet, and we can still do way better than the AI-driven content.

So, our creativity is very necessary, and they think more deeply and more creatively about humans. But AI will be very disruptive in marketing. We're using it in all aspects of marketing right now. We're using it to learn. You can create synthetic research panels.

You can do a focus group overnight; that's 80% accurate and gives you a directional sense of things. We're using it to create content. Immediately, you can chop something up and turn it into lots of versions and see which versions move. We're using it to distribute content, and we're using it to optimize as well.

We took all our knowledge, and we put it into an LLM, so all of the things I've been talking to you about over the last hour. And so, AI can write messages for us well. And so, we can scan a leader's speech in there, and we can improve its responsiveness.

So, it's going to be massively disruptive in the marketing sector. I would view it as any technology transition that's happened in marketing. You know, we went from mass marketing to database Internet to search, to social, to influencer, and now we've got AI. It'll probably be more disruptive.

It doesn't necessarily change marketing economics, so there's no silver, but none of those transitions have changed the cost per acquisition that much. The channels have ended up making most of the money, right? So, there's a reason that, database marketing made Oracle lots of money and search marketing made Google lots of money.

So, I'm not sure it's going to fundamentally change the need to invest capital in marketing, but it'll definitely change the how, and it will change the speed, and it comes with a lot of risks of disinformation. Now, we've got some upside to AI with respect to disinformation, as the sensing tools are great right now.

So, we can detect and learn what different segments are seeing, much more effectively than we could before, because AI enables us to do that. So, it enables us to, if we're good at it enables us to be in the conversation more than we've ever been.

Mike Toffel: It does seem like there's an arms race between the generation of disinformation and the detection of disinformation.

John Marshall: There's an arms race, and who knows when and where regulation may come into play. We should probably assume it'll be slow and long-term. But there's a little advantage we have right now, which I may have put a dose of optimism into this conversation, that LLM's bias science right now, right?

And so, you go into Gemini, or you go into Claude, and you ask them about climate change, and you're generally going to get something that's biasing the UN and Harvard and places that are credible sources. That may change, but if we can align LLMs to science, we can make a big amount of progress on climate communications.

And that's going to be so important cause right now, like seventy percent of clicks or seventy percent of searches are ending in one click, right? Because people are using AI to get to the answer. And so that is really important in terms of controlling disinformation.

Now, that doesn't control the craziness on the distribution side and the slop and so forth. But if you have an agent in your life, right now those agents are on our side. They're on the side of science and truth, and that could be valuable for health, science, and climate, and a whole series of things.

And so, we might view it as having some upside as well as some downside.

Mike Toffel: Yeah. Super interesting. So, John, we've covered a lot of ground. For those listeners who are interested in pursuing work in the intersection of storytelling, marketing, and climate, even if they don't call it climate, what do you recommend they do to learn more?

John Marshall: Yeah. It's a great question, and I talk to a lot of young people about career advice in the general area of business, climate, and communications, which is where I've been operating. I always say there's nothing like having the fundamentals that you can then apply.

And I think something very valuable for our business is we've brought a lot of people on board who have been strong, big brand companies, and have really learned the fundamentals of marketing. Cause no matter what happens with technology or politics or the infosphere, the fundamentals of the discipline of marketing will always be valuable.

And so, I always coach young people to think about where there are places in your career, you can develop those core skill sets. And I've happened to be into marketing as I've made my career choices, and I think learning how to understand other humans is an important skill set.

And the tools for those are multiplying exponentially and so getting. It was always the case when I was growing up in my career that being a brand manager at P&G was the way to go, and that a core discipline of really learning the underpinnings of how marketing works is so foundational.

And so, I always recommend that it's an important thing to do. It's been very valuable for us. We've been able to move the ball forward by going back to fundamentals, and I've been teaching or have been teaching at Dartmouth for the last couple of decades, and those core marketing principles are things that I think are super valuable.

Mike Toffel: Great. Well, John, it's been a real pleasure getting to know you and learning more about your organization's work, so I really appreciate your time.

name: Clean Energy
title: SOLAR THERMAL ENERGY FOR INDUSTRIAL DECARBONIZATION - TERI
description:
India’s commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2070 hinges significantly on industrial decarbonization.
Because replacing fossil fuels for process heat remains a primary challenge, low-carbon thermal solutions must be rapidly deployed across critical manufacturing operations.
To address this gap, TERI has released a new policy brief: “Solar Thermal Energy for Industrial Decarbonization.” The brief focuses on how solar thermal technologies can drive India’s clean energy transition in mid-temperature sub-sectors such as textiles, dairy, pharmaceuticals, and food processing.
Beyond identifying market barriers and cost-optimized emission reduction pathways, the brief advocates for a National Solar Thermal Mission to secure institutional support, mobilize fiscal mechanisms, and scale commercial adoption.
Ultimately, this publication aims to elevate solar thermal energy as a vital, cost-competitive solution for India’s sustainable industrial future.

US appeals court blocks EPA attempt to reclaim $20 billion in Biden-era clean energy grants

A U.S. appeals court has blocked the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) from reclaiming nearly $20 billion in clean energy grants awarded under the Biden administration.

The grants were issued in 2022 through the $27 billion Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund to finance renewable energy projects and expand access to green lending. Zeldin sought to freeze the funding in March 2025 because they did not align with EPA policies. A lower court later blocked the move, allowing the funds to proceed, but the decision was temporarily paused while the EPA appealed.

On Tuesday, a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. reinstated the injunction, saying that the EPA’s attempt to cancel the grants “based solely on a policy disagreement” likely violated the Inflation Reduction Act. The EPA is now considering whether to appeal to the Supreme Court.
