Indiana Governor Mike Braun today announced that the Indiana Energy Saver Program (IESP) has advanced nearly $20 million in residential energy-efficiency investments across Indiana during its first six months of active construction, helping more than 1,200 Hoosier households reduce energy costs, improve home comfort, and strengthen housing affordability.

Program investments are expected to generate nearly $400,000 in recurring annual utility bill savings, providing lasting benefits for households and communities throughout the state.

The milestone reflects the growing impact of Indiana’s statewide effort to help residents lower energy costs through practical energy-saving improvements and is a key component of the Governor’s focus on strengthening affordability in all 92 Hoosier counties.

“Reducing utility costs is one of the best ways we can improve affordability for Hoosier families,” Governor Braun said. “The Indiana Energy Saver Program is delivering practical solutions and producing meaningful results for families and communities.”

Income-qualified homeowners and multifamily property owners are encouraged to apply for the Indiana Energy Saver Program. To get started, applicants provide basic information about their property, household income, and utility usage as part of their online application. Once a complete application is received, the program reviews the applicant provided documentation for eligibility, schedules a free energy audit, and works directly with participants to identify opportunities to reduce energy costs and improve home comfort. The program then works with Indiana Energy Saver Program Qualified Contractors to develop and complete eligible improvements through the program process.

name: EPA
title: The EPA heralds its Omaha cleanup as a success. But we found many yards still have toxic ...
description:
It’s the largest residential lead cleanup in the country.
But by the time the Omaha cleanup started, the method had changed.
But the EPA tested only 32 sites where homes had been demolished and found six exceeded the cleanup level.
Those figures, however, trouble Ian von Lindern, who oversaw lead cleanup at an Idaho Superfund site for more than 30 years.
Local health employees can also test residents’ dirt, and, if it’s above the cleanup level, it may qualify for further remediation.
text:
Leer en español

This article was produced for ProPublica’s Local Reporting Network in partnership with the Flatwater Free Press.

Shortly after buying her house in 2022, Mary Royers learned from a man across the street that her Omaha, Nebraska, neighborhood was contaminated with lead. But her yard, like thousands of others, had been cleaned up, the neighbor said.

Royers wanted to be sure. So the 36-year-old educator checked a website where the city tracks the soil test results of every home in a 27-square-mile area surrounding the site of an old lead smelter. She saw “remediated” written in bright green letters. The federal government had completed the work two decades ago. An expert must have tested the dirt and determined the problem was solved, she thought.

Relieved, Royers set about sowing the garden of her dreams. Hours disappeared as she thrust her hands into the soil, tearing up the grass and planting purple coneflower for bees to harvest and prairie grass to sway in the breeze.

“You have the green light from the city. That means everything’s safe,” she said. “I remember thinking, ‘Thank God I don’t have to worry about that.’”

But a soil test conducted last fall by the Flatwater Free Press and ProPublica found otherwise: Royers’ yard still has more than 1.5 times the level of lead that the Environmental Protection Agency’s cleanup was supposed to have eliminated.

Reading the emailed results, she felt “gut-wrenching disbelief,” she said.

“All I could think about was the dirt under my nails and all over my face,” said Royers, who has largely given up gardening for now. She explained later, “It felt like a betrayal of that trust.”

Since 1999, the EPA has spent $273 million digging up and backfilling nearly 14,000 yards across east Omaha to address contamination left from the smelter and other factories downtown. It’s the largest residential lead cleanup in the country. And the agency’s Superfund program has repeatedly heralded it as a success.

But, it turns out, Omaha’s soil might not be as safe as officials have advertised. The news organizations tested soil from more than 600 properties, including 150 that the EPA said had been cleaned up. In those tests, 1 in 10 yards marked as remediated still had enough lead to qualify for cleanup under the original guidelines. And nearly a quarter of the properties we tested in east Omaha could qualify for further study under new guidance released by the Trump administration last fall.

The results suggest the EPA has more work to do, said Howard Mielke, a longtime researcher of lead-contaminated soil who’s considered one of the field’s foremost experts. Not only should the agency clean up the areas that tested above the remediation level, he said, but it also should test other homes.

“If you find a couple of high results, chances are many high results will be nearby,” said Mielke, an adjunct professor at the Tulane University School of Medicine.

Some experts and environmental advocates said our findings reflect weaknesses in the EPA’s approach to cleaning up residential lead sites, which can leave a lot of lead behind.

Jeff Tittel, former director of the Sierra Club in New Jersey, the state with the most Superfund sites, said he repeatedly watched the EPA declare its work done after wrongly assuming everything had been cleaned up.

“On paper, everything’s wonderful,” he said, “but at the sites, there’s still chaos.”

The EPA declined an interview request with senior officials overseeing the Omaha cleanup.

In an emailed response, spokesperson Kellen Ashford said the EPA is committed to cleaning up contaminated sites to protect residents and the environment. “The diligent cleanup efforts have led to a dramatic decrease in elevated blood lead levels” in Omaha, he said. (While the percentage of kids testing high for lead has dropped significantly, as it has nationally, kids in the Omaha site still test high for lead at rates above the national average.)

Ashford said the EPA could not assess the news organizations’ results without further investigation, but property owners can reach out to the EPA or the city of Omaha, which now manages the site for the federal government, if they have concerns.

“Because it would not be possible to completely remove all lead,” Ashford said, the EPA and the city also try to educate the community about lead risks and precautions.

The city is already responding to the news organization’s findings.

The day after receiving her results, Royers forwarded them to the city’s lead office, asking if anything could be done. An employee tested her dirt and found even higher levels than the news organizations did. The city plans to clean the yard up again in August, Royers said.

But the EPA and the city have refused to clean up or test properties of others who have reached out about their high lead results.

The agency has also not said what it plans to do about properties that are below the current cleanup level but above President Donald Trump’s new screening level, which could prompt further action. Any update would come after a new site study the agency plans to release in October 2027, Ashford said.

Royers and her partner, Stephen Matthews, are thankful for the new cleanup, but they wonder: How many other Omahans may be misled or unaware about lead contamination in their yards?

“We’re one house out of thousands,” Matthews said.

What might have gone wrong

It’s difficult to identify why some cleaned-up properties still test high for lead.

That’s in part because Omaha’s lead problem is almost as old as the city itself. The American Smelting and Refining Company produced lead to make batteries, cover cables and enrich gasoline for more than a century. After the smelter closed in 1997, the EPA estimated the plant and other factories had dumped 200,000 tons of lead dust — enough to fill at least 1,600 rail cars — across Omaha’s east side.

At the time, the Superfund program, which had started only a decade before, was still trying to figure out how to clean up residential sites like Omaha’s, then home to 125,000 people. Old factory sites could be bulldozed and excavated, the contaminated material carted away. But the Omaha site involved people’s homes and yards.

The agency tested nearly every yard in east Omaha and came up with a plan: It would dig up and replace parts of yards that had a concentration of more than 400 parts per million of lead — the equivalent of a marble in a 10-pound bucket of dirt.

But that meant that some properties were cleaned up while neighboring ones that had only slightly lower levels of lead were not.

Hewing to that kind of strict standard doesn’t make sense, said Gabriel Filippelli, an Indiana University earth sciences professor and longtime lead researcher.

“From a scientific standpoint, a 390 is the same as a 410,” Filippelli said. “It’s the same as a 400. They’re all about the same value.”

Failing to clean up neighboring properties can also lead to recontamination over time. When it’s windy and the ground is dry, tiny lead particles in the dirt — generally about one-hundredth the width of a human hair — become airborne and spread, Filippelli said.

When the Superfund program started, the agency cleaned an entire yard if its average lead level among multiple samples was over the limit.

But by the time the Omaha cleanup started, the method had changed. In Omaha, it divided yards into five sections: two in the backyard, two in the front yard and a thin ring around the home’s perimeter called the dripline, which often contains the most contaminated dirt but can also contain remnants of lead paint.

The agency took multiple samples per section of yard and replaced a section’s soil only if the average was over 400 parts per million. This approach could lead them to miss hot spots or leave behind areas that have high lead levels but are just under the cleanup threshold. Contractors also did not dig up the driplines if another part of the yard wasn’t over the limit.

This could explain why the Flatwater Free Press and ProPublica’s testing found that about 1 in 20 homes that didn’t qualify for cleanup originally now tested above the cleanup threshold. In addition, the news outlets found several properties outside the Superfund site that were over the limit.

In the early days of the cleanup, Don Preister, a longtime Omaha lead advocate and former state senator, argued for the EPA to clean up entire yards and to lower the level of lead that would qualify for remediation, calling the agency’s solution a half-measure.

But the EPA decided that its approach made the most of limited money and prioritized the highest-risk areas. One EPA manager told Omahans in 2004 that the choice to remove only sections of yards was “economical,” according to meeting records.

“It brought out feelings of hurt,” Preister said of the EPA’s choice. “Children are likely to still be impacted, and their health affected.”

The EPA’s national guidelines did advise against “‘patchwork clean-up’ patterns which are prone to recontamination” when adjacent sections are high. But the agency didn’t give clear guidance on how to implement that, several former site managers said, and some felt they had to follow the rules strictly or risk violating federal law or agreements with companies paying to clean up their pollution.

Ashford acknowledged that the agency has to adhere strictly to its cleanup plans but said in some cases, like an industrial site near a residential area, the EPA may clean up to a lower level to prevent recontamination.

Another problem was that east Omaha was full of older homes that contained lead paint that could recontaminate cleaned soil over time. Following local pressure, the EPA agreed to test homes’ paint. If it contained lead, the agency repainted the outside. But the EPA did not repaint houses whose soil did not also qualify for cleanup. Studies in urban areas have found homes with deteriorating paint have contaminated nearby gardens.

Ashford said an EPA study found most lead-based paint contamination in Omaha was within 6 feet of the house.

Brenda González Rocha, who has lived in her south Omaha home since 2020, thinks both soil and paint are to blame for the lead that doctors found in her 4-year-old daughter’s blood. Her basement had lead paint, which she hired a company to fix.

But although the EPA cleaned up her yard in 2012, the Flatwater Free Press and ProPublica tests found levels of lead that are higher than before the agency remediated it. González is surrounded by properties with lingering lead. A yard down the street that had high lead levels was never remediated. The banks of the nearby highway were never dug up and replaced. The house next door has lead paint on it, according to the city lead website.

Ashford said it’s unlikely that wind-blown dust from one house to another would recontaminate cleaned areas with enough lead to surpass the cleanup level.

But nearly all the remediated properties the newsrooms tested that were over the cleanup threshold are within 100 yards of a property that originally qualified for remediation but wasn’t cleaned up. A third had two such neighboring properties.

González’s eight kids, between 8 months and 22 years old, love to play outside. They jump on the trampoline, ride bikes and play soccer. Now González is anxious whenever they’re in the yard.

“I worry that this could affect their quality of life,” she said. “I would feel bad if something happened to them during their development. I would feel responsible.”

‘Benign neglect’

Once the EPA chooses a fix for a Superfund site, it is generally required to review the site every five years to update the public on the progress of the cleanup. But the ways those reviews are done leave unanswered questions about whether the solution is working and how much lead is in Omaha today, said experts who examined the reports for the Flatwater Free Press and ProPublica.

In their reviews, government officials in Omaha track how intact the grass is on top of the new soil. If it is exposed or has been disturbed, it could be a sign that any remaining lead is no longer safely underground and could blow around.

But they don’t retest a representative sample of properties.

Cleanups often take several tries to get right, said Tittel, the former New Jersey Sierra Club director, and recontamination or missed contamination can be a huge problem.

Tittel said he has seen similar patterns in New Jersey. In 1979, Tittel helped show EPA employees where the Ford Motor Company dumped industrial waste into abandoned mine pits. Since then, he has seen the mess declared a Superfund site, marked safe, become a Superfund site again and spawn a lawsuit that Ford settled in 2009 as locals continued discovering more hazards.

“It’s sort of a benign neglect when it comes to these sites,” Tittel said. “Government just wants to get it over with because it’s taking so long. They end up cutting corners or looking the other way.”

A Ford spokesperson said the company takes its environmental responsibility seriously and has been working with state and federal officials to clean up the site.

Retesting soil does not appear to be standard at other sites, according to reviews examined by the Flatwater Free Press and ProPublica. But it should be, said Debbie Chizewer, a managing attorney with the environmental law group Earthjustice. Without ongoing testing, the EPA can’t really know if its solution is working, she said, and residents won’t know how toxins in the environment are impacting their health.

“I think for the five-year review to be meaningful, you need to do testing,” she said.

Ashford said the EPA retests properties on a case-by-case basis, such as when construction disturbs the soil. The periodic reviews, which in Omaha have led to an ongoing reevaluation of the site’s cleanup level, allow the EPA to ensure these unique, complex sites protect people and the environment over time, he said.

Steve Zivny, who leads Omaha’s Lead Information Office, also said new testing and cleanup decisions depend on factors such as whether kids live at the home and whether they have tested for a high lead exposure.

The EPA’s reviews of the Omaha site do point to some potential problems. In 2024, inspectors found 98% of the lawns had been disturbed, indicating a risk that buried lead could be exposed. That includes having weeds, bare soil or demolished buildings. But the EPA tested only 32 sites where homes had been demolished and found six exceeded the cleanup level. To them, that indicated the solution was “generally protective; however, more data should be collected to support this conclusion,” according to the report.

Those figures, however, trouble Ian von Lindern, who oversaw lead cleanup at an Idaho Superfund site for more than 30 years. He doesn’t doubt the federal government did a good job hauling away tons of toxins in Omaha. But he’s sure they couldn’t get all of it.

At the Idaho site, the EPA requires people to request permits from a local health district before digging in their yards. Local health employees can also test residents’ dirt, and, if it’s above the cleanup level, it may qualify for further remediation.

Without someone keeping a close eye on the fixes, recontamination can occur as people dig up lead-contaminated soil or unremediated soil is allowed to blow around.

“Those remedies are, I don’t want to use the word failing, but they’re becoming less effective,” he said.

Royers worries many homes in Omaha fit that description.

This summer, the educator is letting the weeds grow freely in her garden. Pretty soon, the city is going to replace it anyway.

The thought makes her feel guilty. More people should know about potential lead in their yard and have access to tests and cleanups. But that would require acknowledging that after decades and hundreds of millions of dollars spent, there are cracks in the cleanup. Royers isn’t sure that will happen.

“The priority is pretending like things are OK,” she said. “Clearly it’s not.”

Melody Kramer and Joel Jacobs contributed reporting.

This reporting was also supported by the 2024 Data-Driven Reporting Project, a grant funded by the Google News Initiative in partnership with Northwestern University’s Medill School of Journalism.

title: What's at stake amid Diablo Canyon's uncertain future? See 3 major local issues
authors: Stephanie Zappelli, Sadie Dittenber, Laura Dickinson
description:
The power plant provides more than 1,500 local jobs, and it once contributed millions of dollars of tax revenue to local schools.
In April, the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission granted PG&E a 20-year license to operate the power plant until 2045.
Jobs at the nuclear power plant The power plant is an economic engine for San Luis Obispo County, according to UC Berkeley economist Dr. David Roland-Holst.
“It’s these gorgeous rolling oak-adorned hills that rise above San Luis Obispo Bay,” he told The Tribune.
“They went on to say that there would be no love money for our district or for our local community.
text:
While the Diablo Canyon nuclear power plant has federal approval to operate for another 40 years, the state must still decide whether the plant can stay open past 2030 — and the fate of the community living in the shadow of the power plant hangs in the balance of that decision.

The power plant provides more than 1,500 local jobs, and it once contributed millions of dollars of tax revenue to local schools. It’s also surrounded by 12,000 acres of undeveloped land.

PG&E representatives, economists, labor organizers, safety inspectors, school representatives and people living and working near the power plant gathered at an information session about the power plant on Thursday night at the San Luis Obispo County Government Center to discuss local implications of keeping the plant open.

The power plant, nestled into seaside hills near Avila Beach, has two nuclear reactors that generate about 18,000 gigawatt-hours of energy per year — enough to serve 4 million Californians, according to PG&E.

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission issued PG&E an operating license for the plant that expires in 2044 for Unit 1 and 2045 for Unit 2. However, the state only approved operation of the plant through 2029 and 2030.

In April, the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission granted PG&E a 20-year license to operate the power plant until 2045. However, PG&E only has state permission to run the plant until 2030. The state Legislature would need to pass a law to extend operations beyond 2030 in order for PG&E to use the entirety of its license.

Meanwhile, a recent test conducted by PG&E and its contractor shows that materials in Unit 1 at the Diablo Canyon nuclear power plant are unlikely to deteriorate and break during the next 60 years — but the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission still needs to review the report.

That process should be completed by Oct. 1, NRC senior resident inspector Mahdi Hayes said at the meeting.

Here are three things to know about the discussion at Thursday night’s meeting.

Jobs at the nuclear power plant

The power plant is an economic engine for San Luis Obispo County, according to UC Berkeley economist Dr. David Roland-Holst.

The plant pays about $85 million in state and local taxes, $163.6 million in federal taxes and contributes about $420 million per year in income benefits in San Luis Obispo County, he said.

Meanwhile, the plant provides 1,567 jobs in San Luis Obispo County, and those employees are embedded in the community, Roland-Holst said.

Some own homes, others coach youth sports teams and send their kids to local schools. All of them are considering their future — a difficult task when they don’t know how long the power plant will be open, IBEW Local 1245 assistant business manager Hunter Stern said.

“We’ve been through a bit of a whipsaw,” he said during a panel discussion.

If the plant closes, those employees would need to find new jobs, and some of them may have to leave the county.

“It would force people to make decisions that they’d rather not make about their future,” Stern said. “I think some of those folks will be able to go take work elsewhere, and those that will remain will work on decommissioning. But it will just take a big chunk out of what makes this community so attractive and vibrant.”

Meanwhile, local tradesmen would lose the opportunity to work on refueling outages, when PG&E hires between 1,000 and 1,200 temporary workers to refuel the reactors and perform maintenance on the plant, Stern said.

Plant employee and IBEW 1245 member Chris Burnham said the plant should stay open because it reduces the state’s carbon footprint and stabilizes the grid.

But also, he wants to keep working in San Luis Obispo County, where he bought a house, performs in community theater productions and takes piano lessons.

“This is the first city I’ve lived in where I felt like I could put down roots,” he said during public comment. “I’m really happy to have found a home here, and I hope that I don’t have to give that up soon.”

The fate of Diablo Canyon lands

The power plant is surrounded by 12,000 acres of undeveloped land.

In December, the California Coastal Commission ordered PG&E to dedicate thousands of acres of that land to conservation to offset the environmental impacts of operating the plant through 2030.

The mitigation package includes:

A 4,500-acre conservation easement on the North Ranch Property. PG&E will also attempt to dedicate the fee title of the North Ranch to a public agency, a nonprofit land conservation organization or a Native American Tribe.

Conservation easements for 25 miles of trails on the property, including a trail that connects Montaña de Oro State Park to Port San Luis.

A $10 million endowment for the design, planning, construction and maintenance of those trails.

A prohibition on the sale of the South Ranch property for purposes other than conservation until 2040.

The option to sell the fee title for the 2,400-acre Wild Cherry Canyon property to a state agency, a nonprofit conservation organization or a Native American tribe that also obtains an agreement to purchase the lease from HomeFed Corp. at fair market value.

A conservation plan for Wild Cherry Canyon is moving forward.

A California-based nonprofit land trust called the Wildlands Conservancy is working on purchasing the lease for Wild Cherry Canyon, according to executive director Frazier Haney.

HomeFed Corp. sold its lease to a private party, which then entered into an agreement to sell the lease to the Wildlands Conservancy by the end of the year, Haney told The Tribune on Monday.

If all goes according to plan, the Wildlands Conservancy will also purchase the fee title for Wild Cherry Canyon from PG&E.

The parties are working on appraising the property to determine a purchase price for the lease by Aug. 17, Haney said. If successful, the State Coastal Conservancy will consider awarding a grant to the Wildlands Conservancy at its Sept. 17 meeting.

State Senator John Laird previously earmarked $40 million of the state budget for Wild Cherry Canyon, so the State Coastal Conservancy can pull from that funding for the grant, Haney said.

The Wildlands Conservancy has three priorities for the property: public access, ecological restoration and tribal co-management, Haney said.

The property is home to coastal prairie, a creek shaded by willow trees and live oak woodlands.

“It’s these gorgeous rolling oak-adorned hills that rise above San Luis Obispo Bay,” he told The Tribune. “It’s just one of the most beautiful parts of the Central Coast, and to have the chance to conserve it is just profound.”

At the meeting on Thursday, Mona Olivas Tucker, the chair of yak titʸu titʸu yak tiłhini Northern Chumash Tribe of San Luis Obispo County, urged state agencies, elected officials and PG&E to create a plan to return the Diablo Canyon lands to her tribe — whose members trace their ancestry to the Pecho Coast.

“If the plant runs to 2045, we want our land back. If it closes tomorrow, we want our land back. We’ll take it any time we’re given the opportunity. Our love and responsibility to this place do not end,” she said. “We’ve been waiting for 250 years, and it’s criminal that we’re being asked to wait even longer.”

Local school district urges PG&E to pay unitary tax

At the top of mind for many public officials is the funding that Diablo Canyon operations once provided.

Previously, local agencies received unitary tax payments from PG&E, providing millions of dollars annually that helped run public programming while the power plant operated in the county.

When it was anticipated that the plant would shut down, legislation was crafted that created a plan to taper off the payments over nine years, with public agencies receiving their final mitigation payments in 2025.

Now, after lawmakers decided to extend the plant’s operations for another five years, the power plant remains operating — but the funding hasn’t been restored to public agencies.

“We weren’t brought into that conversation by way of continued funding and support,” San Luis Coastal school district superintendent Eric Prater said during Thursday’s information session. “It just really, really was a difficult time for us, and continues to be.”

San Luis Coastal has been particularly hard hit — and vocal — about the impacts that the loss in funding has had. The district had to cut about $10 million out of its budget over the last three years to compensate for its loss in unitary tax money from PG&E.

The cuts have affected jobs, class sizes, as well as the availability of programming and services.

During Thursday’s information session, Prater described the cuts as “nothing short of devastating,” with an adamant demand that funding be restored if the plant is authorized for another 20 years.

“That funding that we’ve been accustomed to for decades is, right now, not there,” he said. “And we just need to be honest about it, and know that our kids … and our staff are reeling from that.”

A potential solution to the funding loss is currently moving through the California Legislature — but Prater said he was “very concerned” about recent amendments made to the bill.

Senate Bill 931, sponsored by Central Coast lawmaker Sen. John Laird, D-Santa Cruz, aims to reinstate funding to SLO schools and other public agencies via the Community Impact Mitigation Program, but the bill has not yet gained approval from the full state Legislature.

“I’m an optimist. I believe in this community,” Prater said. “I believe that we will come together with some really positive solutions.”

Prater was not the only person to speak out about the lack of continued funding at Thursday’s meeting.

Several community members used their two minutes of allotted public comment time to demand that any extension of power plant operations be tied to funding for the community.

Ben Lippert, a San Luis Obispo father who has been at the forefront of a local effort by the San Luis Coastal Parent Information Network to lobby PG&E for continued funding amid school budget cuts, was one of the speakers.

“My incentive is for my daughters,” he said. “And so what I think everybody, I hope, can understand is there is a set of policy decisions that are made that determine how much money comes into our community, and goes to PG&E shareholders, and goes to a lot of the different people in the state.

“And all we’re asking for is a baseline for our community,” he continued.

San Luis Coastal school board member Brian Clausen also spoke, describing the meetings he’s had with the school board and PG&E as “one of the most disappointing and rude experiences” of his career.

“The representative from PG&E had the gall to tell us that we are bad at lobbying, and that’s why we lost our funding,” Clausen recalled at the podium Thursday night. “They went on to say that there would be no love money for our district or for our local community. And I’ve just been really disappointed in the partnership, despite really high hopes.”

Clausen concluded his speech with an ask of his community members and fellow elected officials.

“If we don’t advocate for our funding, we’re not going to get it,” he said. “PG&E is not going to provide anything out of goodwill, and we, at this moment, need to advocate for our funding, or the county and the school district will not receive it.”

text:
One year after the federal government suspended approximately $584 million in research funding at the University of California, Los Angeles, researchers say many of the consequences continue despite court orders restoring most of the grants. A federal judge ordered the Trump administration to reinstate the bulk of the suspended National Institutes of Health, National Science Foundation, and Department of Energy awards, but faculty members say funding delays, hiring freezes, and the loss of early-career researchers still affect scientific work across the university.

The grants were suspended after the federal government alleged UCLA failed to adequately address antisemitism, engaged in illegal affirmative action practices, and allowed transgender women to compete in women's sports. UCLA denied the allegations and challenged the funding freeze in federal court.

Restored Funding Hasn't Restored Lost Research Momentum

Carrie Bearden, a professor of psychiatry and biobehavioral sciences, said graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in her NIH-funded neurogenetics laboratory temporarily lost salary support while the grants were suspended, and some junior faculty left UCLA after concluding the research environment had become too uncertain. Even after funding was restored, researchers reported delays receiving the awards, leaving some labs waiting months to start projects that had already been approved.

Those setbacks carry weight beyond a single fiscal year. Federally funded research runs on multi-year timelines, specialized personnel, and continuous data collection, and when a project is interrupted, rebuilding the team and restarting the work can take far longer than restoring the underlying funding did.

Hiring Pipeline Remains Under Pressure

Dimitri Shlyakhtenko, director of UCLA's Institute for Pure & Applied Mathematics, said hiring freezes have cut opportunities for graduate students and researchers finishing postdoctoral appointments. The slowdown extends past UCLA. According to a letter from University of California President James Milliken to California's congressional delegation, the National Science Foundation has awarded 39% fewer new research grants than in prior years, a pattern similar to what's playing out in federal energy research accounts facing their own steep funding cuts. Fewer awards mean fewer new projects entering the pipeline and sharper competition for what's left.

Grant Oversight Rules Could Compound the Setback

Researchers are also watching proposed revisions to the Office of Management and Budget's Uniform Guidance, the government-wide rulebook for managing federal grants. The changes would expand political oversight of certain grant decisions, and university leaders argue they could add uncertainty for institutions that rely on federal support across fields from biomedical science to engineering and energy technology, not unlike the turmoil clean-energy demonstration projects have faced when federal agencies reorganize funding priorities without much notice. The University of California has encouraged researchers to weigh in during the federal rulemaking process while continuing talks with policymakers.

Federal research grants finance more than individual labs. They underwrite graduate training, shared facilities, and joint work with hospitals and national laboratories, the same funding architecture behind the broader federal research strategy shift now underway. Pull on one strand long enough and the rest strains too. Researchers argue that prolonged uncertainty risks slowing discovery precisely where private investment tends to be thin, in basic science, medical research, and clean energy work among other fields.

UCLA's grants came back. The people who left didn't, and neither did the year. Faculty say the episode showed how fast a funding freeze can hit staffing and timelines, and how long the damage lingers after the legal fight is won. For research-intensive universities, the real cost isn't the months of lost funding. It's the longer stretch of rebuilding that follows.

title: Battery industry expands beyond vehicles
description:
Utility-scale energy storage The electric grid has quickly become the largest new source of battery demand.
By early 2026, domestic manufacturing capacity for battery storage systems matched 100 percent of U.S. demand for the first time.
Energy storage deployment surged in early 2026 as data centers added battery systems to mitigate grid stress and ensure uptime.
Supply chain resilience Despite significant domestic investment, U.S. battery manufacturing continues to rely heavily on foreign sources for key materials.
The road ahead The mid-2020s buildout created a strong foundation for domestic battery manufacturing.
text:
Driven initially by the rapid rise of electric vehicles, the battery industry has evolved into a far more complex and strategically vital sector. Lithium-ion technology remains the foundation, but demand now extends across energy systems, defense, and industrial automation. The most successful manufacturers are those that built flexible facilities capable of serving multiple markets. Those early investments are now being repurposed to support a broader and more resilient energy transition.

The demand surge

The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 triggered an unprecedented wave of U.S. battery investment. Federal incentives helped drive more than $127 billion in announced projects within two years, spanning over 225 developments and more than 131,000 projected jobs. A new “Battery Belt” emerged across the Midwest and Southeast, anchored by large facilities such as Ultium Cells in Ohio and LG Chem in Tennessee.

In response to aggressive project timelines, engineering firms have played a pivotal role in supporting the design and commissioning of thousands of gigawatt-hours (GWh) of lithium-ion manufacturing capacity. This work spans the full battery value chain, from electrode and cathode production to cell formation and pack assembly.

As the market shifted

By 2024, EV demand growth slowed due to reduced incentives, higher interest rates, and softer consumer adoption. Production ramp-ups were delayed, leaving some battery lines underutilized. The industry reached an inflection point as billions in manufacturing capacity required new demand sources.

The response was a shift toward diversification. Manufacturers began aligning production capacity with multiple sectors rather than relying solely on automotive demand.

New demand vectors

As the battery market diversifies beyond electric vehicles, demand is now driven by a broad array of sectors, each with unique requirements and growth trajectories. This expansion creates new opportunities and challenges for manufacturers, necessitating flexible production approaches that can serve the distinct needs of emerging applications. Below are some of the fastest growing demand vectors reshaping the industry landscape.

Utility-scale energy storage

The electric grid has quickly become the largest new source of battery demand. In 2025, the U.S. added 58 GWh of utility-scale energy storage, reaching 137 GWh total capacity. Demand is projected to grow another 43 percent in 2026, driven by renewable integration and grid reliability needs. By early 2026, domestic manufacturing capacity for battery storage systems matched 100 percent of U.S. demand for the first time.

Automakers have responded with major investments. Ford committed $2 billion to convert its Kentucky EV battery plant into a BESS production hub targeting 20 GWh annually. Tesla and General Motors have also expanded into grid-scale storage. These applications rely heavily on LFP chemistry for its longevity and safety profile.

Hyperscale data centers

The expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure has transformed data centers into major energy drivers. The U.S. data center energy storage market reached approximately $1 billion in 2025 and is growing at over 6.5 percent annually. Operators are deploying lithium-ion Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) systems and onsite storage to ensure reliability and manage power demand.

Energy storage deployment surged in early 2026 as data centers added battery systems to mitigate grid stress and ensure uptime. These applications closely align with EV battery manufacturing capabilities, allowing existing facilities to transition into this market.

Department of Defense

Battery technology has become a national security priority. The Department of Defense outlined its Lithium Battery Strategy 2023–2030 and is preparing a broader update under the FY2025 National Defense Authorization Act. The updated framework emphasizes domestic supply chains and system standardization.

Military demand is expanding across unmanned systems, electrified platforms, and advanced field equipment. The military battery market is valued at $2.57 billion in 2026 and is projected to exceed $5.22 billion by 2034. Applications require high energy density, reliability, and performance under extreme conditions.

Robotics and autonomous systems

Beyond the grid and the battlefield, robotics and autonomous systems represent a growing and structurally important source of lithium-ion demand. The global robot battery market reached approximately $4.8 billion in 2025 and is projected to grow to $11.6 billion by 2034, with lithium-ion technologies accounting for more than 62 percent of the segment.

This growth is driven by rapid deployment across logistics, manufacturing, semiconductor fabrication, and commercial services. Autonomous mobile robots and automated systems are becoming standard in warehouses and production environments, while service robots are expanding into healthcare and retail applications. Many of these systems operate untethered and continuously, requiring compact, high-energy-density batteries capable of long cycle life.

Summary of demand vectors

The diversity of applications reinforces the need for varied battery solutions. Some use cases prioritize energy density, while others focus on durability, fast charging, or thermal stability. As with other emerging demand vectors, no single chemistry or configuration meets all requirements.

For manufacturers, this segment represents a fragmented but durable source of demand. Facilities designed with flexible production capabilities are best positioned to serve the evolving needs of robotics and autonomous systems.

Supply chain resilience

Despite significant domestic investment, U.S. battery manufacturing continues to rely heavily on foreign sources for key materials. The Inflation Reduction Act mandates increasing proportions of these materials to be sourced domestically or from allied countries, prompting structural shifts throughout the supply chain.

Some companies are leading efforts to close the domestic materials loop by developing recycling facilities that process battery feedstock into recovered metals such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel. These large-scale facilities are designed to handle tens of thousands of metric tons of battery materials annually.

In addition to recycling, advances are being made in lithium extraction projects, alongside plans for the expansion of additional recycling centers. Regional initiatives like the Critical Materials Crossroads are actively working to build domestic refining capacity and foster workforce development in this sector.

Manufacturing complexity

As recycled and multi-source materials are integrated into production, manufacturing complexity increases. Facilities must track material origin, chemistry, and processing history to meet regulatory requirements and qualify for incentives.

Feedstock segregation introduces additional challenges. Different chemistries require separate processing flows or strict cleaning protocols between runs. Variations in material composition affect performance, requiring dynamic process tuning and quality control.

Manufacturing Execution Systems must maintain full traceability at the batch level. As a result, battery plants are evolving into hybrid systems that combine production with materials management. This represents a significant departure from earlier single-product gigafactories.

How to scale confidently

Scaling from a pilot plant to full industrial production is a high-stakes leap that the most successful organizations approach as both a technical and a people-centered challenge. To navigate this complexity, teams should adopt a holistic and incremental strategy, beginning with a thorough understanding of the production process. A pilot plant must be intentionally designed to generate the precise data required for making informed full-scale decisions.

Because the impacts of early choices won’t follow a simple linear path, seemingly minor factors, such as humidity controls or other environmental requirements, can have major long-term consequences on cost and constructability. Incorporating benchmarking against similar facilities is also essential to validate assumptions related to acreage, utilities and layout, enabling teams to right-size the solution and minimize total ownership costs.

With these foundations in place, effective scale-up relies on disciplined early planning, a high-functioning project team, and a flexible program management system. Defining the project’s core values and translating them into clear KPIs that reflect long-term success is critical. Progressing through stage gates allows teams to progressively lock in decisions as design evolves, a process particularly vital when fast-tracking necessitates starting procurement and construction before design completion.

Teams should also ensure dedicated staffing, adopt a contracting strategy that encourages collaboration, and establish clear decision rights to prevent delays. Lastly, robust project controls and a formal Management of Change process are important to monitor performance, proactively manage inevitable changes, and prevent cost and schedule overruns as project complexity grows.

The road ahead

The mid-2020s buildout created a strong foundation for domestic battery manufacturing. U.S. battery production increased significantly between 2020 and 2025, and domestic manufacturing capacity for energy storage systems reached 100 percent of demand in 2026.

The challenge now lies in deploying that infrastructure across a more complex demand landscape. Leading manufacturers are treating facilities as adaptive assets capable of multi-chemistry production and rapid reconfiguration.

Global battery demand is expected to rise from approximately 1.6 TWh in 2025 to about 4.2 TWh by 2030 and 6.8 TWh by 2035, with lithium-ion technologies accounting for the majority of that growth.

The industry is no longer building toward a single outcome. It is learning to operate across multiple demand vectors simultaneously, with adaptability emerging as its most critical capability.

Tesla’s AI lead Ashok Elluswamy doubled down on the company’s strategy regarding Full Self-Driving’s speed settings, and owners are definitely confused.

Earlier versions of Full Self-Driving allowed owners to set a max speed that the vehicle could travel while operating under the semi-autonomous driver assistance platform. This allowed more customization for the driver, giving them the ability to experience FSD’s robust performance with their own personal preferences.

Speed is massively important for obvious reasons — it’s not only a question of keeping the vehicle occupants comfortable by traveling at a safe speed, but it’s also something that could contribute to a ticket or infraction from law enforcement.

With the release of FSD v14 last year, Tesla removed the ability to set a max speed and instead opted for five Speed Profiles, ranging from “Sloth,” the most conservative, to “Mad Max,” the most aggressive and spirited. These profiles not only control speed, but also how frequently the vehicle will execute passes, perform lane changes, and other contributing factors.

The removal of the Max Speed setting was a major complaint amongst the Tesla community because it left owners scrambling for a way to experience suitable behaviors while traveling at an appropriate speed. Most felt the driving profiles would be a good indicator of the behaviors, while speed would still be left up to the discretion of the driver.

Instead, Tesla’s Speed Profiles determine both, and the constant tinkering of how they behave has been a major bottleneck and point of confusion for both owners and the company. From update to update, the Speed Profiles will change, sometimes more drastically than others. Some owners have complained that the “Standard” profile is too fast, while others have experienced “Mad Max” traveling below the speed limit:

These things change with each update, but the big complaint is that owners are on the hook for any tickets that come from FSD’s infractions; that’s the caveat of the suite being named FSD (Supervised). It ultimately means the driver is responsible, and the automaker has no liability when it comes to speeding tickets or general traffic infractions.

It is the driver’s responsibility to take over or adjust based on this.

Elluswamy essentially confirmed that there are no plans to bring back Max Speed control, because it is what he referred to as “an anti pattern.” He then echoed something that CEO Elon Musk has started to really push with FSD, and that’s the idea that Tesla is really honing in on the preferences of the driver.

Owners were confused by Tesla’s decision, stating that there must be a better way, especially considering disengagements for incorrect speeds are common:

From personal experience and using FSD for over 72 percent of my driving miles since v14 was released late last year, I make Speed Profile adjustments constantly. If FSD is traveling a tad too quickly, I will scale it back, and if it’s too conservative, I’ll make it more aggressive.

I don’t complain about making the Speed Profile changes too frequently, but it would certainly be nice to have it happen less frequently. There are far too many times I am concerned about getting a ticket, even in Standard mode.

The biggest issue for me, personally, which seems to be echoed throughout the community, is the fact that Tesla’s goal is to minimize disengagements. Many drivers are stating that speed is a major reason for disengagements.

However, Tesla is not willing to bring back this one level of input because it would technically be a regression.

Whether it’s right or wrong in your opinion, it is what Tesla is going with, and it seems like it has pivoted quite a bit from its other strategies for minimizing interventions by pushing its AI to behave in a way that would fit the occupant’s personal preferences.

As autonomous driving technology advances, Lemonade’s state-by-state expansion of usage-based pricing that directly reflects real-world safety data represents a notable shift in how insurers evaluate risk.

name: Congress
title: Congress should rein in EPA overreach to protect affordable and reliable energy - The Hill
authors: Sarah Wagoner, opinion contributor, Sarah Wagoner, opinion contributor
description:
Over the past decade, the EPA has increasingly used the Clean Air Act not just to regulate pollution, but to reshape the nation’s energy system.
The need for reforms such as the End EPA Abuse Act is especially clear because the U.S. is in a period of rapidly growing electricity demand.
For American families and businesses, the consequences of bad energy policy show up in higher utility bills, fewer choices, a less reliable power system, and, eventually, electricity rationing.
It preserves environmental protections while ensuring that major decisions reshaping America’s energy system are made by Congress, not imposed through regulation.
At a time of rising demand, Congress should act to keep energy affordable, reliable, and driven by consumer choice.
text:
At a time when Americans are facing higher utility bills and the grid is under growing strain, getting energy policy right is crucial. The End EPA Abuse Act, introduced by Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga.), would prevent the Environmental Protection Agency from imposing rules that undermine reliability, raise costs, and restrict consumer choice while still protecting the environment.

Over the past decade, the EPA has increasingly used the Clean Air Act not just to regulate pollution, but to reshape the nation’s energy system. Consider the Obama-era Clean Power Plan’s “generation shifting” approach.

Under the Clean Air Act, the EPA determined that the “best system of emission reduction” required not just efficiency improvements at individual plants, but changes across the entire power sector. In practice, that meant pushing utilities to shift electricity production away from coal and toward “green” sources such as wind and solar. The Supreme Court ultimately rejected that theory of authority in West Virginia v. EPA, holding that Congress had not authorized the agency to restructure the nation’s electricity mix.

Further, the EPA’s original 2024 tailpipe emissions rule for model years 2027 through 2032 set emissions targets so stringent that conventional gasoline vehicles cannot meet them at scale. While this rule is currently being reevaluated, automakers faced a forcible and dramatic increase in electric vehicle production to comply with the proposed rule.

EPA’s own projections indicated that electric vehicles would need to account for roughly 30 to 56 percent of new vehicle sales by the early 2030s, with earlier proposals suggesting even higher levels. While framed as “technology neutral,” the practical effect of such a rule is to steer the market away from internal combustion engines, regardless of consumer demand or producer readiness.

The same pattern appears in the EPA’s 2024 power plant rule requiring carbon capture. This requires certain coal and natural gas facilities to meet emissions limits equivalent to capturing up to 90 percent of their carbon emissions, effectively mandating the use of carbon capture technology or forcing early retirement. Industry groups warn the technology is not ready for wide-scale deployment within the required timeframe, and that enacting the plan would increase costs.

Those requirements remain in effect for now, but they are being challenged in court and are under active reconsideration by the EPA, which has proposed repealing the rule.

The End EPA Abuse Act is designed to draw a clearer line by prohibiting rules such as these that would force fuel switching, restrict the use of gas-powered vehicles, undermine grid reliability, or require technologies that are not economically or practically feasible.

Critics will likely characterize the legislation as an attack on environmental protections. In reality, it leaves the EPA’s traditional authority to regulate known pollutants intact. What it does not allow is for the agency to use that authority as a vehicle for imposing major energy and transportation policies that Congress never enacted.

The need for reforms such as the End EPA Abuse Act is especially clear because the U.S. is in a period of rapidly growing electricity demand. Federal analysis warns that the grid could require roughly 100 gigawatts of additional peak capacity by 2030 to keep pace with rising demand from artificial intelligence, data centers, and industrial growth, even as the system faces increasing reliability risks from the retirement of dispatchable generation.

Data centers, artificial intelligence, and advanced manufacturing are placing new and constant pressure on the grid, and even short outages can have severe consequences for their operation. These facilities require electricity that is available around the clock, something intermittent resources like wind and solar cannot provide on their own because they depend on weather conditions and are not always available when demand is highest.

At the same time, energy supply is facing new constraints. Analyses of the grid warn that rising demand, combined with the forced retirement of baseload power generation and increased reliance on intermittent sources such as wind and solar, will lead to shortfalls in available capacity.

One federal assessment again finds that about 100 gigawatts of new capacity will be needed to maintain reliability. Yet despite thousands of proposed projects, more than 2,300 gigawatts of generation and storage capacity were waiting in interconnection queues in 2024. Of these, only a small share will ultimately be built.

When dependable generation is forced offline without adequate replacement, the result is less supply, higher prices, and greater risk of outages. For American families and businesses, the consequences of bad energy policy show up in higher utility bills, fewer choices, a less reliable power system, and, eventually, electricity rationing. Americans should be free to choose the vehicles they drive and the energy that powers their lives.

The End EPA Abuse Act offers a practical path forward. It preserves environmental protections while ensuring that major decisions reshaping America’s energy system are made by Congress, not imposed through regulation.

By forbidding mandates that force fuel-switching or rely on unproven technologies, the bill would restore certainty for energy producers, encourage investment in reliable capacity, and strengthen both the grid and the broader economy.

At a time of rising demand, Congress should act to keep energy affordable, reliable, and driven by consumer choice.

Sarah Wagoner is a Policy Analyst in Environmental and Energy Policy at the Heritage Foundation.

description:

LDEQ’s “expedited” permit process for the Hyundai steel mill follows a dangerous trend by the Landry administration of rushing through complex industrial siting and permitting processes in total secrecy.

Not even close,” said Glenn Price, President of the Sunrise Community Group of Donaldsonville.
text:
DONALDSONVILLE, La. — Labor, environmental health, civil rights, and community groups are warning that the recently published proposed air permit for Hyundai’s steel mill will have a severe impact on community and worker health, exacerbating cancer, asthma, and respiratory and nervous system disease.

The warning from the Good Neighbors Louisiana coalition, which includes the United Steelworkers, the Sunrise Community Group of Donaldsonville, the Sierra Club, and the NAACP Louisiana State Conference, follows the issuance of a proposed air permit by the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality that imposes weak, inadequate restrictions on the $5.8 billion Hyundai facility. This is despite warnings by the Sierra Club, United Steelworkers, and other groups filed to the department over the past several months outlining the health risks.

"Hyundai’s project should be held to the highest standards, backed by meaningful commitments to neighboring communities and the future workforce,” said Jacob Horwitz of the United Steelworkers. “USW supports responsible investment in new industry and knows firsthand the value that a good union job in the steel sector can provide — but economic development should not come at the expense of worker protections, public health, or community accountability."

Good Neighbors Louisiana is also raising concerns about LDEQ’s short, 30-day timeframe for public comment, and is calling on the Department to provide at least 60 days for the community to engage with the 2,165 pages of draft permit materials.

LDEQ’s “expedited” permit process for the Hyundai steel mill follows a dangerous trend by the Landry administration of rushing through complex industrial siting and permitting processes in total secrecy. Louisiana’s $2.6 billion taxpayer-funded incentive package for the steel mill was negotiated under the cover of non-disclosure agreements Hyundai signed with local elected officials, which continue to restrict access to information by journalists and community members.

“Hyundai knows they’re asking LDEQ for a blank check to pollute, and that’s exactly what this draft permit represents,” said Dr. Angelle Bradford Rosenberg, a medical researcher. “Now that they’ve amended their application just a few weeks ago, following months of community pressure, they can’t feign ignorance that cleaner, better technology is available. We won’t stop campaigning until we secure legally binding commitments to the use of that technology.”

LDEQ’s proposed permit does not address serious concerns about Hyundai’s air permit application, including:

Failure to consider comprehensive electrification of finishing processes, which would significantly reduce the facility’s pollution,

Failure to control toxic dust that blows off the trucks and storage piles, which include slag and cement dust and other fine particulate matter,

Failure to provide any details about its carbon capture and sequestration plans,

Failure to establish a credible timeline for transitioning away from methane gas towards zero-emissions green hydrogen in the ironmaking process,

Inadequate planning for pollution events, industrial accidents, and other dangerous incidents at the plant, and how the company would deal with community notification.

“Hyundai’s proposed air permit neglects to consider readily-available electric technologies, toxic dust control methods and the green hydrogen that would significantly minimize harmful pollution at its greenfield plant,” said Andrea Issod, Sierra Club Senior Attorney. “We urge LDEQ to follow the law and require Hyundai to evaluate cleaner technologies and conduct a thorough environmental justice review to ensure the permit protects local communities and plant workers from harmful pollution. If they do not, Hyundai Steel will be just another source of pollution in a region already known as Cancer Alley.”

Sierra Club’s previous comments on the permit application included analysis showing that if Hyundai used electricity instead of pollution-intensive methane gas for ‘steel finishing’ operations at the steel mill, the company could potentially save $2.7 million per month in operating costs while reducing greenhouse gas emissions and other toxic emissions.

Good Neighbors Louisiana has yet to receive a reply to the coalition’s letter to Hyundai CEO José Muñoz demanding that the steel mill meet strong health and environmental standards while providing quality jobs.

The coalition has held several town hall meetings of local residents informing them about the potential impacts of the facility and their rights, and gathering support for a Community Benefits Agreement, which would hold Hyundai to account on limiting pollution and promises about delivering for local residents.

“This permit is simply not good enough. Not even close,” said Glenn Price, President of the Sunrise Community Group of Donaldsonville. “We need them to come to the table, not throw us scraps from it. To Hyundai, we say: come to Modeste and have a real conversation with the community.”

The local community in Donaldsonville, where the facility is planned, have voiced concerns about health impacts from methane gas iron and steelmaking at the facility, which is known to release toxins such as nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, and airborne lead and mercury, which are linked to cancer and other chronic illnesses.

title: 500-megawatt battery plan in New Jersey aims to address bill hikes, grid strain
description:

Andrew Hendry, region president for Atlantic City Electric, said the filing is meant to address the region's growing power supply problem.
By sending stored electricity into the grid when demand spikes, battery storage can reduce some exposure to those price swings.
The proposal also comes as New Jersey relies on imports for nearly half its energy use, according to Atlantic City Electric.
Atlantic City Electric is presenting the battery as both a reliability measure and a way to help with affordability.
text:
With electricity costs climbing, Atlantic City Electric is pointing to a storage project in South Jersey as a possible way to ease pressure on household bills.

The proposal centers on a large battery installation in Salem County that would hold electricity for later use and release it when the grid is busiest and power prices rise.

What happened?

According to Shore Local News, the utility has asked the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities to approve up to 500 megawatts of battery storage on land it owns in Salem County. Atlantic City Electric said that amount of capacity could serve about 400,000 homes.

If regulators approve the plan, Invenergy would help develop the project, which is aimed for completion in late 2030. The facility would not produce electricity itself; instead, it would store energy and feed it back to the grid during high-demand periods, when wholesale power tends to cost the most, and the system faces the most strain.

Andrew Hendry, region president for Atlantic City Electric, said the filing is meant to address the region's growing power supply problem.

"Battery storage is a practical solution that can be deployed quickly to help manage rising energy costs for customers, strengthen reliability, and support the grid during periods of peak demand," Hendry said.

Why does it matter?

Atlantic City Electric said the average residential customer is paying about $40 more per month than in 2024, and that PJM energy supply costs account for 86% of that increase.

By sending stored electricity into the grid when demand spikes, battery storage can reduce some exposure to those price swings. It can also help curb price surges, support the grid during heat waves, and make the power system more resilient when it is under stress.

The proposal also comes as New Jersey relies on imports for nearly half its energy use, according to Atlantic City Electric. More in-state storage could give the region another tool to keep the lights on during extreme weather or peak-usage periods while helping cities, businesses, and households avoid some of the disruption that comes with grid strain.

What's being done?

The project still requires regulatory approval, and the BPU review process is expected to examine whether it provides clear value for customers. Atlantic City Electric said there would be no effect on customer bills during the first five years after the project begins operating.

The company said early-year federal tax credits, along with revenue from PJM markets, could offset nearly 70% of the project's cost over time. Atlantic City Electric is presenting the battery as both a reliability measure and a way to help with affordability.

Storage projects like this can help utilities respond more quickly to demand swings, reduce reliance on volatile energy markets, and create a more dependable backup layer for a cleaner, more flexible power system.

"This project is a direct response to the energy supply challenges facing our region," Hendry said. "Now we are stepping up to take action to address this challenge."

LIVONIA, Mich., Aug. 04, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- As the average transaction price of vehicles continues to rise, new research from Escalent reveals car buyers believe sticker prices have reached unprecedented heights. Sitting well beyond car buyers’ perceived range of affordability (between $31,865 and $47,838), the current average price of a new electric vehicle (EV) ($55,211 according to Kelley Blue Book) is viewed as a financial stretch for many buyers.

This is according to Escalent’s 2026 Affordability DeepDive from EVForward®, the largest, most comprehensive study on EV buyers and electrified powertrain adoption. The report explores how new-vehicle buyers define “affordable,” how it varies for different vehicle segments and how alternative approaches to affordability resonate with consumers. The report also analyzes what vehicle features buyers are willing to compromise on for price, how used EVs fit into the equation, and what automakers can do to address affordability concerns and support EV adoption.

“Affordability is a considerable hurdle for the automotive industry,” said Nikki Stern, a senior insights manager in Escalent’s Automotive & Mobility practice. “This challenge is particularly pronounced for EVs, with more than half of buyers perceiving the powertrain to be financially out of reach, especially in the absence of federal tax credits. While buyers have increased their anticipated spend over the past few years to an average of $43,950 in response to rising vehicle prices, concerns over high costs are leading buyers to ignore the powertrain entirely, creating a major obstacle to EV adoption.”

Escalent’s research revealed buyers evaluate vehicle affordability through a matrix of purchase price, monthly payments and total cost of ownership. EV Intenders—identified by Escalent’s algorithms as buyers who are over 15 times more likely to purchase an EV than the average new-car buyer—placed even greater emphasis across these three considerations. More than four in five (87%) EV Intenders agreed operating costs matter just as much as sticker price. Three-quarters (75%) of EV Intenders also agreed manageable monthly payments can make an expensive vehicle more affordable and an equal number indicated they’d be willing to pay more up front to lower the total cost over time. These attitudes suggest that EV Intenders think about affordability in a more holistic and multifaceted way.

The report also highlights how EV-specific concerns impact new-vehicle buyers’ perceptions of the powertrain’s affordability. The risk of needing to replace the battery (42%) and the cost to set up home charging (37%) outrank the purchase price (26%) as reasons EVs feel unaffordable to buyers.

Similarly, battery degradation and potential replacement costs are the leading concerns associated with purchasing a used EV. These risks are a significant barrier even though a used EV is perceived as a more affordable entry point. Despite this, the study found buyers are open to used EVs, with more than half (55%) saying they would definitely, probably or maybe consider them.

“Today’s auto buyers are looking beyond the sticker price when weighing the cost of a new vehicle. For most buyers, both short- and long-term costs are important considerations for whether buyers perceive a vehicle to be affordable,” said K.C. Boyce, vice president of Automotive & Mobility at Escalent. “As affordability concerns persist, maintaining EV purchase consideration among buyers will require more than just price cuts. Automakers will need to explore alternative incentives and personalized solutions that better resonate with individual customer needs, or risk losing customers’ interest altogether.”

About the EVForward ® 2026 Affordability DeepDive

This EVForward DeepDive study was conducted among a national sample of 1,088 respondents—including 94 EV Owner, 270 EV Intender, 336 EV Open and 308 EV Resistant respondents as identified by Escalent’s algorithm. These respondents are a re-contact subset of the EVForward database, an insights platform focused on identifying and understanding the next generation of EV and electrified powertrain buyers. The EVForward database consists of new-vehicle buyers selected to represent the US population, with quotas for race, Hispanic ethnicity, gender, age, vehicle ownership and region. Results are weighted by race, Hispanic ethnicity, condensed vehicle segment intention and luxury versus mainstream vehicle intention. The sample for this research comes from an opt-in online panel. title: Texans Can Have Data Centers and Affordable Energy Too - Daily Signal
description:
Data centers consume a lot of electricity and will therefore raise electricity demand across the country, but demand alone does not determine whether household rates rise.
Texas’ data centers can strengthen the state’s economy without forcing households to pay higher electricity rates.
In a recent poll, 14% of Texans “somewhat” opposed new data centers in their community, and a whopping 42% “strongly opposed” their construction.
These policies can work well in Texas’ energy environment, where, apart from market-distorting subsidies, the energy market is meant to determine what type of energy is cost-effective and reliable.
It’s reasonable to expect data centers to cover the costs of the generation, transmission, substations, and reliability services they require.
text:
There is no need to choose between winning the AI race and having affordable electricity. Data centers consume a lot of electricity and will therefore raise electricity demand across the country, but demand alone does not determine whether household rates rise. Texas’ data centers can strengthen the state’s economy without forcing households to pay higher electricity rates.

Data centers have been around for years, making everyday online services possible: websites, cloud storage, email, streaming, online banking, artificial intelligence, government networks, and business software. A data center provides the essential, physical infrastructure that supports “the cloud.”

Despite the useful services they supply, not everyone is convinced. In a recent poll, 14% of Texans “somewhat” opposed new data centers in their community, and a whopping 42% “strongly opposed” their construction.

Often people assume that allowing a new data center nearby will ensure their electricity prices increase rapidly. This doesn’t have to be the case. Electricity prices aren’t driven by demand growth alone. Instead, they’re driven by how the grid and infrastructure respond to that growth.

Take China, for example: It is experiencing a similar data center boom, but its electricity prices are significantly lower. China doesn’t unnecessarily restrict its supply chains, as we do in the U.S. Additionally, while gullible media and government officials point to China’s development of wind and solar, the Chinese government has fully committed to supplying abundant, cheap electricity for its industrial and commercial needs.

That commitment means China now operates the most coal-fired electricity generation on the planet, and its government has approved the construction of more new coal generation than is currently operating in the U.S. In contrast, overregulation hinders American energy from reaching its full potential.

A solution to meeting growing demand despite metastasizing regulatory restrictions on American electricity markets is a bring-your-own-energy style policy. These policies can work well in Texas’ energy environment, where, apart from market-distorting subsidies, the energy market is meant to determine what type of energy is cost-effective and reliable.

Texas Senate Bill 6 requires data centers using a lot of energy to fund grid connection and infrastructure upgrades, including transmission and distribution studies. Although SB6 doesn’t guarantee that every dollar charged to a data center equates to a dollar of infrastructure for that specific facility, it embraces the right principle of taking meaningful steps to protect ratepayers.

In states such as New York, Washington, or Oregon, where zero-emission requirements are abundant, a bring-your-own-energy style policy would serve as an additional cost on developers. But mandates in these states already force data center operators to fund wasteful climate initiatives that distort investment decisions, raise operation costs, and ultimately raise prices for consumers and businesses.

It’s reasonable to expect data centers to cover the costs of the generation, transmission, substations, and reliability services they require. However, these businesses (and their investors) should not be viewed as piggy banks for green political agendas. Loading costs onto an industry based on climate initiatives backed by faulty science is a cardinal sin in a free market.

Instead, these states would do well in the short-term to focus on expanding electricity supplies with grid-enhancing technologies that could help to provide data centers with the power they need.

A Columbia University analysis found that these commercially available technologies can unlock meaningful capacity within months, making them especially useful as data-center electricity demand rises through 2028. Examples include advanced conductors that can nearly double line capacity, and power-flow controls that have already freed 2 gigawatts—approximately 4.4% of Britain’s national peak demand—of additional capacity on Britain’s grid.

These technologies move electricity; they unfortunately do not generate it. Deregulation, paired with innovation, is the solution to meeting the data center electricity demand. Faster permitting and local responsiveness, especially around community concerns, are key to data centers being good neighbors and to America winning the AI race.

title: PJM "Hunger Games" Pits Solar And Storage Against Gas, Nuclear - CleanTechnica
description:

Energy Storage And Renewables Go Mano-A-Mano With Natural Gas The raw numbers look good for the combination of energy storage and renewable energy.
