text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

The massive logjam of power projects awaiting a connection to the equally massive PJM grid has finally shown signs of cracking open. To the surprise of nobody, applications from energy storage projects lead by a long shot in terms of raw numbers, followed by natural gas, solar, and wind, with coal slotted far behind into the measly category of “other.” As for which projects actually get off the drawing boards, well, that depends on who or what is prepared for a fight…

The PJM Logjam Breaks Open

The US grid is divided up in to several regions managed by a cohort of grid operators. The regional system was formalized in the late 1990’s to streamline coordination between power generation resources in different parts of the country. Some grid operators, like PJM, periodically call for new capacity proposals to secure new power sources to meet future demand.

PJM is short for Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Maryland, the territory it initially covered at launch. Over the years PJM has grown beyond those three states to encompass all or part of Delaware, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Virginia, West Virginia and the District of Columbia, an area with a population of 67 million.

In recent years PJM has weathered a barrage of criticism for its dilly-dally pace of approving new power projects for grid connection. As described by a press statement on August 3, PJM now aims to speed up the application process by deploying the Tapestry AI-enabled tool developed by Google, among other steps it has taken.

Energy Storage And Renewables Go Mano-A-Mano With Natural Gas

The raw numbers look good for the combination of energy storage and renewable energy. After sorting through 811 proposals, PJM has winnowed the total down to 715 projects. Natural gas clocked in at 147 projects, but it was easily beaten by energy storage at 314, with solar turning in a respectable number of 117 projects.

The domestic wind industry also proved that it still has a beating heart despite a concerted effort by the Trump administration to cut it off at the knees. PJM lists wind at 61 projects, with solar-plus-storage hybrids contributing another 37 projects.

Bringing up the rear are nuclear at 24 and hydropower at 5, with the remaining projects piled into one “other” lump. “The ‘other’ category includes biomass, coal, fuel cell, fusion energy and methane,” PJM explains.

So much for coal.

Moving on to the breakdown by gigawatts of nameplate capacity, by that measure natural gas wins by a mile, accounting for almost half of the total. All together, the 715 projects add up to 201.5 gigawatts, broken down as follows:

Natural gas: 99.8 GW

Storage: 60.0 GW

Nuclear: 17.3 GW

Solar: 11.8 GW

Solar-plus-storage: 7.5 GW

Wind: 3.9 GW

Other: 1.1 GW’

Hydro: 0.07 GW

Let The Games Begin

Again, so much for coal, which Trump has tried — and clearly failed — to somehow “save.” For that matter, Trump’s much-hyped “American Energy Dominance” policy also embraces biomass, geothermal energy, and hydropower, none of which make any particular appearance in the 201.5-gigawatt tranche of projects to be assessed by PJM.

PJM emphasizes that the selection of the 715 proposals is just the first step towards approval, and that’s where the rubber hits the road. The potential for 201.5 new gigawatts is impressive, but PJM only foresees demand increasing by a fraction of that — 70 gigawatts — over the next 10 years, with growth primarily driven by data centers and other large load users. Something’s gotta give, and PJM hints that the quickest-to-build projects have an advantage.

“Demand growth is outpacing the addition of new supply, risking reliability and making the timely interconnection of new resources critical to keeping the lights on for 67 million people in 13 states and the District of Columbia.” PJM emphasizes (emphasis added).

“The rigorous process that is now in place is designed to encourage projects that will get built,” adds PJM VP of Planning, Jason Connell for good measure.

“Based on historical performance, only a percentage of projects that apply for interconnection will sign interconnection agreements and become operational,” PJM adds yet again.

The Solar-Plus-Storage Advantage

Energy storage and solar have made a powerful showing on the nation’s grid in recent years, which is no surprise considering they are the most economical, and most accessible (and least polluting), domestic power generation resources available today. Once construction begins, a typical solar array can be up and running in 12-18 months.

Gas power plants, in contrast, have a much longer construction timeline of three years or more for a modern, combined cycle system. That’s assuming the developer can get their hands on the necessary gas turbines, which are in short supply globally. A backlog of five years is the current rule of thumb.

Nuclear power also fails to beat solar and storage on the timeline, and then there’s public opinion to consider. Despite a sharp partisan split over fossil fuels, and some alarming headlines about local opposition to new solar power plants, a recent study of 686 solar projects completed from 2022 to 2023 shows that only 19% involved a high level of conflict, with 56% falling into the “low” or “no” conflict definition.

If gas and nuclear stakeholders think they can do better, let them try. Trump is stacking the deck in favor of polluters, but local opposition to new development of any kind has been rising at a furious pace. In particular, the blistering anger over new data centers makes the solar battles of years past look like a middle school lunch food fight in comparison.

Communities across the US are organizing against new data centers hand over fist. Red and blue voters alike have also organized against Trump’s ICE warehouse plan, giving them a taste of their power to reshape local elected offices. If anything, the past years’ battles over solar power plants have also provided local residents with the tools and experience to monkey-wrench other new power proposals.

As if on cue, PJM also notes that its previous attempts to wade through the backlog have been stymied. “PJM currently has 51 GW of generation with signed agreements, but many of these projects are either not being built at all or are being slowed by hurdles such as state permitting and supply chain backlogs,” PJM explains.

Hmmm, supply chain backlogs. Ya think? If the voting public wants more electricity, more quickly, more cleanly, and more economically, they already know what to do. Like they say, all politics is local…

title: America's permitting crisis lives at City Hall | Utility Dive
description:

text:
Justin Lopas is COO and co-founder of Base Power, an Austin-based energy company that installs and operates home backup batteries. He previously led manufacturing at the defense company Anduril and was a lead manufacturing engineer at SpaceX.

I run a company trying to make American electricity cheaper and more reliable. The single biggest operational constraint is not the technology, the financing, or the physics of the grid. It is the thousands of city building departments that each have a different way of saying yes — and many more ways of saying no.

Case in point: Two of our members — homeowners who let us install a backup battery, about the size of an outdoor AC unit, and who get below-market electricity rates in return — live eight miles apart. Each of their installations, on nearly identical homes, involved identical batteries and an identical installation team. But the red tape was anything but identical.

One installation was permitted online in a single afternoon, photo-inspected the day of install, and cost the homeowner $45. The other took twelve weeks, three visits to city hall, two separate in-person, half-day inspections, and cost the homeowner $992.

This is the part of the permitting story that almost never gets told. When people talk about “permitting reform,” they usually mean the federal kind: NEPA, environmental review, Manchin-Barrasso, executive orders from the last two administrations. Those debates are real. But if you build things for a living, frame houses, lay fiber, or install batteries, the federal government usually isn’t the one slowing you down. The municipal building department is, and there are roughly 23,000 of them, each with their own rules.

My company has spent the last three years installing home batteries in Texas to deliver affordable, reliable power. We see the same pattern documented in rooftop solar, where “soft costs” — the bureaucratic overhead that isn’t the panel, the inverter, or the wiring — now account for 78% of what a homeowner pays.

The usual defense of the system is safety. “Localities know best,” the argument goes. But our batteries already pass UL 9540, a rigorous national third-party safety certification, before they reach a customer’s house. When the product is already nationally tested, a twelve-week municipal review isn’t producing more safety — it’s producing friction.

Australia proves the point. Same language, same legal tradition, comparable electrician wages. Roughly 33% of Australian homes have rooftop solar versus 7% in the United States. A 10-kW system costs about $5,700 there and $19,000 to $27,000 here. Australia accredits the installer rather than reviewing every project. Most residential permits take a day, handled online. Fire rates per installation are comparable to ours.

The harder fact is who pays for the U.S. version. The cities with the longest timelines, the highest fees and the most bespoke rules are disproportionately dense urban ones. Those are also the cities with the highest electricity bills and the most households behind on paying them.

National utility bill debt has risen to $25 billion, up from $15 billion three years ago. When a permit takes three months and costs four figures, we and every other installer route around it. The families who would benefit most from home backup and a lower bill are the ones who can’t get one. Through their own paperwork, the places that have most loudly championed clean energy and affordability have written themselves out of receiving it.

None of this is partisan. More than a year after the Palisades Fire, Los Angeles has issued only a handful of rebuild permits. The previous administration green-lit roughly $100 billion in clean energy tax credits and watched many of those projects stall in local queues. The current one came in promising “build, baby, build” and cancelled offshore wind permits already in state and federal review. The machinery is roughly as dysfunctional regardless of who is nominally in charge.

Read More in Energy Storage

There is precedent for federal action. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 preempted local interference with wireless siting under the Commerce Clause, and is a meaningful reason nationwide cell coverage exists. Product safety, vehicle safety, food safety and drug approval are all national. We do not need federal review of every energy system install. We need national standards that local governments can’t quietly undermine, and federal infrastructure funding that flows to states which meet permitting benchmarks, the same way highway funding flowed to states that adopted seatbelt laws in the 1980s.

The state playbook is just as clear. Delete what doesn’t need a permit at all. The Department of Energy’s SolarAPP+ platform auto-approves code-compliant residential solar in seconds and is free for cities to adopt. Simplify what’s left. Florida HB 683 imposed a statutory clock on single-trade residential permits, with real consequences for missed deadlines. Standardize across jurisdictions, the way Texas SB 1252 did for residential batteries, so one installer can serve fifty cities with one document package instead of fifty.

The timing is what makes the delay self-defeating. After nearly two decades of flat demand, American electricity use is climbing again, and the cost of keeping up is already landing on bills. The grid needs new capacity faster than it has in a generation — and a battery on an existing home is among the fastest capacity there is: no new power plant, no transmission line, no years-long queue.

Read More in Energy Storage

Permitting is the throttle. Every month a city spends re-reviewing a battery it has already certified safe is capacity the grid doesn’t get and a bill a family doesn’t see fall — and it lands hardest on the households already behind. Federal preemption of local rulemaking is the clearest path to letting America build what it suddenly needs. Delete what you can. Simplify what you can’t delete. Standardize what’s left.

text:
A North Carolina homeowner looking to heat and cool a 620-square-foot garage ran into a familiar home-upgrade dilemma: Spend about $1,500 now on a lesser-known mini-split brand, or pay roughly three times as much for one with a better reputation.

The question struck a nerve because many homeowners weigh the same trade-off as interest in electric heating and cooling continues to grow.

What happened?

After getting surprisingly low quotes for a garage mini-split installation, the homeowner brought the question to Reddit's heat pumps forum.

They said they had the option to choose from Prime, PG American, and Confortotal equipment, and they wondered whether anyone had experience with them. "All come with a five-year condenser warranty and one-year labor. I'm getting these all in for about $1,500 with electric work included, versus a Mitsubishi, which I'm getting at about $4.5k all in," they explained.

The discussion broadened into a discussion about balancing immediate savings against long-term dependability. Some people fixated on how low the bid was, while others debated whether an 18k BTU mini-split would be enough in the Tar Heel State, where coastal and mountain climates can create very different needs.

"18k for 620sf in a garage is oversized unless you're doing serious heat load. I'd have run the math first," one person advised. Another incredulously wrote: "$1,500 all in??? In the U.S.??"

Heat pumps are attractive to homeowners because they are significantly more energy-efficient than traditional HVAC systems, and they provide both heating and cooling.

That can translate to lower utility bills and long-term savings. If you want to explore which heat pump is right for you, EnergySage's heat pump marketplace makes it easy to compare your options. For small spaces and targeted heating and cooling, Merino offers single-room, ultra-efficient HVAC systems at a low price point.

Why does it matter?

The exchange highlights a challenge for homeowners.

A mini-split can be a smart electrification upgrade that improves comfort and lowers energy use, but sizing, service support, and parts availability can make big differences in whether the investment actually pays off.

Saving on a heat pump upfront can be especially tempting for a garage or bonus space, but a low price may stop looking cheap if reliability problems show up later.

"TL;DR: Mitsubishis are zombies that never die. Buy Mitsu if you don't want to think about it for 15 years," one commenter recommended.

Others shared cautionary tales about cheap equipment. "Mine came with internal pumps that failed after about four years. They can't be fixed, only replaced," someone said.

What can I do?

If you're comparing mini-split brands, there are a few practical steps. Ask about parts availability, verify the installer's experience, compare warranty coverage, and make sure the system is properly sized for your climate and insulation.

It can also help to compare multiple quotes rather than focusing on sticker price. Resources such as EnergySage's heat pump marketplace can make it easy to compare equipment, incentives, and installer options before committing to the cheapest bid or most expensive brand name.

Homeowners interested in leveling up their energy systems can also use EnergySage, which offers a free solar quotes comparison tool.

For one commenter, the original poster had come out with a win either way. "The fact they let you choose options aside from the one with the most markup is phenomenal," they wrote.

title: Reuse of Wartime Lands in Volunteer State Launches Nation's Next American Energy Hub
description:

Bill Lee launched Tennessee’s Nuclear Energy Fund in 2023.
By leveraging federal investment and bipartisan support, the initiative is positioning East Tennessee as a leader in the nation’s energy future, fostering job creation, supporting local communities, and driving long-term prosperity.
I’m excited that these efforts are setting the stage for historic levels of investment and development for the Volunteer State,” said Fleischmann.

text:
OAK RIDGE, Tenn. — The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Environmental Management (EM) recently highlighted its American Energy Hubs, an initiative that is transforming former Manhattan Project and Cold War sites into engines for innovation, affordable energy production, advanced manufacturing, and economic growth.

Oak Ridge has become a trailblazer for President Donald Trump’s ambitious vision for DOE and EM. Federal teams, working in partnership with state and local officials, have established a successful model for restoration and revitalization that is giving these lands a new chapter as the Oak Ridge American Energy Hub – an epicenter for the United States’ ongoing nuclear renaissance that will sustain the nation’s growing energy demands.

That was the message from EM Assistant Secretary Tim Walsh at this year’s Nuclear Opportunities Workshop, where he addressed a capacity crowd at the Knoxville Convention Center.

“Our work is transforming sites that were instrumental in powering and protecting our nation decades ago and making it possible for them to do it again,” said Walsh. “These efforts are paving the way for projects and investments on a scale unseen since these sites were first constructed. Now they are creating high-paying jobs for the next generation, supporting technological advances, and ramping up to generate historic levels of power to the grid to increase affordable energy.”

Partnerships with the Tennessee Department of Economic and Community Development, City of Oak Ridge, Roane County, Anderson County, Roane Alliance, Oak Ridge Industrial Development Board, Oak Ridge Corridor Development Corporation, and Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) are driving major private-sector investments that are creating economic opportunities and building crucial infrastructure to increase energy production in the United States.

To date, EM has transferred more than 2,500 acres of federal land in Oak Ridge to the community for economic reuse, with hundreds more acres expected to be transferred in the near term. That land is now home to businesses that have announced approximately $10 billion in projected capital investment and are expected to create thousands of private-sector jobs.

Among them are companies that represent the complete nuclear lifecycle.

Orano USA’s announced enrichment facility will provide a domestic capability for producing fuel for power plants, while BWXT is enriching fuels for national security missions. LIS Technologies is developing new laser enrichment technology. TRISO-X is producing fuel for next generation reactors, including those being constructed locally by Kairos Power. Radiant Nuclear has announced a factory to manufacture microreactors, and Oklo Inc. has announced a nuclear fuel recycling facility.

A major contributor to the pace and scale of this redevelopment is the support of the governor’s office in attracting companies to the region, along with the leadership of Tennessee’s congressional delegation representing the region, including Sens. Marsha Blackburn, Bill Hagerty, and Rep. Chuck Fleischmann. All three provided remarks at this year’s Nuclear Opportunities Workshop earlier today.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee launched Tennessee’s Nuclear Energy Fund in 2023. Since then, the state has allocated $95 million to support the expansion of nuclear-related businesses, workforce development and site infrastructure.

"Tennessee is leading America's nuclear renaissance because we've built an unmatched ecosystem of innovation, investment, and opportunity," said Lee. "Our selection as a finalist for a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus reinforces the Volunteer State's commitment to advancing safe, reliable energy solutions for generations to come. I thank the Trump Administration and our federal, state, and local partners as we strengthen America's energy dominance, enhance our national security, and create greater opportunity for Tennesseans."

“Congressional backing is breathing new life into the nuclear industry by revitalizing once-dormant land and attracting substantial industry and investment through the ambitious American Energy Hubs initiative. By leveraging federal investment and bipartisan support, the initiative is positioning East Tennessee as a leader in the nation’s energy future, fostering job creation, supporting local communities, and driving long-term prosperity. I’m excited that these efforts are setting the stage for historic levels of investment and development for the Volunteer State,” said Fleischmann.

The land for many of these economic development opportunities in Oak Ridge is made available from the environmental restoration conducted by EM and contractor United Cleanup Oak Ridge. Their work has transformed a shuttered government-owned uranium enrichment complex into a privately owned industrial park.

That transformation process involved demolishing and removing more than 500 facilities with a combined footprint covering the equivalent to 225 football fields and excavating more than 50,000 dump truck loads of soil, clearing the way for this revitalization.

text:
Automakers and truck-makers play a double game, proclaiming their greenness to the public while lobbying policymakers to water down or eliminate environmental regulations. Environmental and public health advocates write letters to the companies politely asking them to stop doing so.

In the latest round, a coalition of 24 organizations, including the Sierra Club, the Center for Biological Diversity, GreenLatinos and the Natural Resources Defense Council, have sent a letter to the CEOs of Paccar, Cummins and Daimler urging the companies to reverse their efforts to weaken implementation of the EPA’s heavy-duty nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions standards, which are set to take effect in 2027.

The letter calls out the companies’ recent public statements backing a rollback of the standards—a position the groups say directly contradicts assurances the manufacturers have given investors about their readiness to meet the 2027 requirements. The groups point to manufacturers’ own earnings calls: Paccar stated it was “prepared” for the 35 mg NOx standard and Cummins said it would “be ready to launch” products under the 2027 rule.

“Paccar, Cummins, and Daimler must end their attempts to undermine implementation of heavy-duty NOx standards, threatening the health of the communities and drivers upon which the heavy duty industry relies,” the groups wrote.

The letter notes that heavy-duty trucks make up just 6% of the on-road fleet but account for 59% of the transportation sector’s NOx emissions and 55% of its particulate pollution, and cites American Lung Association findings that truck drivers face elevated exposure to diesel exhaust and higher lung cancer mortality.

“Cummins is marketing an aftertreatment system built for EPA27. Daimler is selling engines it calls compliant today. PACCAR told investors it was ready last year,” said Andrea Marpillero-Colomina, Policy, Research & Data Analytics Advisor at GreenLatinos. “They can’t sell readiness to shareholders while simultaneously buying delay from Congress.”

name: Louisiana Environment
title: Sierra Club: Meta is underestimating emissions from its Hyperion data center
description:
The Sierra Club is challenging Louisiana’s approval of revised air permits for Meta’s Hyperion data center in Richland Parish, arguing that the facility should have been classified as a major source of air pollution rather than receiving a less restrictive minor source permit, Louisiana Illuminator reports.
The environmental group contends that Meta’s revised permit underestimates the facility’s emissions by excluding emissions from emergency diesel generators.
According to the Sierra Club, including those emissions along with the site’s 44 natural gas water boilers would push the project above the 100-ton annual threshold for a minor source permit.
The Sierra Club is also urging the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality to require on-site air monitoring, consider battery storage as a cleaner alternative and hold a public hearing on the permit revisions.
While the permit covers the data center’s generators, boilers and fuel storage, it does not include emissions from 10 natural gas turbines that Entergy is constructing to power the facility because those emissions will be permitted separately.

text:
BP is to sell its Archaea Energy biogas business, it disclosed in Q2 results today.

It bought the Houston-based firm for $4.1bn in October 2022, as part of a triple strategy to expand its presence in the US biogas industry, support customers’ decarbonisation goals and reduce the average carbon intensity of the energy products it sells.

But now, under a corporate portfolio simplification drive, it is cutting back on non-core assets. It follows last week’s news that it has started to process to sell North Sea assets after 60 years of production.

Archaea specialises in the development and construction of RNG (biomethane), and landfill gas-to-electric and dairy digester facilities that capture waste and convert it into low-carbon energy.

While the sale marks a strategic pivot from biogas, BP maintains a partnership with Clean Energy Fuels Corp to build anaerobic digestion facilities to process dairy cow manure into scalable renewable natural gas (RNG) for commercial use.

CEO Meg O’Neill said its costs and liabilities are “not resilient enough” in a low price environment, although its underlying quarterly profit jumped $2.5bn in three months to $5.7bn, thanks largely to soaring energy prices as a result of the Middle East war. Net debt stands at $22.3bn, down from $25.3bn in Q1. Impairment charges totalled $0.8bn, under the amount forecasted in a previous statement.

She said performance over the last few years has met neither its own expectations nor those of shareholders. Future investments will be based on value creation and not “sentiment, history, or legacy attachment”.

“We need to move faster, and we have both the opportunity and the technology to do this. Operational excellence is also about working safely with people, communities and the environment; it helps us work to deliver energy that is secure, affordable and lower-carbon, where it makes business sense – and it is how we will make BP more competitive,” she said.

Full year divestment proceeds are expected to be in the range of $8 to 9bn, buoyed by the sale of the Gelsenkirchen refinery in Germany on 31 July.

KNOXVILLE, Tenn.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 4, 2026-- Pilot Company (Pilot), General Motors (NYSE: GM) and EVgo Inc. Well-lit, fully staffed locations open 24/7 with free Wi-Fi and clean restrooms

On-site retail, restaurants and a variety of food, beverage and convenience options

title: Climate change is changing how Texas farmers handle their peach harvests | WUNC News
description:

The Texas peach crop was wiped out.
The fruit trees need chill hours, a certain number of hours where winter temperatures stay below 45 degrees Fahrenheit but above freezing.
Unpredictable weather can also throw a wrench into peach production too, even if the trees get enough chill hours.
JIM POKLUDA: You can accumulate chill hours, but if it gets really, really warm, then you can negate those chill hours and so take them away.
text:
SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

In the summer months, signs along Texas highways usually advertise fresh local peaches. But this year, Texas farmers say the warmest winter on record since 1895 has hurt their summer peach harvest. From Houston Public Media, Natalie Weber reports.

UNIDENTIFIED VENDOR: So you have a great weekend. Thanks for coming by.

NATALIE WEBER, BYLINE: On a hot, bright Friday afternoon, Bridget Stunz is buying produce at the Peach Creek Country Market, about an hour southwest of Houston.

BRIDGET STUNZ: I was here last week, and I'm here again. Whenever they got peaches or, you know, they're getting the cantaloupes in and the watermelon, I'll come.

WEBER: Many of those peaches, however, may not be from Texas this year. That's according to Jeff Pavlock, the store's owner.

JEFF PAVLOCK: So what we've been doing this year is we've been carrying a lot of South Carolina peaches. The Texas peach crop was wiped out.

WEBER: Pavlock says it's always a bit of a challenge to grow peaches in Texas. The fruit trees need chill hours, a certain number of hours where winter temperatures stay below 45 degrees Fahrenheit but above freezing. This year, he says, peach trees didn't get enough chill hours, and a late spring freeze also wiped out much of the harvest. That freeze was followed by heavy rains and fungus growth.

PAVLOCK: It's like one week you'll get a peach in that'll knock your lights out, and the next week, you got to deal with the brown rot. And that's from all the rain.

WEBER: It's hard to say exactly how many peaches Texas produces each year. The state doesn't participate in the U.S. Department of Agriculture's peach count. However, Tim Hartmann, a fruit crop researcher with Texas A&M, predicts that this year's crop will be less than half of last year's harvest. He says Texas weather is highly variable, but he has noticed a pattern.

TIM HARTMANN: In recent history, though, we've seen a trend of getting less chilling.

WEBER: Hartmann compares a lack of chill hours to a lack of sleep.

HARTMANN: You're going to be more likely to snooze through your alarm clock - right? - and then you're not going to be very productive that day. That's the same thing these plants are doing.

WEBER: Climate change is creating new challenges for farmers and ranchers, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. Higher temperatures are impacting everything from corn harvests in the Midwest to cherry crops in Michigan. Unpredictable weather can also throw a wrench into peach production too, even if the trees get enough chill hours. Jim Pokluda, who owns a farm north of Houston, says he didn't harvest a single peach this year.

JIM POKLUDA: You can accumulate chill hours, but if it gets really, really warm, then you can negate those chill hours and so take them away. And then you can gain them again, but now you've confused the plant. And then if, all of a sudden, you throw in a freeze, then you'll just kill everything.

WEBER: At the Peach Creek Country Market, a large loud fan runs nonstop near the produce to keep shoppers cool. A worker uses a forklift to load pallets into a trailer that will deliver the fruit stand's produce across the region. Jeff Pavlock, the owner, says he feels fortunate that he has cultivated relationships with out-of-state farmers so he can still sell peaches this year.

PAVLOCK: And we will say our prayers for a better season next year 'cause I know the good Lord'll take care of us (laughter).

WEBER: Still, as he sits outside his produce store on the side of a Houston highway in the July heat, he says he misses the taste of a juicy Texas peach. For NPR News, I'm Natalie Weber in Houston.

Colorado Gov. Jared Polis signed legislation May 29 extending the Job Growth Incentive Tax Credit through to 2035. The credit was previously set to expire after 2026. No changes were made to the eligibility or administration of the credit. The incentive offers businesses a state income tax credit, which is equal to 50% of the Federal Insurance Contributions Act taxes paid for each new job created. To qualify, businesses must create at least 20 net new jobs in Colorado, or five jobs in Enhanced Rural Enterprise Zones. The credit can be claimed for up to eight years. If the tax credits exceed the business’s income tax liability, they can carry forward the unused credits for up to 10 years.

PLANO, Texas (Aug. 4, 2026) – Smooth driving, electric exhilaration, and SUV practicality enhance every drive in the 2027 Toyota bZ battery electric vehicle (BEV). Returning for its fifth year in the lineup, the 2027 bZ remains unchanged from the prior model year. It is available in XLE and Limited grades in a choice of Front- or All-Wheel Drive (FWD or AWD).

At the heart of the bZ is Toyota’s continued focus on real-world usability. The 2027 Toyota bZ features a sleek exterior that emphasizes a low and planted stance. Its front-end design delivers a sleek, contemporary look with a hammerhead hood and standard LED light bar. While available details such as distinctive wheel treatments, black accents, and available two-tone styling help differentiate grades and personalize the vehicle’s appearance.

It also has a color keyed front center bumper, thin lower grille, and rear spoiler, standard. Color matched overfenders are also available. There is privacy glass on all rear side, quarter, and liftgate windows for added privacy. The overall result is an electric SUV with a polished, aerodynamic profile that looks purpose-built for the modern era while remaining unmistakably Toyota.

Interior Features: Spacious, Modern, and Driver-Focused

Inside, the 2027 bZ presents a clean, contemporary cabin with a horizontal dashboard design and a strong emphasis on usability. A standard 14-inch Toyota Audio Multimedia display anchors the interior, while available premium touches add comfort and refinement throughout the cabin.

Thoughtful details include standard dual wireless charging, front and rear interior ambient lighting with 64 available colors, dual zone climate control, and heated front seats. Premium climate amenities, like heated and ventilated front seats, heated rear seats, and front radiant foot-and-leg heaters are standard on the Limited grade models. Seating materials are available in SofTex® with fabric mixed media trim or SofTex trim, depending on grade.

Passenger and cargo space are practical for everyday use, with 42.1 inches of front legroom, 35.3 inches of rear legroom, and 27.7 cubic feet of cargo volume behind the second row (without subwoofer). The rear cargo area has 56.9 cubic feet of space with the second row down (without subwoofer).

Driving Dynamics: Smooth, Responsive, and Confident

The Toyota bZ delivers electric driving that feels composed and responsive. Toyota’s compact, lightweight and energy-efficient eAxles use silicon carbide semiconductors to help deliver thrilling output while maximizing range. Front-wheel-drive models produce either 165 total system horsepower (XLW FWD grade) or 221 total system horsepower (XLW FWD Plus and Limited FWD), while available all-wheel-drive models deliver up to 338 total system horsepower, giving the bZ strong acceleration and confident passing power.

Toyota engineers have also tuned the bZ for a refined ride and stable handling. Toyota’s BEV-dedicated e-TNGA platform supports a low center of gravity and a rigid foundation by placing the battery pack flat under the floor. Combined with the battery cross-framing structure, lightweight body construction and dynamic suspension, the architecture is intended to enhance ride quality, stability and handling precision.

Available all-wheel-drive capability adds traction in challenging weather and road conditions, reinforcing the bZ’s versatility as a daily-driver EV. Additional driving-related features include:

Vehicle Stability Control to help maintain vehicle control in adverse conditions

The 2027 bZ has a standard North American Charging System (NACS) port. Under ideal conditions, DC fast charging can replenish the battery from 10% to 80% in approximately 30 minutes.** The model also has Plug & Charge*** capability, which helps streamline the charging experience at supported networks.

It can also use Level 1 and Level 2 power sources to charge and includes a standard dual-voltage charging cable. Each bZ model also has a standard adapter kit for compatibility with SAE J1772 and Combined Charging System (CCS) stations, providing even greater charging convenience and flexibility.

text:
DC fast EV charging manufacturer Kempower has deployed eight new charging points in its first UK leased EV charging project.

The project, which sees the chargers installed at a Highway Stops Retail Limited (HSRL) site in Astwick, Bedfordshire, was funded through a flexible finance agreement provided by Kempower’s leasing partner, financial services provider DLL.

The agreement with HSRL is a UK-first for Kempower and a first for the partnership.

The financing model means HSRL is provided with hardware and regular maintenance services from Kempower, meaning operational support comes alongside the financial backing.

Kempower and DLL partnered in late 2024 to enable Kempower to offer customised financing solutions and lower the upfront cost of EV charging installations across the UK and Europe.

The leasing model means customers can spread the cost of Kempower’s equipment and maintenance over several payments during a term period.

“This flexible funding model opens the door for customers like HSRL who are in the early stages of expanding their EV charging services. The agreement we have with DLL helps remove the financial risk for operators,” Kempower’s head of sales for the UK and Ireland Rolle Nieminen explained.

At the Astwick site, which was commissioned in February this year, four of Kempower’s Double Satellite chargers, which altogether provide eight CCS2 connection points, have been installed. The chargers are supported by two Kempower Power Units—rack-style, modularly scalable converter cabinet solutions that deliver up to 1,200kW of charging power in 25kW granularity—to supply up to 400kW to two connected EVs.

Kempower, which is headquartered in Finland but ships globally, just saw its hardware deployed in a major rollout across Coles supermarkets in Australia.

With its primary manufacturing based in Lahti, Finland, Kempower has localised North American headquarters and a manufacturing plant in Durham, North Carolina.

text:
LIVONIA, Mich., Aug. 04, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- As the average transaction price of vehicles continues to rise, new research from Escalent reveals car buyers believe sticker prices have reached unprecedented heights. Sitting well beyond car buyers’ perceived range of affordability (between $31,865 and $47,838), the current average price of a new electric vehicle (EV) ($55,211 according to Kelley Blue Book) is viewed as a financial stretch for many buyers.

This is according to Escalent’s 2026 Affordability DeepDive from EVForward®, the largest, most comprehensive study on EV buyers and electrified powertrain adoption. The report explores how new-vehicle buyers define “affordable,” how it varies for different vehicle segments and how alternative approaches to affordability resonate with consumers. The report also analyzes what vehicle features buyers are willing to compromise on for price, how used EVs fit into the equation, and what automakers can do to address affordability concerns and support EV adoption.

“Affordability is a considerable hurdle for the automotive industry,” said Nikki Stern, a senior insights manager in Escalent’s Automotive & Mobility practice. “This challenge is particularly pronounced for EVs, with more than half of buyers perceiving the powertrain to be financially out of reach, especially in the absence of federal tax credits. While buyers have increased their anticipated spend over the past few years to an average of $43,950 in response to rising vehicle prices, concerns over high costs are leading buyers to ignore the powertrain entirely, creating a major obstacle to EV adoption.”

Escalent’s research revealed buyers evaluate vehicle affordability through a matrix of purchase price, monthly payments and total cost of ownership. EV Intenders—identified by Escalent’s algorithms as buyers who are over 15 times more likely to purchase an EV than the average new-car buyer—placed even greater emphasis across these three considerations. More than four in five (87%) EV Intenders agreed operating costs matter just as much as sticker price. Three-quarters (75%) of EV Intenders also agreed manageable monthly payments can make an expensive vehicle more affordable and an equal number indicated they’d be willing to pay more up front to lower the total cost over time. These attitudes suggest that EV Intenders think about affordability in a more holistic and multifaceted way.

The report also highlights how EV-specific concerns impact new-vehicle buyers’ perceptions of the powertrain’s affordability. The risk of needing to replace the battery (42%) and the cost to set up home charging (37%) outrank the purchase price (26%) as reasons EVs feel unaffordable to buyers.

Similarly, battery degradation and potential replacement costs are the leading concerns associated with purchasing a used EV. These risks are a significant barrier even though a used EV is perceived as a more affordable entry point. Despite this, the study found buyers are open to used EVs, with more than half (55%) saying they would definitely, probably or maybe consider them.

“Today’s auto buyers are looking beyond the sticker price when weighing the cost of a new vehicle. For most buyers, both short- and long-term costs are important considerations for whether buyers perceive a vehicle to be affordable,” said K.C. Boyce, vice president of Automotive & Mobility at Escalent. “As affordability concerns persist, maintaining EV purchase consideration among buyers will require more than just price cuts. Automakers will need to explore alternative incentives and personalized solutions that better resonate with individual customer needs, or risk losing customers’ interest altogether.”

About the EVForward® 2026 Affordability DeepDive

This EVForward DeepDive study was conducted among a national sample of 1,088 respondents—including 94 EV Owner, 270 EV Intender, 336 EV Open and 308 EV Resistant respondents as identified by Escalent’s algorithm. These respondents are a re-contact subset of the EVForward database, an insights platform focused on identifying and understanding the next generation of EV and electrified powertrain buyers. The EVForward database consists of new-vehicle buyers selected to represent the US population, with quotas for race, Hispanic ethnicity, gender, age, vehicle ownership and region. Results are weighted by race, Hispanic ethnicity, condensed vehicle segment intention and luxury versus mainstream vehicle intention. The sample for this research comes from an opt-in online panel. MILWAUKEE — We Energies announced today that construction is underway on three Wisconsin energy projects that will provide customers with reliable energy as power demand continues to grow. The new solar, wind and battery storage projects will produce enough energy to power about 100,000 homes and support the grid during peak demand.

The projects are part of We Energies “all of the above” power generation approach to serve customers with safe and reliable energy every second of every day.

Dawn Harvest Solar and Battery Park — a 150-megawatt solar project with

50 megawatts of battery storage in Rock County. Construction broke ground in June.

Badger Hollow Wind Energy Center — a 110-megawatt wind project in Iowa and Grant counties. Construction broke ground in July.

600 megawatts of battery storage projects in service, under construction or filed for regulatory approval.

The projects were developed and are being constructed by Invenergy, North America’s largest privately held developer, owner and operator of innovative, reliable power infrastructure. description:

America has roughly 77,000 wind turbines, making wind power one of the largest sources of renewable electricity in the nation.
Claim: Wind turbines are 'ugly' and damage the environment Trump has frequently criticized turbines for their appearance, often calling them "ugly," particularly offshore wind projects.
Claim: Wind energy is too expensive Trump has often argued that wind power is economically inefficient and depends on government support.
Benefits of Wind Energy Wind energy became one of the fastest-growing sources of electricity in the United States over the past two decades.
text:
President Donald Trump has spent years criticizing wind turbines, calling them unsightly, expensive and harmful to wildlife while arguing they should be replaced by fossil fuels and other energy sources.

His opposition resurfaced Monday during remarks in the Oval Office, where he again criticized "windmills" while discussing Europe's economic challenges, continuing a theme that has become one of the most consistent features of his public rhetoric.

Trump's stance has evolved from a fight over an offshore wind farm near one of his Scottish golf courses into a broader campaign against wind energy, culminating in executive actions during his second term aimed at slowing new wind projects across the United States.

Read More on News

Newsweek has reached out to the White House via email for comment.

When Did Trump Start Criticizing Wind Turbines?

Trump's opposition to wind energy dates to the mid-2000s, when plans emerged for an offshore wind farm near Trump International Golf Links in Aberdeenshire, Scotland. He argued the turbines would spoil the coastal landscape, damage tourism and reduce the value of his golf resort.

Trump fought the project for years through public campaigns and legal challenges but ultimately lost, with Scottish courts allowing the development to proceed. Many observers have pointed to that dispute as the beginning of Trump's long-running criticism of wind power.

His criticism intensified during his 2016 presidential campaign, when he increasingly linked wind energy to broader attacks on climate policies and government support for renewable energy.

The president has argued they are "ugly," damage scenic landscapes and hurt tourism, while he also claimed they are inefficient, expensive to maintain and harmful to wildlife, particularly birds. More recently, he has increasingly framed wind power as part of what he sees as misguided climate and energy policies that disadvantage fossil fuels and raise energy costs.

Although Trump signed a 2009 open letter supporting action on climate change, his rhetoric shifted dramatically over the following decade as renewable energy became a more prominent political issue.

Trump's Wind Turbine Timeline

2006

Trump purchased land in Aberdeenshire, Scotland, where he developed Trump International Golf Links. Shortly afterward, he opposed plans for a nearby offshore wind farm, arguing the turbines would ruin the view and hurt tourism.

2011-2015

Trump spent years challenging the Scottish wind project through lawsuits and public campaigns. Despite those efforts, the wind farm was eventually approved and constructed.

2012

Trump began making increasingly frequent public attacks on wind power, criticizing the appearance, economics and environmental impact of turbines.

2015-2016

During his presidential campaign, Trump incorporated criticism of wind energy into his broader message supporting expanded oil, gas and coal production.

2017-2021

Throughout his first term, Trump repeatedly criticized wind turbines while his administration rolled back a number of climate and clean-energy initiatives.

2019

Trump drew widespread attention after claiming that noise from wind turbines could cause cancer—a statement rejected by medical experts and public health authorities.

2021-2024

Out of office, Trump continued attacking wind energy at rallies and campaign events, frequently calling turbines unreliable and expensive while pledging to reverse Biden administration renewable-energy policies if elected.

2025

Within days of returning to office, Trump signed executive actions aimed at pausing or slowing approvals for new offshore wind projects. His administration later expanded those efforts, drawing criticism from the renewable-energy industry and praise from fossil fuel advocates.

2026

Trump has continued to raise the issue during speeches, campaign-style appearances and Oval Office remarks, frequently citing wind turbines while discussing energy policy, inflation and Europe's economy.

How Has Trump Acted Against Wind Energy?

Trump's criticism has extended beyond rhetoric. Trump's views on wind energy now influence federal energy policy as well as political debate over climate change and renewable power.

During his first term, his administration prioritized expanding oil, gas and coal production while rolling back a number of environmental regulations and clean-energy initiatives. Although wind development continued during those years, Trump frequently questioned the value of federal support for renewable energy.

After returning to office in January 2025, Trump took more direct action against the wind industry. His administration moved to pause or slow approvals for new offshore wind projects, ordered reviews of existing permits and signaled that future wind-energy development would face greater federal scrutiny.

Supporters say the measures are intended to strengthen American energy independence by emphasizing reliable domestic fossil fuel production and reducing regulatory burdens. Critics, including renewable-energy companies and environmental groups, argue the policies threaten investment, delay major infrastructure projects and could slow the transition to lower-carbon sources of electricity.

How Many Wind Turbines Does the US Have?

One of Trump's harsher criticisms of wind power came earlier this year at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, when he said countries investing heavily in wind power were "losers."

“There are windmills all over Europe. There are windmills all over the place, and they are losers,” Trump said. “One thing I’ve noticed is that the more windmills a country has, the more money that country loses, and the worse that country is doing.”

The U.S. ranks second in the world in wind power capacity, trailing only China.

America has roughly 77,000 wind turbines, making wind power one of the largest sources of renewable electricity in the nation. The latest U.S. Wind Turbine Database, maintained by the U.S. Geological Survey, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and the American Clean Power Association, lists 77,379 turbines across 45 states, Guam and Puerto Rico.

Those turbines are spread across approximately 1,700 wind power projects and represent nearly 160 gigawatts of installed capacity. Texas has the largest number of wind turbines of any state, followed by other major wind-producing states across the Great Plains and Midwest.

Wind energy now supplies a significant share of U.S. electricity, with turbines contributing power to the grid in states ranging from Texas and Iowa to Oklahoma, Kansas and California.

Despite Trump's repeated criticism of wind turbines, the technology has become a major part of America's electricity infrastructure.

Trump's Wind Turbine Claims: Fact Check

Trump has repeatedly criticized wind turbines, arguing that they are harmful to wildlife, unreliable as an energy source and damaging to communities. Some of his most repeated claims have been challenged by scientists, public health experts and energy researchers.

Here are some of Trump’s claims and what the evidence shows.

Claim: 'They say the noise causes cancer'

Trump has repeatedly claimed that wind turbine noise can cause serious health problems. Speaking in 2019, he said, “They say the noise causes cancer.”

Fact check: No credible scientific evidence links wind turbines to cancer.

Public health experts have found no evidence that exposure to wind turbine noise causes cancer. While turbines can produce audible sound and low-frequency noise, research has focused primarily on possible issues such as annoyance, sleep disruption or stress for some people living very close to turbines—not cancer.

The American Cancer Society and other medical organizations have not identified wind turbine noise as a cancer risk factor.

Claim: They kill 'all the birds'

Trump has repeatedly criticized wind turbines by arguing they are especially harmful to birds. During the final presidential debate with Joe Biden in 2020, he said to the former president: "I know more about wind than you do. It's extremely expensive. Kills all the birds. It's very intermittent. Got a lot of problems."

Fact check: Wind turbines do kill birds, but experts say they are not the largest human-caused source of bird deaths.

Scientists acknowledge that wind turbines can cause bird deaths, particularly among certain species such as raptors and migratory birds. However, studies have found that other human-related causes—including collisions with buildings, vehicles, power lines and predation by domestic cats—kill far more birds annually.

Conservation groups say the impact of wind turbines depends heavily on location and design. Proper siting, monitoring and technology such as improved turbine designs can reduce risks to wildlife.

Claim: Wind turbines are 'ugly' and damage the environment

Trump has frequently criticized turbines for their appearance, often calling them "ugly," particularly offshore wind projects.

In June 2025, he told Fox News that wind turbines "Cover up a half a mountain" and "are ugly as hell." A day earlier, during a meeting with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, he said he would not allow them to be built in the U.S. because "They're killing the beauty of our scenery, our valleys, our beautiful plains—I'm not talking about airplanes, I'm talking about beautiful plains. Beautiful areas in the United States, and you look up and you see windmills all over the place. It's a horrible thing."

Fact check: The visual impact is subjective, but environmental effects are more complex.

Wind turbines do change landscapes, and some communities have opposed projects because of concerns about views, tourism or local character. However, environmental researchers generally distinguish between visual impacts and broader environmental effects.

Unlike fossil fuel power plants, wind turbines do not burn fuel during operation and do not directly produce greenhouse gas emissions or air pollution while generating electricity.

Wind projects can have environmental impacts, including land use, effects on wildlife and the materials required for manufacturing, but experts say those impacts must be weighed against the environmental costs of fossil fuel energy production.

Claim: Wind energy is inefficient and unreliable

Trump has repeatedly argued that wind power does not work because turbines only generate electricity when the wind is blowing.

Speaking at the Shell Pennsylvania Petrochemical Complex in Monaca, Pennsylvania, in 2019, during his first term, Trump said, “When the wind stops blowing, it doesn’t make any difference, does it? Unlike those big windmills that destroy everybody’s property values, kill all the birds ... And then all of a sudden, it stops. The wind and the televisions go off."

Fact check: Wind power is variable, but energy experts say it is a reliable part of a modern electricity grid.

Wind generation does depend on weather conditions, meaning turbines do not produce electricity at maximum capacity at all times. However, energy experts say that does not make wind unusable or unreliable.

Grid operators manage changes in wind output through forecasting, geographic diversity, transmission networks, energy storage and combining wind with other sources of electricity.

The U.S. Department of Energy and National Renewable Energy Laboratory have found that wind energy can provide significant amounts of electricity while being integrated into a reliable grid.

Claim: Wind energy is too expensive

Trump has often argued that wind power is economically inefficient and depends on government support.

During a July 24 Oval Office news conference this year, Trump said about wind energy, "It's very expensive. It's probably the most expensive form of energy."

Fact check: Wind economics vary, but utility-scale wind has become one of the lowest-cost sources of new electricity generation in many regions.

The cost of wind projects depends on location, financing, transmission needs and policy incentives. While some projects require government support or face higher costs due to infrastructure challenges, energy analysts say technological improvements have significantly reduced the cost of wind power over time.

Critics of wind energy argue that subsidies distort the market and that intermittency creates additional costs. Supporters argue those costs are offset by fuel savings and reduced pollution.

Benefits of Wind Energy

Wind energy became one of the fastest-growing sources of electricity in the United States over the past two decades. Unlike coal and natural gas, wind turbines generate electricity without burning fuel, meaning they produce no direct greenhouse gas emissions or air pollution during operation.

According to the Energy Department and other federal agencies, wind power can diversify the nation's energy mix, reduce dependence on imported fuels and create jobs in manufacturing, construction and maintenance. Offshore wind projects can also generate large amounts of electricity near densely populated coastal regions where demand is high.

Supporters argue that expanding wind generation helps reduce carbon emissions, improves long-term energy security and lowers electricity costs in some markets. However, they acknowledge that wind energy also presents challenges, including the need for transmission infrastructure, energy storage and backup generation when wind speeds are low.

Energy Hub gives managers real-time vehicle data, including battery state of charge (SoC) and estimated remaining range. Building on Teletrac Navman’s existing telematics platform, Energy Hub supports configurable alerts and exception-based reporting that can identify overcharging, unusual fuel transactions and inefficient charging behavior.

Energy Hub’s dashboard provides fleet-wide visibility into energy consumption, transaction volumes, cost per kilowatt-hour and overall spend. Fleet managers can analyze trends, monitor live charging status, track charging events, and locate public charging infrastructure.

“The challenge is no longer simply collecting information but bringing it together in a way that supports better operational decision-making,” said Teletrac Navman CEO Alain Samaha. “Energy Hub helps businesses reduce fragmentation and gain clearer insights into energy performance, bringing these data points together into one platform and enabling a more integrated, data-driven approach to fleet management.”

Transforming the Global Battery Supply Chain The adoption of dry electrode coating could have profound implications for the global battery supply chain.
The Future of Battery Manufacturing Dry electrode coating represents a significant step forward in the evolution of battery technology.

text:
Lithium-ion batteries have transformed energy storage, but their production process has long relied on liquid-based methods that are both time-consuming and resource-intensive. In a recent breakdown by Ziroth, the spotlight is on dry electrode coating, a solvent-free manufacturing technique that eliminates the need for liquid slurries and energy-intensive drying stages. This approach not only reduces production costs by an estimated 20-25% but also enables the creation of thicker cathodes, which can increase energy density. By addressing both cost and performance, dry electrode coating could significantly advance the accessibility and efficiency of technologies like electric vehicles and renewable energy systems.

Explore how this method is reshaping the global battery supply chain, from reducing reliance on traditional infrastructure to allowing localized production in regions like the U.S. and Europe. Gain insight into the technical challenges manufacturers face, such as optimizing polymer blends for scalability and learn how companies like Tesla are driving innovation in this space. Whether you’re interested in the mechanics of dry electrode technology or its implications for future energy solutions, this overview provides a clear look at the path forward for battery manufacturing.

The Importance of Reducing Battery Costs

Although lithium-ion batteries are more affordable than ever, further cost reductions are critical to accelerating the global shift to sustainable energy and transportation. Dry electrode coating has the potential to lower manufacturing costs by an additional 20-25%, making it a fantastic option for the industry. By eliminating the need for liquid slurries and energy-intensive drying ovens, this process significantly reduces production expenses. For consumers, this translates to more affordable electric vehicles, energy storage systems and other advanced technologies. Lower costs could also help bridge the gap between clean energy solutions and widespread adoption, making sustainable options more accessible to a broader audience.

The Mechanics of Dry Electrode Coating

Traditional lithium-ion battery production relies on liquid slurries to bind active materials, followed by lengthy drying processes that consume significant energy and time. Dry electrode coating replaces this method with a solvent-free approach. Using polymers like PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene), electrode powders are bound into a cohesive, dry film without the need for liquid solvents. This eliminates the drying stage entirely, streamlining the manufacturing process and reducing energy consumption. The result is a more efficient, cost-effective and environmentally friendly production method that could reshape the battery industry.

Overcoming Technical Challenges

While dry electrode coating offers numerous advantages, scaling the technology for mass production presents several challenges. One major hurdle lies in the interaction between cathode materials and PTFE binders, which can sometimes compromise battery performance. To address this, manufacturers are experimenting with polymer blends, such as combining PTFE with PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride), to enhance chemical stability and performance. Additionally, roller-based techniques are being developed to improve scalability and ensure consistent quality during production. These innovations are essential for overcoming technical barriers and making dry electrode coating a viable solution for large-scale manufacturing.

Performance Enhancements and Energy Density

One of the most compelling benefits of dry electrode coating is its potential to improve battery performance. By avoiding binder migration, a common issue in traditional methods, this process enables the creation of thicker cathodes, which directly increases energy density. Higher energy density allows batteries to store more energy, resulting in longer-lasting electric vehicles, more efficient portable electronics and improved renewable energy storage systems. Furthermore, dry electrode coating is compatible with solid-state batteries, which require moisture-sensitive manufacturing environments. For consumers, this means access to next-generation batteries that are not only more powerful but also more reliable and durable.

Transforming the Global Battery Supply Chain

The adoption of dry electrode coating could have profound implications for the global battery supply chain. Traditional wet electrode processes require specialized infrastructure, much of which is concentrated in Asia. In contrast, dry electrode coating eliminates the need for such infrastructure, creating opportunities for regions like the U.S. and Europe to establish localized battery production facilities. This shift could reduce reliance on foreign supply chains, enhance energy security and foster greater independence in battery manufacturing. By decentralizing production, dry electrode technology has the potential to reshape the global manufacturing landscape and promote a more balanced distribution of resources.

The Future of Battery Manufacturing

Dry electrode coating represents a significant step forward in the evolution of battery technology. While challenges remain, ongoing research and development efforts are steadily addressing these obstacles, paving the way for broader adoption. Companies like Tesla are leading the charge, investing in the refinement and scalability of this innovative process. As dry electrode coating becomes more widespread, it is expected to play a pivotal role in both current lithium-ion batteries and emerging solid-state technologies. For consumers, this means a future where energy storage solutions are not only more affordable but also more sustainable and efficient, driving progress toward a cleaner, greener world.

text:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency wants to remove public notice and public comments for state-level air quality permits, a significant change to the 1973 Clean Air Act. The change — which could occur in a few weeks — would take away a common form of public awareness for a new data center and public participation, speeding up the review process.

In a July 1 news release, the EPA called the current public participation rule “burdensome” and said removing public comments will “streamline” the process.

Dry cleaners, auto body shops and gas stations are typical applicants for a Clean Air Act “minor source” permit. Gas and diesel generators for data centers, especially in the past few years, have been a sustained newcomer to the permit application pool. These minor source permits are reviewed by state agencies, like the Georgia Environmental Protection Division, while “major source” permits for big power plants or large industry above the minor threshold are reviewed by the EPA (known as a Title V permit).

Critics of the EPA’s proposal, such as environmental lawyers, clean air advocates and data center opponents across the country and in Georgia, called this proposal “alarming”, “anti-democratic” and “bypassing community notices” in a July 22 EPA hearing considering the rule change.

“This proposal could allow pro-polluters to move forward with permitting new pollution sources while bypassing community notices and the current channels of communication,” Kiya Stanford, Georgia state organizer for Moms for Clean Air Force, said during the hearing. “This is especially alarming to me in Georgia with the rise of possible pollutant sources like AI data centers rapidly moving into communities throughout the state.”

More permits in two years than the previous 10

The Georgia EPD does not have a running list of data centers with air permits, and not all data centers have air permits, according to communications director Sara Lips. They are not tracked separately or categorized separately in a database, she wrote.

But Lips shared industry codes (SIC codes) to search for data center permits for “most but not all” in the state that have “minor source” site implementation plan permits.

According to an SIC search, 20 minor source permits have been approved for diesel generators at data centers in Georgia since January 2025. From 2014 to 2024, there were nearly the same number (17) of minor source data center permits.

Diesel generators are used for backup power when the grid can’t supply power during a storm or an outage and, in some cases, as a main power source while the developer waits to connect to the grid.

Finding out about a permit application is a critical way for watchdog groups and advocates to confirm a data center or polluting industries are coming to town, community organizers argue, because most people don’t search for air permits.

“Even current announcements don’t reach the residents who will be impacted directly,” Treva Gear the Georgia community organizer for North Carolina-based environmental justice advocate Dogwood Alliance, said during the July 22 EPA hearing. “It’s up to groups like mine to notify them. Once they know, they are always ready to speak up and speak out.

“The idea that the EPA is considering removing this 1973 requirement is alarming and anti-democratic. (It would make) it easier for polluting industries to move into communities under a cloud of secrecy is not the mandate of the EPA or state regulatory agencies.”

Gear has notified residents and reporters about biomass plants in southern Georgia, like the Altamaha Green Energy plant. That biomass plant’s minor source permit was approved in October 2025 and received 15 comments for or against the plant.

In Upson County, Rusty Blackston, a community activist against a Brightmark Plastic plant, thanked the Georgia EPD for allowing a public hearing in-person in Thomaston in May. Of the 29 people who spoke, only one was in favor of the plastic-recycling plant. The permit is being reviewed now. Blackston said the minor source permit review exemplifies a founding principle of this country.

“The public needs to have an input into this,” he said during the July 22 EPD hearing. “Damage to our environment is not acceptable, and we need to keep the process going to allow people to attend hearings, to submit comments and to be able to voice their opinions. If you take this away, you are infringing on our rights to freedom of speech.”

While public notice has been a way for watchdog groups to notify the community, public comment for data center permits hasn’t been popular until recently.

The permits issued between 2014-2024 had no public comments, according to the Ledger-Enquirer SIC list.

The first hyperscale data center project in Georgia, Project Excalibur, by QTS in Fayetteville, received a permit in 2023 and had no comments during the draft review.

In June, two projects out of the 20 found since 2025 had public comment participation: Project Pegasus in Troup County and Equinix xScale in Henry County.

Minor permits could have major implications

But starting in January 2025, the Sierra Club consistently commented on all 20 projects, saying: data center diesel generators would degrade air quality, battery storage should be considered rather than diesel generators, stricter emissions control technology should be considered, and a study about the cumulative impact on Georgia from all data centers should be conducted, given their unprecedented rise in development.

The Georgia EPD responded to the Sierra Club’s comments with consistent remarks. On air quality, they point to the facility’s Toxic Impact Analysis (TIA), showing pollutant levels below the state’s Allowable Ambient Concentrations (AACs). They do not dictate facility design, and battery tech isn’t a viable replacement for diesel backup. No federal rule requires more stringent technology, so EPD won’t mandate beyond the existing rule, and the cumulative study request has been “acknowledged,” and they are “monitoring” the growth.

The QTS Fayetteville project had 205 diesel generators approved in 2023. Project Pegasus had 180, in May, according to their air permits. Alone, these might not seem like a substantial amount, but that is why the Sierra Club has pushed for the review of a cumulative impact.

“The main reason why we’re so invested in this is the air pollution that comes out of these plants has real impacts in the air, even though it’s called minor source,” Isabella Ariza, a staff attorney for the Sierra Club, told the Ledger-Enquirer.

The Sierra Club analysis found adding together all approved minor source permits in Georgia are set to house more than 2,600 diesel generators, according to the Sierra Club’s analysis in a public comment submitted May 11. They could be more than two coal and gas plants worth of nitrous oxide emissions.

“These 24 data centers alone provide 5.2 gigawatts of backup power,” their letter says. “At a minimum, if we assume all 212 data centers in Georgia operate 100 diesel generators rated at 2,000 kW, the total backup power comes to 42.4 gigawatts. Georgia’s power sector had 39.7 gigawatts of net summer capacity online in 2024. There may now be enough diesel backup generators at Georgia’s data centers to power the state’s entire electric grid.”

Ariza, told the Ledger-Enquirer via email that, when clustered together, the data centers’ minor sources act as a major source, leaving folks with difficult decisions during the summer heat.

“If Georgia’s 212 data centers are each allowed 99-ton annual NOx emissions limits, they could emit roughly 21,000 tons of NOx per year, close to double the annual NOx emissions of Georgia’s coal plants, Plant Scherer and Plant Bowen,” Ariza wrote.

“During power outages in the summer, individuals who live near data centers will be without AC and will be faced with a decision of whether to open their windows and be exposed to unnecessarily high emissions from the data center’s diesel generators or else keep their windows shut and bear the brunt of the heat,” Ariza said via email.

Burden of proof or proof of burden?

The Ledger-Enquirer asked the EPA about the burdensome process that the state-level agencies are experiencing.

When asked specifically how much time it would save, they did not give a specific answer, only operational procedure and their reason for the change.

“The time required for any specific agency to review and respond to public comments varies across air agencies,” EPA spokesperson Carolyn Holran said via email. “The purpose of the proposed rule, per the best reading of the Clean Air Act is to provide state, local and Tribal permitting authorities with greater discretion to identify the requisite level of public participation that is appropriate in their minor NSR programs…it would put state and local agencies most familiar with local issues in the driver’s seat to determine whether, when, and for how long to provide opportunities for public participation for proposed new minor sources and modifications.”

Ariza said the Sierra Club, and other “allied organizations” have filed Freedom of Information Act requests for surveys and meetings about the burdensome process. The EPA has not responded, and rejected the Sierra Club’s request to expedite the process.

After comments are reviewed by the Aug 21 deadline, the EPA can act as soon as they want, Ariza said.

Lips explained where the EPD stands with the EPA decision and other means of communities being notified through other permits.

“EPD is determining whether the proposed rule changes would affect public participation requirements per the state regulations,” she said in an email to the Ledger-Enquirer. “Not all data centers require an air permit, and some data centers do require water withdrawal or wastewater permits. Those that require water from local governments do not require public notice. But if a new water permit is requested, public hearings will be held.”

In July, the EPD issued a stop-work order for a data center in Newton County because it was illegally constructing a data center. Activists in Covington say the public participation in these processes made this possible.

‘Pop-up power plant’ delayed because of public comment

In Newton County, the data center in Covington has been delayed thanks to public participation and comments from the group, said Sustainable Newton president and co-founder Maurice Carter. He told the EPA this story during the July 22 hearing in hopes of not letting this new proposed rule come to fruition.

The nonprofit organization with 50 members was concerned when they heard about the California-based Serverfarm data center being built in Covington last fall. The data center wanted to use on-site power because Georgia Power couldn’t yet supply this site, as it was an old warehouse that would be transformed into a data center, according to Carter.

VoltaGrid, a Texas-based power provider, permitted 33 gas generators to provide 90 megawatts of electricity “behind the meter,” Carter said. At the same time, Serverfarm applied for 37 diesel generators for backup power, all in one permit.

The Southern Environmental Law Center, on behalf of Sustainable Newton, filed public comments challenging the technical aspects of the VoltaGrid permit in December.

“We raised and challenged (Georgia) EPD’s December decision to allow VoltaGrid and Serverfarm to apply for separate minor source permits rather than undergoing full review of their combined emissions from a co-located operation,” Carter said during the July 22 EPA hearing.

Georgia EPD published a draft permit in March. Sustainable Newton reiterated the same comments in the draft permit and noted the EPD proposed the two entities to separate sources, allowing both to escape more rigorous Title V permitting, Carter said. The “behind-the-meter” arrangement also violates state law, Carter told the Ledger-Enquirer.

“We again filed comments challenging that arrangement and also pointing out that under Georgia law, under the Georgia Territorial Electric Service Act, a business can’t sell electricity to another business unless one of those businesses is a regulated utility,” Carter told the Ledger-Enquirer. “So VoltaGrid could sell power to Georgia Power, or they could use it themselves, but they can’t sell it to Serverfarm. That’s not allowed.”

Despite this, VoltaGrid still constructed their generators, and Sustainable Newton took aerial photos resulted in EPD’s stop-work-order to VoltaGrid. Serverfarm has since received a permit, but they remain liable for penalties and further enforcement actions. VoltaGrid has not received a permit, according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution.

“It’s very obvious,” Carter said. “If we had not been notified and invited to comment, then nothing we’ve done would have happened. This thing would probably have been operating back in March, you know, when they got the draft permit. Nonprofits like ours rely on a transparent review process, giving local communities an opportunity to hold polluters accountable. Without that, people suffer.”
